Don’t get sucked in by bad GTA 6 Black Friday deals – read this first.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If you want to play GTA 6 and get a Black Friday deal, it's a minefield of iffy offers and disappointment, but some hidden-away deals are actually worth it.

At a glance, Amazon, Best Buy, GameStop, Target, and Walmart are all reporting low stock of GTA 6 Standard Edition at $79.99, with no Black Friday price cuts. The one US price drop I have found is at key retailer Loaded (formerly CDKeys): the PS5 and Xbox digital code is $69.99, down from $79.99, or £69.99 £55.79 in the UK, but that's for the digital edition (okay, they're all digital, but there's no box to collect).

Xbox players can do better there. Loaded lists the Xbox Series X/S edition at $67.49 (was $79.99) and the Ultimate Edition at $85.99 (was $99.99), with the sale running through 1 December, so it's genuinely time-limited. It's a third-party key seller, so check the region before you pay.

Prefer to buy straight from the PlayStation Store? Discounted gift cards are the workaround. Newegg has about $5 off $70 PSN cards, and promo code BFF3538 takes $25 off $250 cards.

Or UK readers can head to Amazon and get the same £5 off GTA 6 on PlayStation 5, now £69.99 £64.95, without the PSN workaround.

Sony has no official GTA 6 console bundle, and it raised US PS5 prices on April 2: the Slim Digital now lists at $599.99, the Slim with a disc drive at $649.99, and the PS5 Pro at $899.99, so keep these numbers in mind if you see a console and GTA 6 bundle deal. Couple that with Microsoft saying Xbox Series X/S won't be discounted, and you need to watch any bundle deals.

For example, the only US console-plus-GTA 6 package I've found is a PS5 Slim with GTA 6 and an accessories kit at Walmart: $929.99, down from $999.99. Best Buy lists the same bundle at $1,199.99. It saves $70 on paper, but the price is high compared to buying the pieces separately, so check exactly what's in the listing first.

The good news? The best actual GTA 6 related deals I've found are Amazon's GTA 6 + accessory offers, for PS5 and Xbox, so I've listed them below.

#9054. PGYTECH RetroVa Gives the iPhone a 400mm Reach and a Real Camera Feel

PGYTECH RetroVa Gives the iPhone a 400mm Reach and a Real Camera Feel

PGYTECH is best known for camera bags, tripods and straps, and in the phone world for telephoto extender lenses designed for Vivo and Oppo flagships. Its RetroVa kit brings that lens work to the iPhone.

The system first appeared on Kickstarter in January 2026 for the iPhone 16 Pro and 17 Pro families, combining a camera-style Bluetooth grip, retro-style case, and a 2.35x teleconverter for the phone’s telephoto lens. The newest version designed for the iPhone 17 Pro/Pro Max and 18 Pro/Pro Max series brings in a lighter and smaller 2X lens, along with a 4X telephoto lens as an alternative.

This all provides focal range that simply doesn’t work as well when using the phone itself. With 200mm, 235mm, and 400mm equivalents, the iPhone can reach farther with more optical clarity. A dedicated app also offers old school film simulations and manual controls for composition to let you decide how you want your images to look.

The RetroVa All-in-One Ultimate Gift Set comes in Graphite Black, while the 4X lens, grip, and the case are also sold separately and in smaller bundles, offering users different ways to put the kit together.

RetroVa Black Friday deal: From November 19 to 30, the RetroVa All-in-One Ultimate Gift Set (Graphite Black, iPhone 17/18 Pro Max) is 10% off, and PetaPixel readers can take an extra 10% off with code BYTEDDYK. Buy it on Amazon or directly from PGYTECH.

The Ultimate Gift Set brings them all together in the box: the 4X telephoto lens, a lens adapter bracket, lens pouch, RetroVa phone case, grip, a photography strap, and an Arca-Swiss compatible tripod collar for the lens. The case is polycarbonate and works with MagSafe, leaving the proverbial door open for additional magnetic accessories. Though it has a lip over the edges, you can still use the case with a screen protector on the phone itself.

The lightweight grip weighs 63 grams for the Pro and 65.4 grams for the Pro Max. It carries physical controls, a built-in microSD slot, and a standard 1/4-inch socket on the base for tripods and monopods. It slides into the phone’s USB-C port with a lock switch that holds it firmly in place, though it actually pairs and connects to the device via Bluetooth.

It’s important to get the right size because there are separate variants for the Pro and Pro Max. While the lens mount is the same on either build, you can’t slide a Pro grip into the Pro Max, for instance. That also goes for the case, which is the most integral piece because that’s what everything else in the kit attaches to. Fortunately, since the iPhone 17 Pro and 18 Pro models share the same dimensions, you don’t need to worry about compatibility in that regard.

The shutter button functions a lot like a typical camera would: half-press to focus, press to take the shot, or hold it down for a burst. The zoom lever right under it can either skip between focal lengths in Vintage mode or adjust zoom more freely in the Standard setting. Below that is the control dial that you can choose to adjust exposure, ISO, white balance, or shutter speed. Lastly, the multi-function button acts as power on/off, switches modes, and sets up Bluetooth pairing. A small LED next to it indicates pairing and a solid connection.

The microSD card slot (UHS-I or UHS-II) underneath is another handy way to save excess photos or video, albeit with some key parameters. You can readily save RAW photos or 4K video to it, only you’re limited to HEVC-coded footage and max 120fps. Plug the grip into a laptop where you can then offload the content directly.

If you record in Apple’s Camera app, video automatically goes to the card when you use supported formats, while PGYTECH’s app supports more recording formats. Even third-party apps that can record to external storage can recognize the card, too.

PGYTECH also makes 62mm and 67mm filter adapter rings sold separately from the available kits. They’re not included in any of them, though will work just fine with any filters in those two respective sizes. Being a separate piece, you just slide out the lens adapter ring and bring in the filter adapter instead. There is no way to use a filter with the teleconverter lenses themselves, since the filter adapter covers the iPhone’s entire rear array.

PGYTECH designed the kit to work with a dedicated companion app called PGYTECH: Pro Camera & Editor. It’s free to download, only requiring iOS 17 or later to run. You do, however, need to be diligent about keeping it up to date because if you don’t, the app may lock you out of all the manual control settings. A pop-up notice stating that a subscription is required to unlock those pro features isn’t actually necessary. Update the app and that message disappears.

While there is an Auto mode available, Manual provides controls for exposure, shutter speed, ISO, white balance, tint, and filters, which you can then map to the grip by going to Settings->Hardware Settings. You will need to ensure the grip is on and once connected via Bluetooth, select RetroVa in the drop-down menu to pick what you want. At any point within that section, you can always look at tutorials on connecting the grip and a video FAQ as well.

Unless you explicitly make your own manual adjustments, the app’s camera interface treats everything as if it was in Auto. So, shutter speed, ISO, white balance, and tint will all dynamically shift based on what’s in frame. Tap to focus works just like any other camera app would. One difference, though, is if you have Focus Assist on (focus peaking by another name), you will see where the camera is actually focusing after you tap, giving you an indication of where the focal plane is.

Other manual controls, like a histogram and priority facial recognition (the camera will always focus on a face first in this setting), are elective. Standard bits, like a timer, live photo, watermark, and aspect ratio (1:1, 4:3, and 16:9) round out much of what’s left. There is a Dive Mode that switches controls to physical buttons for underwater photos and video, while also applying an “underwater filter” as a copy of the original when captured. You can make separate manual settings adjustments for this mode, too.

In addition to about 15 standard filters, PGYTECH offers a series of nostalgic film simulations, ranging from Classic Negative and Nostalgic Negative to Kodak Gold 200, Fujifilm PRO Neg Std, Velvia 100, Classic Chrome, FujiColor C200, Tungsten 500, and Bleach Bypass. Choose any one at any time and adjust the intensity from 0-100. These simulations apply no matter what image format you shoot with and aren’t limited to still photos: they work with video, too.

The app includes a Retro Film mode that features the same set of film simulations, except it changes the hybrid zoom ranges to include 35mm and 50mm equivalents to better match traditional prime lenses. Otherwise, images process the same way as the Photo mode.

It’s also possible to apply any of these filters on a photo after you capture it within the in-app editing suite, including HSL for some color grading. Beauty features also present a variety of options for those seeking that kind of detail. Under Creative, there are templates for sharing or social media.

An on-device AI tool in the Adjust section lets you try enhancing detail in images by either using HD to improve clarity or AI HD to restore detail in softer images. You need to download it to make it work on-device rather than in the cloud but once it’s there, you can utilize it any time. If you’d rather avoid AI completely, you don’t have to use it.

Mind you, you’re not forced into PGYTECH’s app for basic shooting (without the lenses) since the grip also works with the native Camera app. To make that work with iOS, go to the Settings app, then Accessibility->Zoom->toggle On->Full Screen Zoom. At that point, having already paired it to the phone, you gain access to Apple’s own Camera app where pressing the shutter or zooming in responds onscreen. PGYTECH says it’s working on more third-party app integrations, so we’ll see where that leads.

The 4X lens is both the newest and the headline of the trio. It uses an 11-element, 3-group optical design with fluorite-grade low-dispersion glass and weighs about 137 grams. It feels sturdy in hand, which is why it’s smart to use it with the tripod collar when you need to prop it up for a long exposure or timelapse.

It’s a 400mm equivalent optical focal length, going up to 1200mm with a digital crop. The 4x lens also comes with a case and slightly different bracket that also includes a mount for the iPhone’s main camera. That gives you a 240mm optical equivalent or 400mm with an in-sensor crop with more background separation, which PGYTECH pitches for portraits.

The 2x lens, at about 104 grams, gives 200mm optical and 400mm cropped over the telephoto camera, or 105mm and 200mm over the main camera. This lens doesn’t come with a case but does include the same lens bracket the Ultimate Gift Set does, which only covers the phone’s telephoto camera. That’s an important distinction if you’re looking to use any of the lenses on both the main and telephoto cameras.

In the case of the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max, the PGYTECH app can’t control the main camera’s mechanical aperture, so you can’t benefit from stopping down to f/4 for certain photo or video opportunities. Either way, all three lenses fit any of the RetroVa cases and brackets made for the iPhone.

One thing to always keep in mind is how much attaching the lenses considerably increases minimum focusing distance. PGYTECH lists 16.2 meters for the 4x over the telephoto camera and three meters over the main camera, against 5.22 meters and 60 centimeters for the 2x. There’s no optical image stabilization in any of them, so PGYTECH relies on its app’s stabilization algorithm for steadier handheld results. Handheld, the kit is better now than it was just a few months ago.

There’s nothing electronic communicating between the lenses and the app, so you have to manually select the lens you’re using and then turn that off or switch if you end up putting on another one. Doing so makes corresponding changes to available focal lengths and ensures focusing and processing fall in line with what you’re using. It’s one of the easiest things to forget while shooting with it in the field but it’s vitally important.

Technically, the lenses aren’t supposed to work with Apple’s own app, though I randomly found no obstruction in doing so. Other times, it didn’t work at all. This has nothing to do with the kit and everything to do with how Apple engineers its camera array. Because it functions as one virtual system, the software can decide what it thinks is the best camera, even though you’ve already chosen one over another. PGYTECH’s app doesn’t do that, leaning purely on whichever camera you’ve attached the lens to capture images or video.

If you get lucky enough to make Apple’s app work, it gives you access to manual controls (in the 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max) as well as the possibility of manipulating the variable aperture with the main camera. It’s just a very hit-or-miss proposition, so your experience may truly vary.

As a kit, the RetroVa is trying to present a camera-like feel to capturing photos and video on the iPhone. That’s the basic gist, but in practice, the handling offers a fairly high degree of versatility in both perspective and ergonomics. Without having to stretch out a thumb or finger to hit the onscreen shutter, the grip’s controls make low or high-angle shots easier to manage. Double-clicking the iPhone’s Camera Control will launch Apple’s Camera app but if you prefer to switch that to PGYTECH’s app within iOS, go to Settings->Camera->Camera Control and tap on it to make that the default.

In the four months I’ve been using the kit (both with the iPhone 17 Pro and 18 Pro), multiple updates over that time have either added new features or refined existing ones. One thing you have to always remember is that this app processes images slower than Apple’s app does, especially when shooting in ProRAW. You can see that in the preview window where a yellow indicator shows that it’s rendering what you just shot.

The reason that matters is because it’s easy to ruin a photo by quickly moving the camera after capture. That very brief window between snapping the shutter and seeing the resulting image populate the preview window can feel like an eternity when shooting action, like I did at multiple WNBA games with this kit. It’s faster if you’re purely shooting JPEG or HEIF but the same thing can happen if you’re a little too eager to see what you just got.

Part of what PGYTECH is up against is the smaller 1/2.55-inch sensor Apple uses for the telephoto camera on both the 17 Pro and 18 Pro series. Adding significant optics to that lens certainly gets you closer to the subject or action but it’s best to also learn the subtleties of PGYTECH’s app. Lighting conditions are of paramount importance, as noise can creep in at higher ISO levels when you need to raise the shutter speed.

While you can shoot in either ProRAW, JPEG, or HEIF at either 12 or 48-megapixels, you don’t really wield any outsized control over the imaging pipeline. Apple’s processing engine still kicks in, forcing you to lean more on RAW images if you feel more comfortable with the higher degree of manual control available. PGYTECH isn’t necessarily only targeting seasoned mobile photographers with the RetroVa kit but it’s still worth dealing with the learning curve.

The controls include manual focus, with focus peaking as an elective option where you get to choose between red, green, or blue as the visual aid. It applies no matter if you’re tapping to focus manually or adjusting it in the slider. One key tidbit is tapping to focus doesn’t always work as you’d expect because focal length (even for the iPhone’s own lenses) behave natively. Within the app, there’s no fusion between them to enable, say, macro shooting at closer distances where the main or ultra-wide might step in to help the cause.

All that aside, the handling is a big part of the appeal here. As a slab device, the iPhone can prove tough to work with under different perspective and angles, so the grip turns it into something you can maneuver in more interesting ways. With a finger on the shutter and the ability to make granular adjustments with the dial, plus the strap to take off the weight, the creative possibilities certainly stand out.

Focusing is the biggest challenge because subject tracking isn’t the same as Apple’s own implementation, and you often still need to tap on the screen to hone in on what you want the composition to look like. One workaround for that is to get a separate screen primarily used for rear camera selfies as a way to wirelessly compose a shot when it’s hard to contort yourself to see the real time preview on the phone.

PGYTECH says it’s working on tracking autofocus and on controlling the iPhone’s aperture from the grip, which would address two key challenges in using the RetroVa kit. A universal lens adapter and further lens types are also on PGYTECH’s wish list, though no firm commitment.

For now, RetroVa is an iPhone-only system built around the Pro and Pro Max models, albeit with some nuances noted earlier. Not everything made for the iPhone 17 and 18 Pro series applies to what’s available for the iPhone 16 Pro series.

It’s also worth noting the kit isn’t a qualitative replacement for a mirrorless camera. The iPhone’s image sensors aren’t in the same league to begin with, but the app’s manual controls are far more extensive and the lenses a big upgrade over the awful hybrid crops the iPhone offers on its own. Compared to a bigger mirrorless, however, this kit is easier to carry, especially when you take off the lenses.

The RetroVa All-in-One Ultimate Gift Set is 10% off through November 30, plus an extra 10% with code BYTEDDYK, on Amazon and at PGYTECH.

#9053. RIBA president rejoins ARB register to restore architect title

The president of the Royal Institute of British Architects, Chris Williamson, has decided to renew his membership with the Architects Registration Board, nearly a year after terminating it.

In a LinkedIn post, Williamson said he was rejoining the Architects Registration Board’s (ARB) register because he no longer wanted “to face the prospect of legal action”.

Specifically, he said he feared the potential “legal proceedings and financial penalties” from referring to himself as an architect, which ARB does not permit if a person is unregistered.

Williamson’s post comes nearly a year after he revealed he was not going to renew his membership to draw attention to what he called the “absurdity of the current regulatory framework”.

This ARB framework currently only regulates the protected title “architect” and the competence of those on its register, meaning it does not oversee the competence of unregistered providers of architectural services.

His withdrawal from ARB last year aligned with the launch of a campaign by the Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA) calling for a new regulatory model for UK architects.

Though he has now rejoined the ARB register, Williamson said his position on the need to reform remains unchanged.

“Today, I have decided to rejoin the ARB register,” he posted on LinkedIn on Friday.

“Over the last year, I have sat in meetings and roundtables with Ministers, MPs and Peers, spoken at party conferences and COP31, and had the pleasure of awarding the Stirling Prize,” he continued. “Throughout, I have felt the fear of legal proceedings and financial penalties all for referring to myself, in these settings, as an architect – something that’s so fundamental to my identity.”

Williamson, the co-founder of Weston Williamson + Partners, began his two-year term as president on 1 September 2025.

In the LinkedIn post – a shortened version of an open letter shared with RIBA members – he said he will now continue to “push for a stronger system” for regulation.

The current RIBA campaign calls for three steps to reform architects’ regulation, including repealing the Architects Act – a UK law that sets the framework for the regulation of the title architect, under which ARB is the regulator.

It also proposes new legislation outlining reserved activities, such as submitting full planning applications, and who can execute them. The final step calls for the introduction of a Built Environment Council to oversee the competence of individuals and companies working in the construction industry.

“I know my decision to return may surprise or disappoint some of you, particularly those who followed my lead,” concluded Williamson.

“I want to stress this is not a step backwards and it does not reflect a change in my views. In fact, the year I’ve spent outside of the Register has only cemented my commitment to reform,” he continued.

“While my title may change, RIBA’s campaign for regulatory reform will not. I will use my experience on both sides to push for a stronger system that protects what we call ourselves – and what we do.”

Williamson was selected as RIBA president in 2024. Prior to this, he held several roles within the RIBA, including the vice president international from 2017 to 2019.

In 2014, ARB gave Dezeen 14 days to amend an article describing John Pawson as an architect, claiming it was “in the public interest” for Dezeen to use an alternative description, as Pawson is not registered with the board.

The Aful Ember-01 DAC/Amp dongle comes with volume buttons and goes LOUD!

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Today Aful has officially launched the Ember-01, a budget-friendly portable USB headphone DAC/Amp dongle for $89.99. And I think it's a bit special.

Clearly not satisfied with making some of my favourite IEMs under $500 this year, Aful has also been busy with making some of the coolest-looking bits of kit for audio enthusiasts too. The Ember-01's metallic chassis is paired with a transparent glass panel, showing the internal circuitry and a bitrate-reactive RGB light inside. It's very cool, but there's more to it than that.

The Ember-01 also comes with a 10-band PEQ, through the Aful app. This theoretically will allow you to alter the sound of your music to exactly what you want, which is pretty exciting.

If you're still looking for some headphones to go with this dongle, check out my list of the best-sounding wired headphones at any price.

Equipped with physical media buttons, a dedicated hardware gain switch – which literally blew my mind – and in-line microphone support, the Ember-01 aims to bridge the gap between everyday smartphone use and audiophile performance. Though for the sake of total transparency, early impressions have suggested that its ambitious software features still need a bit of polish.

Under the hood, the Ember-01 pairs its AKM AK4493SEQ DAC with a CB5100 Pro USB bridge, supporting high-res playback up to 32-bit/768kHz PCM and native DSD512, alongside UAC 1.0 compatibility for gaming consoles...

In English, that means it uses high-end audio chips to convert digital files into ultra-crisp, studio-grade analog sound, supporting virtually every ultra-high-resolution music format around. And that's while also including a compatibility mode so you can plug it into gaming consoles like a Nintendo Switch. Hoorah!

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

Its 3.5mm single-ended port outputs 125mW (and supports headset microphones), while the 4.4mm balanced output ramps things up to a massive 500mW into 32 ohms with a 121dB dynamic range.

A major selling point for me is its built-in 10-band Parametric Equaliser (PEQ), offering customisable frequencies, gain, Q-values, and digital filters. However, early testers have reported launch-day limitations, including the Android app not being properly ready at release, leaving users reliant on a web-based desktop interface.

However, once Aful get this fixed, I can see this being a popular bit of kit for audiophile on the go.

#9051. Photographer Captured Northern England in the 1970s Before It Disappeared

Photographer Captured Northern England in the 1970s Before It Disappeared

In the 1970s, Peter Mitchell drove a delivery truck around the British city of Leeds and photographed the city between drops: shopkeepers in their doorways, factory gates, cafés, scrapyards, and terraced streets halfway to demolition.

Mitchell worked slowly, with a medium-format camera and a stepladder, and his subjects posed willingly. The result is an affectionate portrait of a city on the edge of change.

“Leeds is a city in the North where I’ve ended up and it’s now where I’m from,” says Mitchell, now 83 years old. “I’m surprised (though I shouldn’t be) as I go through the neg files and notebooks just how familiar all the people and places are.”

“All gone now,” he adds. “But as I stride down the new canyons of glittering emptiness that litter our cities, I hear my photographs chattering away.”

As Mitchell says, Leeds is now a very different city. While it still has plenty of Victorian housing, it is now permeated with modern apartment blocks.

Mitchell’s long out-of-print photobook Strangely Familiar returns in a remastered and expanded edition. On Strange and Familiar Ground introduces a new audience to the work that brought Mitchell recognition in the 21st century, remastering the 47 photographs Martin Parr originally selected for the 2013 Nazraeli Press edition and adding new images and recent discoveries.

Mitchell was a pioneer of British color photography. In 1979 his exhibition A New Refutation of the Viking 4 Space Mission at Impressions Gallery in York was the first color show by a British photographer at a British photography gallery. In his introduction, Martin Parr recalls a show “so far ahead of its time that no-one knew exactly what to say or how to react, apart from with total bewilderment.” It took decades for Mitchell to receive his due.

Strangely Familiar was published in 2013 in a first edition of 1,500 copies, part of a series of 10 books selected by Parr for Nazraeli Press. The book sold well and became a sought-after collector’s item, and its success led directly to RRB’s long collaboration with Mitchell.

This new edition has been newly scanned and remastered from Mitchell’s archive. It keeps Parr’s original introduction and sets the familiar images alongside photographs that have rarely or never been seen before.

“When the history of colour photography in the U.K. is written about, Mitchell’s name is often omitted. One of the roles of this volume is to correct this oversight,” Parr wrote in 2013.

On Strange and Familiar Ground is published by RRB Photobooks and can be purchased here.

#9050. Museum acquisitions round-up: a Simone Leigh monumental bronze and an atmospheric early Rothko

© Simone Leigh, courtesy Matthew Marks Gallery

The American Friends of the National Gallery of Australia bought this sculpture by Simone Leigh last year from Matthew Marks Gallery in New York. The monumental bronze, measuring 3.3m long and 1.5m tall, is named after the Nigerian American artist and actress Okwui Okpokwasili. It shows a reclining woman in a cast raffia skirt, exploring the resilience and cultural memory that merges the semi-abstract female form with the African vernacular. This cast is the second from an edition of two (with one artist’s proof). In 2022, Leigh became the first Black woman to represent the US at the Venice Biennale.

Untitled (wharf, Gloucester, Massachusetts) (1934) by Mark Rothko

Cape Ann Museum, Gloucester, Massachusetts

Christopher Rothko, the son of the artist Mark Rothko (1903-70), says that while his father thought “all art was inherently of its time”, sometimes “even with a master of abstraction like Mark Rothko, art can also be inherently of its place”. He is referring to this painting—an atmospheric early watercolour-and-gouache work depicting the harbour in Gloucester—which Christopher recently donated to the Cape Ann Museum from his private collection. Mark Rothko frequently summered on Cape Ann, painting alongside two other New York artists: his mentor, Milton Avery, and his friend Adolph Gottlieb. This painting is included in Avery, Gottlieb & Rothko: By the Sea—a touring exhibition currently on view at the Phillips Collection in Washington, DC (until 24 January 2027).

Arc-en-ciel no. 5 (1913-14) by Robert Delaunay

It may not be instantly recognisable, but the lilac spire behind the rainbow in this painting is the Eiffel Tower—the tallest building in the world when the work was painted by Robert Delaunay (1885-1941). The French artist was the husband of Sonia Delaunay, and in 1912 they co-founded the short-lived Orphism movement—an offshoot of Cubism that prized bright colours and geometric shapes. This vivid oil-on-canvas work, measuring 35cm by 40cm, is one of several variations of the composition and shows Delaunay moving away from strict geometry to a looser, more expressive and rhythmic style. The painting, which sold at Christie’s in 2025 for $317,500 (with fees) from the collection of Arnold and Joan Saltzman, was exhibited by the London-based dealer Willoughby Gerrish at Tefaf Maastricht in March—where the sale to the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, was initially agreed.

Only Gorky and Pollock of his peers has so far been catalogued

A new book by the art historian Ben Street attempts to demystify how we look at art and argues for reacting instinctively to what we see

#9049. IKEA's Color of the Year "unexpectedly fits in"

Photography courtesy of IKEA (unless stated otherwise)

Swedish retailer IKEA has unveiled its prediction for 2027’s Color of the Year – a dark, reddish-purple shade called Wild Fig.

Although revealed by IKEA US as part of its 2027 Style Guide, keen eyes would’ve already seen the shade pop up earlier this year in the sell-out floor lamp created by Dutch designer Lex Pott for IKEA’s PS Collection.

The company describes Wild Fig as “a deep, botanical shade with a rich purple tone”, although in certain lights, it looks closer to an earthy oxblood red.

“Full of character and the unexpected, it brings depth and a daring mindset to everyday spaces,” said Abbey Stark, home furnishing direction leader at IKEA US.

Used across furnishings and accessories, it can provide a subtle touch of colour without being overly aggressive, especially paired with warm woods and neutral shades, IKEA US suggests.

But the company equally pictures it being splashed across entire walls and argues it “unexpectedly fits in” with even brighter colours like baby pink and electric blue – IKEA US’s previous colours of the year.

The company’s Style Guide also pulled out a number of other interior design trends to look out for in 2027, including pattern clashing and Japandi minimalism.

Interior designers have already started making liberal use of Wild Fig, as seen in Note Design Studio’s scheme for the Lammhults showroom in Stockholm, where it blankets walls, floors and ceilings in the entrance, as well as an entire kitchen.

Other predictions for 2027’s colour of the year are set to start rolling in any minute, with Pantone’s set to be unveiled at the start of December.

Paint brand Dulux got ahead of the game when it named a muted green called Soulful Sage as its contender in September.

Some interiors industry insiders, including Dezeen columnist Michelle Ogundehin, have argued at least since the end of the pandemic that “it’s time to reconsider the whole colour of the year carnival”, which was originally invented as a marketing stunt for Pantone’s colour-matching system, much like the Michelin Guide was invented to sell more tyres.

#9048. What It’s Actually Like to Shoot With Viltrox’s 35-Pound, $100,000 Cinema Lenses

What It’s Actually Like to Shoot With Viltrox’s 35-Pound, $100,000 Cinema Lenses

For the last couple of years at photo and video trade shows, Chinese lens maker Viltrox has always had a pair of very attention-grabbing optics on display: the Luna 30-300mm T4 Zoom 10x ($100,000) and 42-420mm T5.6 Zoom 10x ($100,000). These beefy, incredibly expensive bright white lenses sent a signal that Viltrox was serious about the high-end cinema lens market.

Seeing them always had us thinking: Why are these lenses so big and expensive?

A few months ago, Editor-in-Chief Jaron Schneider asked if I wanted to test these lenses to find out for ourselves. “Sure, that could be fun,” I responded at that time, blissfully unaware of the daunting task I had just signed up for.

Cinema “Super-Zooms,” which cover a wide-angle-to-telephoto zoom range, have historically been big and expensive, but only covered a Super35 sensor or film negative, a size quite similar to the APS-C sensor size common in photography. The Canon 30-300mm T2.95-3.7 ($48,500) is a great example of this.

Despite the floating aperture and Super35 coverage, it still tips the scales at a substantial six kilograms (13 pounds). By comparison, the Viltrox 30-300mm T4 can cover larger full-frame sensors like an Alexa LF and it has a fixed T4 aperture. The unfortunate side effects are the enormous dimensions and back-breaking weight of 15 kilograms (33 pounds).

The 42-420mm T5.6 is even more extreme, with a huge image projection suitable for an Alexa 65 or Fujifilm Eterna 55. Despite the slower aperture, this leads to a 16kg (1 Sisyphus Boulder) weight. Fortunately, both lenses include 19mm mounting rods and a dovetail tripod plate to keep everything secure. Unfortunately, that adds even more weight to the total package.

In order to test these lenses, I needed some outside assistance as my camera supports are designed for much more compact creator camera packages. Fortunately, Calgary rental shop MPR was able to outfit me with the rig, follow focus motors, and tripod needed to take the 30-300mm T4 into the field. The Panasonic S1R II with a PL-L adapter would make it easy to record full-frame 8K for image quality tests, though admittedly the whole package looked pretty silly.

The 42-420mm was more difficult as it uses the LPL mount designed for short-flange-back, large-sensor cinema cameras. Thankfully, my friend and AC/Cinematographer Alexis Moar was able to get me into Calgary’s Panavision to test that lens on an Alexa Mini LF. We’ll discuss the results a little later in this article.

Both Viltrox lenses are designed to be used interchangeably, so the design is the same. Like all cinema zoom lenses, these have geared rings for focus, zoom, and iris controls. Neither lens has a built-in zoom motor, so you will need to attach your own. I used the Tilta Nucleus for focus and zoom control during my testing.

There is a massive 165mm front element on both lenses, so an extremely large matte box will be required. This is essential for using NDs, as there is no rear filter drop-in. A back-focus adjustment screw is found close to the lens mount to make sure the zoom is parfocal and the indexed focus distances are accurate. Finally, a large removable handle is attached to the top of the lens to make schlepping more tolerable.

In terms of the image quality, I was expecting great things due to the exorbitant price and my increasing lower back pain. However, what I found upon running some tests is that having such a big zoom range with a fixed aperture clearly necessitates some optical compromises. I found very similar results with both lenses, so the following observations apply to both of the Luna optics.

In terms of sharpness, these lenses have something of a split personality. When shooting wide open at either end of the zoom, there is a dreamy haziness across the image. This gives the footage a nostalgic look, but it certainly doesn’t resolve a ton of detail. However, upon stopping down even one stop, sharpness and contrast improved dramatically, to the point that it looked quite good even in 8K. Basically, if fine detail is important to your shot, I would treat these as a 30-300mm T5.6 and 42-420mm T8, respectively.

In terms of bokeh, I was again a bit underwhelmed. There is a bit of truncated bokeh in specular highlights that doesn’t look like a conventional cat’s-eye and is quite distracting. This gives most out-of-focus areas a slightly harsh rendering. The bokeh on these lenses isn’t bad, but it’s far from exceptional.

Breathing is also a concern with cinema lenses, where the field of view changes when focusing from near to far or the reverse. It can be quite distracting if focus is changed during a scene and gives a slight zooming effect. Both lenses do exhibit strong breathing, particularly at the longer focal lengths.

One last thing I was surprised to see was the prominence of LoCA, or longitudinal chromatic aberration. This is where there is color split behind and in front of the plane of focus when shooting wide open, and it was not only noticeable on Panavision’s test charts, but in much of my real-world footage as well.

So I wasn’t terribly impressed with the optical performance of these lenses, but I wanted to see how they compared to industry-standard zooms. I was able to test the Super35-compatible Angenieux 24-290mm Optimo Zoom ($45,000), and despite its legendary reputation, it exhibited similar limitations in terms of sharpness, breathing, and LoCA.

My takeaway is that optimizing these lens formulas for cinema leads to some of these optical qualities, even if price and size are no object.

Despite all the aforementioned limitations, these lenses still definitely fill a niche in high-end film production. With the sudden rise of cinema cameras with substantially larger sensors than traditional Super35, many industry-standard optics will no longer suffice. Previously, if a cinematographer wanted a wide-angle-to-telephoto zoom in a single shot, a Super35 camera would need to be used. Now, even when working with full-frame or even larger sensors, Viltrox has a solution with the Luna line.

That said, this can never be a comprehensive review as these are intended to be used in massive film productions and very high-end documentary work, something I’m not currently engaged in. As well, I have not used any of the similar cinema lenses in the field in order to have an informed opinion about how the Lunas compare.

Rather, this was a fun experience, and a good reminder that even if price, size, and weight are no object, the physics of lens optics mean you still can’t have it all.

Cathay Pacific or Qantas Business Class via Alaska Mileage Plan — no fuel surcharges

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Picture this: you're reclining in a fully flat bed at 38,000 feet somewhere over the Pacific, a glass of Château Léoville Barton in hand, watching the Australian coastline slowly materialize through your window. The cabin is hushed. The seat — Cathay Pacific's renowned Business Class throne on the Airbus A350-1000 — cocoons you in a private pod with a sliding door, direct aisle access, and a mattress pad that makes a five-star hotel bed feel like an afterthought. This is the LAX–HKG–SYD route in Cathay Pacific Business Class. And you booked it for 55,000 Alaska Mileage Plan miles. Now consider what the person three rows up in economy paid in cash for their seat — and what the couple beside you in business paid for theirs. A Cathay Pacific Business Class ticket on this route typically retails between **$5,000 and $12,000**. That's not a typo. Premium cabin pricing on transpacific routes is notoriously aggressive, and Australia amplifies it further because of the sheer distance involved. At 55,000 miles for a one-way business class redemption, you're extracting somewhere between **9.1 and 21.8 cents per point (CPP)** — a range that makes most loyalty program strategists stop and stare. The ChooseFI community benchmarks a "good" redemption at 1.5–2 CPP for most programs. You are obliterating that benchmark. At the high end of this range, 55,000 miles is doing the work of $12,000 in cash. That is what the FI mindset calls asymmetric value. This is also a premium *experience*, not just a premium number. Cathay Pacific consistently ranks among the world's top airlines for business class. The A350-1000 is their flagship long-haul aircraft, featuring a 1-2-1 configuration with every single seat having direct aisle access. There are no middle seats. There are no awkward climbs over sleeping strangers. There is a full dine-on-demand menu, a curated wine list, noise-canceling headphones, and a ground service team that treats you like a valued guest before you even board. For the FI traveler, this redemption represents something rare: a genuine luxury experience — the kind that recalibrates your sense of what travel can feel like — made nearly free through a well-understood system. The math works. The experience delivers. And once you've done it, you'll understand exactly why the ChooseFI community talks about this one.

Alaska Mileage Plan is one of the most valuable frequent flyer programs in the world despite being a relatively small airline. The secret is their partner award chart: Alaska uses fixed pricing for partner airline awards, meaning costs do not fluctuate with demand the way dynamic programs do. This creates structural pricing inefficiencies — especially on premium cabin routes to Asia and Oceania — that savvy travelers can exploit. Alaska has partnerships with Cathay Pacific, Qantas, Japan Airlines, Emirates, Fiji Airways, and others. The primary way to earn Alaska miles is through the Alaska Airlines Visa Signature card (Bank of America), through flying, or via Marriott Bonvoy® transfers at a 3:1 ratio.

Free calculator shows when you could reach financial independence — plus a savings rate tracker, expense audit, and more.

Here's the insight that transforms this from "interesting" to "actionable": Alaska Airlines Mileage Plan uses a fixed partner award chart, and that chart prices Cathay Pacific Business Class to Australia at 55,000 miles one-way — a number that hasn't kept pace with the explosive cash price inflation of premium cabin fares.

Most major U.S. loyalty programs have migrated to dynamic pricing, where award costs fluctuate with cash fare demand. Alaska hasn't done this for partner awards. Their chart is fixed. That means when Cathay Pacific's cash fares spike to $12,000 during Australian school holidays or peak summer travel, your award cost stays exactly where it was: 55,000 miles. This is the pricing inefficiency at the heart of this redemption, and it's why the ChooseFI community treats Alaska Mileage Plan as one of the most valuable programs in the industry.

Alaska Mileage Plan has only one meaningful transfer partner for most people: Marriott Bonvoy®, at a ratio of 3 Bonvoy points to 1 Alaska mile. That's a steep ratio — you'll need 165,000 Bonvoy points to generate 55,000 Alaska miles — and transfer times run 1 to 5 days, so plan accordingly. There is no direct credit card transfer path into Alaska Mileage Plan from Chase, Amex, or Citi, which is why the "Easy to Earn" score for this redemption is a 2 out of 5. The miles must be earned directly: through Alaska's co-branded credit card (the Alaska Airlines Visa from Bank of America), through flying Alaska or its partners, or via Marriott transfer.

This is crucial and often overlooked. Alaska charges no fuel surcharges on any partner award bookings. This matters enormously for a Cathay Pacific redemption. If you were to book the same Cathay flight through Cathay's own Asia Miles program or through British Airways Avios, you could face fuel surcharges of $400–$900 or more on top of the points cost. With Alaska, your out-of-pocket cost is taxes and fees only — typically in the range of $50–$150 depending on the routing. That's it. A $12,000 experience for 55,000 miles and roughly $100 in fees.

Alaska allows a free stopover on one-way awards — a benefit that is genuinely rare among U.S. programs. On the LAX–HKG–SYD routing, this means you can build a stopover in Hong Kong at no additional points cost. Spend a few days exploring one of the world's most dynamic cities — the markets of Mong Kok, the skyline from Victoria Peak, the dim sum temples of Kowloon — then board your continuing flight to Sydney. Two destinations. One redemption. Same 55,000 miles.

The 55,000-mile rate applies to both Cathay Pacific and Qantas for business class to Australia. Cathay routes you through Hong Kong (HKG); Qantas has its own metal and routing options. If Cathay availability is thin, checking Qantas can open up alternatives without changing your points cost.

Do not start at Alaska's website. Alaska's own search tool for partner availability can be unreliable for Cathay Pacific. Instead, go to ba.com (British Airways' booking site) and run a one-way business class search for your desired route — for example, LAX to SYD or LAX to HKG. British Airways and Cathay Pacific are oneworld partners, and BA's search engine surfaces Cathay award availability with remarkable accuracy. Look for "Reward" seats in the business class (Club World or equivalent) cabin. Any dates showing availability on BA.com are almost certainly bookable through Alaska as well. Screenshot or note the specific dates before moving on.

Alaska opens its award booking window 331 days in advance. If you're targeting peak travel dates — Australian summer (December–February), for example — set a calendar reminder to search and transfer 331 days ahead. Your miles also never expire in Mileage Plan, which gives you flexibility to accumulate without pressure.

Confirm you have at least 55,000 Alaska miles available. If you're converting Marriott Bonvoy® points, you'll need 165,000 Bonvoy points at the 3:1 ratio. Initiate transfers at least one week before you plan to call, as Marriott-to-Alaska transfers can take 1 to 5 days.

Log into your Marriott Bonvoy® account, navigate to "Transfer Points," select Alaska Airlines as the recipient program, and enter your Mileage Plan number. Transfer in increments of 3,000 Bonvoy points (yielding 1,000 Alaska miles). Do not transfer until you've confirmed availability in Step 1 — points transfers are generally non-reversible.

This redemption cannot be booked online — Alaska's web portal does not support all partner award bookings, particularly for Cathay Pacific. Call Alaska Airlines at 1-800-252-7522. Tell the agent:

Have your Mileage Plan number, passport information, and a credit card for the taxes and fees ready. The call typically takes 20–40 minutes. Agents are generally knowledgeable, but if you encounter confusion, politely ask for a senior agent or call back.

If Cathay availability is limited on your preferred dates, ask the agent to check Qantas availability to Australia at the same 55,000-mile rate. Qantas Business (The Business) has its own award inventory and may have open seats when Cathay is fully allocated.

If you're routing through Hong Kong on Cathay, explicitly ask the agent to add a free stopover at HKG. This is a program benefit, not a favor — Alaska's routing rules allow one free stopover on one-way awards. Specify how many nights you want in Hong Kong before the continuing flight to Sydney.

The best way to find Cathay Pacific Business Class award availability is through the British Airways website (ba.com). Search for one-way flights from your U.S. gateway to Sydney or Melbourne, and look for dates showing Cathay Pacific-operated flights with Business Class availability. British Airways shows oneworld partner availability more reliably than most tools.

If Cathay Pacific shows no availability on your preferred dates, search for Qantas Business Class on the same route. Qantas availability can be found through the Qantas website or through British Airways. The Alaska Mileage Plan price is the same 55,000 miles for either carrier.

Earn miles through the Alaska Airlines Visa card sign-up bonus (typically 60,000 to 75,000 miles), through flying Alaska or partners, or by transferring from Marriott Bonvoy®. If transferring from Marriott, allow 1 to 5 business days for the transfer to complete before your booking window closes.

Call Alaska Mileage Plan at 1-800-252-7522 and request a partner award booking on Cathay Pacific (or Qantas) Business Class. Provide your desired dates and routing. Ask about adding a free stopover in Hong Kong if routing through HKG. The agent will process the booking and deduct 55,000 miles plus taxes and fees (typically $50 to $150).

After booking through Alaska, manage your seat selection directly through the Cathay Pacific website or app using your booking reference. Select a window or aisle seat in the 1-2-1 configuration — every seat has direct aisle access, so there is no wrong choice. You can also pre-order meals and manage other preferences through Cathay's platform.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Let's make this concrete. You and your partner want to celebrate a milestone — a sabbatical, a paid-off mortgage, financial independence itself — with a trip to Sydney. Here's exactly how this redemption plays out.

The Route: Los Angeles (LAX) → Hong Kong (HKG) → Sydney (SYD), on Cathay Pacific Business Class, with a 3-night stopover in Hong Kong.

Cash Price: A quick search on Google Flights confirms what you suspected — this itinerary in business class retails for approximately $8,000 per person during the shoulder season. During the Australian summer or holiday periods, it climbs closer to $11,000–$12,000.

Your Cost: 55,000 Alaska Mileage Plan miles + approximately $85 in taxes and fees. Per person.

CPP Calculation: At $8,000 cash value, your 55,000 miles are worth 14.5 cents per point — more than seven times what you'd get redeeming Alaska miles for domestic economy. At $12,000, you're at 21.8 cents per point, which is among the highest CPP figures available anywhere in the U.S. loyalty ecosystem.

In Hong Kong, Cathay Pacific's The Pier Business Class Lounge awaits during your stopover travel. It's widely regarded as one of the finest airport lounges in the world — noodle bar, live cooking stations, a spa treatment center, and a wine selection that rivals dedicated restaurants.

After three days exploring Hong Kong, you reboard for the six-hour SYD leg, arriving in Sydney ready — genuinely ready, not depleted — to start your adventure.

Total cost for two: 110,000 Alaska miles + roughly $170 in fees. That's the FI mindset applied to travel: extraordinary experiences made nearly free through a system anyone can learn.

Alaska's booking window opens 331 days out. Cathay Pacific releases business class award space to partner programs in limited quantities, and the best dates disappear quickly. Set a calendar alert for 331 days before your target travel date and be ready to search — and call — that morning.

The single best technique for this redemption: run your search on ba.com before calling Alaska. BA's search engine is faster, more reliable for Cathay availability, and lets you visually scan a full month of dates. Identify two or three date options before you pick up the phone. This dramatically shortens your call time and reduces the chance of getting an agent who says "I'm not seeing anything."

Don't treat the Hong Kong stopover as a layover — treat it as a destination. Alaska's routing rules explicitly allow a free stopover on one-way awards. Two to four nights in Hong Kong costs you nothing extra in miles. Pair this with a cheap positioning flight or use it as an anchor for a broader Asia itinerary.

This is the most common and most painful mistake. Marriott-to-Alaska transfers are generally not reversible. If you transfer 165,000 Bonvoy points to Alaska and then discover no award space exists on your dates, you're stuck with miles you may not use optimally. Always confirm availability on ba.com before initiating any transfer.

Book two one-way redemptions rather than a round-trip. This gives you full flexibility on return routing — you might come back on Qantas through another city, or extend your trip without penalty.

Since there are no major flexible currency transfer paths into Alaska (no Chase, Amex, or Citi transfers), the Alaska Airlines Visa Signature from Bank of America is your most efficient earning vehicle. The welcome bonus alone can cover a significant portion of this redemption. Pair with everyday spending in categories that earn elevated miles.

If Cathay availability is closed on your dates, Qantas Business Class to Australia prices at the same 55,000 miles. Qantas' "The Business" product on their A380 Sydney routes is exceptional in its own right — and availability patterns differ from Cathay, so checking both genuinely doubles your options.

This redemption is purpose-built for the FI-minded couple or solo traveler who is willing to invest some effort in the booking process in exchange for an extraordinary, nearly free experience. If you've been dreaming about Australia and refuse to pay $8,000–$12,000 for a business class ticket — but you're also not willing to spend 20+ hours crammed in economy for a trip this significant — this is your answer.

Minimum requirements: You need 55,000 Alaska Mileage Plan miles per person. For two travelers, that's 110,000 miles. If you're building from zero through the Alaska Visa, factor in 6–12 months of earning runway before booking.

Within a broader FI travel strategy, this redemption pairs well with a Marriott Bonvoy® credit card for point accumulation and an Alaska Visa for direct mile earning. It's a medium-complexity move with a very high ceiling on value.

This redemption earns a **moderate difficulty rating** — and that rating is honest. It's not complicated in concept, but it has two specific friction points that trip up even experienced travel rewards enthusiasts. **Challenge 1: Earning the Miles** Alaska Mileage Plan's isolation from major flexible currency programs (no Chase Ultimate Rewards, no Amex Membership Rewards, no Citi ThankYou transfers directly) means you can't simply funnel points you already have into Alaska. The primary path is the Alaska Airlines Visa (Bank of America) or a Marriott Bonvoy® conversion at an unfavorable 3:1 ratio. Plan your earning strategy well in advance. **Tip:** Prioritize the Alaska Visa signup bonus as your foundation, then supplement with Marriott points if needed. **Challenge 2: The Phone Booking Requirement** You cannot book this online. The call-in process intimidates people who've only ever booked travel digitally. **Tip:** Do your homework on ba.com first, have your dates ready, and approach the call as an informed customer — not someone asking for help finding availability. Agents respond well to specific, prepared callers. **Challenge 3: Cathay Award Availability** Cathay Pacific releases partner award space selectively and often in small quantities. Availability rated 3/5. **Tip:** Search exactly at the 331-day booking window, keep Qantas as your backup at the same price point, and be flexible with travel dates by even one or two days — a Tuesday departure often has inventory when Saturday doesn't. The good news: once you've done this once, you'll understand the system deeply enough to replicate it. The ChooseFI community has members who've booked this exact route multiple times. The first time takes effort. After that, it's a process you know cold.

The fastest path is the Alaska Airlines Visa Signature card from Bank of America, which typically offers a 60,000 to 75,000-mile sign-up bonus. That alone nearly covers the 55,000 miles needed. You can also transfer Marriott Bonvoy® points at 3:1 (165,000 Bonvoy points equals 55,000 Alaska miles) or earn miles through flying Alaska and its partners.

Yes. You would book two separate one-way awards at 55,000 miles each. You could fly Cathay Pacific one direction and Qantas the other, or mix carriers based on availability. Each one-way can include its own free stopover.

Cathay Pacific typically releases Business Class award space 90 to 330 days before departure. The sweet spot for finding availability is usually 90 to 120 days out, when airlines release unsold premium cabin seats. Check frequently, as availability can appear and disappear quickly.

Alaska allows one free stopover on one-way awards. On a routing from the US to Australia via Hong Kong, you can stop in Hong Kong for any number of days at no additional miles cost. Simply tell the agent when booking that you want a stopover in HKG. This effectively gives you two destinations for the price of one redemption.

The Alaska Mileage Plan redemption for Cathay Pacific or Qantas Business Class to Australia is one of the most extraordinary sweet spots in travel rewards. At 55,000 miles for a seat that costs $5,000 to $12,000 in cash — with zero fuel surcharges and a free stopover in Hong Kong — this redemption delivers 9 to 22 cents per point. It requires more planning and effort than a simple hotel booking, but the payoff is a genuine luxury travel experience that proves the asymmetric value the FI community builds its travel rewards strategy around.

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

#9045. ‘Imperfection is everywhere. It is a great element’: Yuko Mohri on her exhibition of found objects at London's Barbican

Mohri at work during her residency at the Barbican earlier this year Photo: © Toby Coulson/Barbican Centre

After picking up the 2025 Calder Prize, the multidisciplinary Tokyo-based Yuko Mohri artist has been on a recent roll, opening institutional shows from Santander in Spain and her first US solo show in Miami Beach to bringing her 2024 Venice Biennale presentation home to her native Japan.

Among the highlights is In Concert (until 24 January 2027), her solo exhibition at the Barbican Centre’s The Curve gallery in London. At the show’s core is a series of site-responsive kinetic and sound installations made with objects she found at the Barbican. These objects, either stored away or nearly tossed out, embed the history and memories of this famed cultural centre, which will be closed for a year from June 2028 for a £191m revamp ahead of its 50th anniversary in 2032. According to Mohri, the pieces represent an ongoing process that may lead to imperfection, which she finds more profound than a picture-perfect scenario.

The Art Newspaper: How did your Barb­ican residency come about?

Yuko Mohri: When I was approached for a project at The Curve, I discussed with Inês Geraldes Cardoso, the curator of this exhibition, the possibility of researching the Barbican Centre.

The Curve is a unique and challenging space, and they accept experimental projects with artists. I am not the kind of artist who needs to work within a white cube. I understand why they chose me to create something unique. I am, however, the kind of artist who needs time to understand the environment and identify interesting elements that already exist in that context. A research residency is necessary.

But rather than focusing on just this curved gallery space, I wanted to see what the Barbican really is. It is a huge centre involving many different departments and activities. Thousands of people are also living here in the attached residential complex.

After rounds of negotiations, I was offered a two-week residency to look for objects and meet the people living and working here. I got a temporary studio at The Pit, a small theatre space located in the basement.

“Imperfection is everywhere,” Yuko Mohri says. “It’s a great element.” Photo: © Toby Coulson/Barbican Centre

The centre has many departments, but they seem very separate from each other and don’t have a lot of communication between them. But since they are going to have a major renovation, they want to revamp the centre’s system, too, and strengthen communication.

We started researching different departments and looked for objects across all the spaces. I wanted to collect objects from here that resonate with the space.

Among the most iconic ones are the original Barbican lamps featured throughout this exhibition. These were once used as street lamps surrounding the centre and also in the building. But as time went on, they were replaced with those of a new design. They were dusty and strange, but I immediately knew that I wanted to use them for my installation. So I spent a lot of time washing these lamps in my temporary studio.

The speakers that I use for the new iteration of the ongoing Decomposition series (begun 2021) located near the entrance to The Curve are old speakers from the Barbican. The found cables that I use to connect the fruit with the lamps and the sound are also very important to me. I also found these metal junk pieces that were discarded in a workshop, and I reappropriated them as triggers for the lamps in the installations in the middle part of the exhibition.

Throughout this project I met many people outside the gallery space, from engineers to the caretakers of the parking space. The extensive communication helped me connect with a lot of open-minded people who accept me and my work.

Yuko Mohri’s Moré Moré (Leaky) is an ongoing installation inspired by the water leaks at Tokyo metro stations Photo: Sun Shi; courtesy the artist, Project Fulfill Art Space, mother’s tankstation, Yutaka Kikutake Gallery, Tanya Bonakdar Gallery and WHITE SPACE

How do you relate the centre’s characteristics with your practice?

The Barbican has many water leaks. There’s also a leak of sound because The Curve wraps around the concert hall. So these leaky elements resonate with my practice, especially my ongoing Moré Moré (Leaky) series (begun 2017), which was inspired by the water leaks at Tokyo metro stations and how the staff contain these water leaks with temporary fixes using everyday items. I presented a version of this in Venice.

This time at the Barbican, I created a large-scale installation located towards the exit of The Curve, using found objects such as a pot, an umbrella, plastic bottles, Wellington boots, traffic cones and old water sinks designed for the Barbican apartments.

I also keep the space open and transparent by removing the covers on the entrances and the back so that people can see what’s going on there from the outside. I also exposed the inner layers of the walls to give people a peek into what is behind them.

Are you building an ecosystem within the Barbican that makes the inaudible heard and the invisible seen?

Instead of building, I see it as repairing. Inspired by attending concert rehearsals at the Barbican, I chose the title In Concert, which mirrors the Latin root consertare. It carries the meaning of repair and adjustment, resembling the process of making an organisation.

The process is also similar to making an installation. When I started, I had no idea how it would turn out eventually. I constantly make adjustments to the elements of my installations, like a conductor making adjustments to the tempo or the volume of the musical instruments. The title also reflects that what you see is not stable. Water leaks, gravity and the audience’s presence will change even some very tiny elements. It is not a finalised show. It’s an ongoing process.

Would you say that you are in control and at the same time you also let go?

I am a human being and I have a desire for a certain outcome. But somehow, it doesn’t always work. This trial and error process is a very learnable process for me.

We all have our expectations, but our society and environment have become increasingly unstable. For example, this summer Tokyo rained non-stop for a record 36 consecutive days. We need to adjust our lives. It’s also a necessity when we are based in Tokyo, constantly facing natural disasters like earthquakes. Japan has long been isolated, but now we have many immigrants. Our society is changing. I see this as a kind of training and accept these changing forces. It’s not necessarily about making things perfect. Imperfection is everywhere. It is a great element.

An edition of Mohri’s ongoing installation Decomposition from 2022 in Kanazawa, Japan Photo: Yuu Takagi; courtesy the artist, Project Fulfill Art Space, mother’s tankstation, Yutaka Kikutake Gallery, Tanya Bonakdar Gallery and WHITE SPACE

Education: 2004 BFA, Tama Art University; 2006 MFA, Tokyo University of the Arts.

Key shows: 2026 The Bass, Miami Beach; 2026 Yokohama Museum of Art; 2026 Centro Botín, Santander; 2025 Pirelli HangarBicocca, Milan; 2024 Japan Pavilion, Venice Biennale; 2023 14th Gwangju Biennale

Represented by: Tanya Bonakdar Gallery, New York; Yutaka Kikutake Gallery, Tokyo; Mother’s Tankstation, London; White Space, Beijing; Project Fulfill Art Space, Taipei

#9044. Meet AMAA, Neri&Hu’s pick for the most influential architect of the next 20 years

Photography by Mikael Olsson unless stated

An innovative approach to the reuse of existing buildings defines the output of Italian architecture office AMAA, which Neri&Hu has selected as one of 20 names to watch in architecture and design as part of Dezeen’s 20×20 project, sponsored by Kohler.

Led by Marcello Galiotto and Alessandra Rampazzo, over the past 14 years AMAA has become known for its approach to the reuse of post-industrial structures in northern Italy, with the transformation of a former factory building into its own studio, a typical example of its approach.

According to Galiotto, these buildings are a taste of what the studio wants to achieve.

“What we have done in the past 10 years is really just a sketch of what we can do in the future,” he told Dezeen.

“Our research is still growing, and it can be applied to various programmes and contexts,” he continued, “but in 20 years we will both be 60 so we want the studio to be able to evolve and grow in new directions.”

The preservation and adaptation of existing buildings, which is central to AMAA’s practice, is a key reason why architects Lyndon Neri and Rossana Hu selected the studio for Dezeen’s 20×20 series.

“AMAA is significant for its fierce commitment to adaptive reuse,” said the duo, adding that the studio’s ability to repurpose historic structures “positions them as leaders in circular, life-cycle thinking in contemporary Italian architecture”.

AMAA is significant for its fierce commitment to adaptive reuse, [which] positions them as leaders in circular, life-cycle thinking in contemporary Italian architecture

Galiotto and Rampazzo met Neri and Hu when they participated in the 2023 Venice Biennale and have since been invited to host lectures at the University of Pennsylvania, where Hu is chair of the architecture department.

“We have a long relationship with Lyndon and Rossana who we consider to be both amazing people and great architects so it’s truly an honour to be selected by them,” said Galiotto.

Rampazzo added that she saw a clear overlap between Shanghai-based Neri&Hu’s work, which also has a focus on adaptive reuse approach, and their approach at AMAA.

“I’m a fan of their work and I see similarities in the way we do architecture and also the way we teach, despite our different cultural backgrounds,” she said. “I also love how they really support students and young architects by sharing their knowledge. We have a lot to learn from them but I hope we can have the same kind of legacy.”

Rampazzo and Galiotto have known each other for more than 20 years after meeting while studying architecture at the Iuav University of Venice.

The studio now has offices in Venice and in the industrial town of Arzignano, and has gradually become established among Italy’s most respected architecture firms thanks to projects such as their own office and a cafe housed within a 19th-century town hall.

We felt our education hadn’t provide us with knowledge of how to run a medium or large-scale practice, so my experience with Sou Fujimoto was about closing the gap between the present and future of our studio

The pair studied together at Iuav under the professorship of Massimo Carmassi, who they cite as an important influence on their approach to restoration and reuse.

After graduating in 2010, they assisted Carmassi and briefly set up a studio with friends to work on competitions. Then Galiotto went to Japan to work for Sou Fujimoto, while Rampazzo travelled to India for her PhD studies.

“We felt our education hadn’t provide us with knowledge of how to run a medium or large-scale practice,” said Galiotto, “so my experience with Sou Fujimoto was about closing the gap between the present and future of our studio.”

This global travel and work experience helped open their minds to alternative approaches and opportunities, as well as giving them the confidence to set up their own studio back in Venice.

“We’re still evolving, and evolving our identity,” said Galiotto. “But the important thing was to find ourselves. That’s why the path was complicated.

“Stay in Italy… going outside of Italy… travelling the world as much as we can to see things. That was the key, I think, to the position that we are covering right now in the panorama of architecture in Italy.”

In 2015, they opened a branch office in Galiotto’s hometown of Arzignano, which has been described as an “AMAA playground” due to the number of projects the practice has completed there.

Galiotto pointed out that their work in the town is part of an ongoing research into how architecture can blur the line between private and public spaces, with the Caffe Nazionale project providing a good example.

“Although the cafe is privately owned, it also forms the edge of a plaza so we wanted to give the space back to the people,” the architect explained, adding that the studio has coined the term “super public” to describe this aspect of their practice.

Alongside their work in Arzignano and Venice, AMAA now has commissions across Italy, including hospitality and residential projects, as well as schools and a theatre. Along with a focus on reuse, especially industrial buildings, Galiotto believes that the studio’s work is united by its considered eclecticism.

“We’re influenced by art, artists, travels and whatever we can be – by curiosity,” he said. “I would say it’s something that’s very important and it gives us this kind of eclecticism. Our architecture in this moment is very eclectic and at the same time has a strong direction.”

“It’s like a piano symphony, very complicated and very up and down, but at the same time very right like a poem, very well taught and very well executed, but very complicated in terms of ingredients.”

The studio’s expanding list of projects has caused it to swell in size to approximately 30 members of staff, which Galiotto suggested is necessary to facilitate their detailed, research-led approach.

We often collaborate closely with other architects, but we are also influenced by painting, sculpture and photography which enhances the eclecticism of our projects

Looking ahead, the architects said their main objective is to continue developing their team and consolidating their approach so that others can carry it on in the coming decades.

One concern they have is maintaining the same quality of output as demand for their services grows and they take on an increasing number of projects.

In just the past year they have completed 10 projects – as many as they delivered during the first decade of their practice – with public commissions now joining their work for private clients.

Despite the rapid growth, Galiotto and Rampazzo insisted their approach remains consistent whatever scale of project they are working on, whether it’s a chair, a public plaza or a museum, which they both agree would be a dream next project.

Asked for her view on the future of architecture over the coming decades, Rampazzo said there is a trend in Italy towards involving other creatives in the design process, which represents an alternative to the more autocratic approach of the past.

“Sharing ideas and opinions leads to more interesting outcomes,” she claimed. “We often collaborate closely with other architects, but we are also influenced by painting, sculpture and photography which enhances the eclecticism of our projects.”

In their teaching roles at institutions including Kent State University and Universidade do Minho in Portugal, Galiotto and Rampazzo are responsible for helping to shape the attitudes of the next generation of architects, who they recognise are entering the workplace in challenging times.

Galiotto said if there is one thing he tries to pass on to his students and the staff in his studio it is to “have passion and to keep pushing for what you believe in.”

“If you are humble, passionate and curious then you can find success,” he added. “Sometimes it can be tough, but when you love what you do you can live your life feeling like you never worked for a single day.”

To celebrate Dezeen’s 20th birthday, we asked 20 of the most influential architects and designers of the last 20 years to identify someone they think will have a major impact in the next 20 years. Over the next four weeks, we’ll reveal their picks in a series of profile interviews. The series is presented in partnership with Kohler.

Photography by Mikael Olsson unless stated

From a bargain 4K set to a stunning OLED, these are the Black Friday TV deals we'd buy ourselves.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If you've been holding out for a new TV, now's the time to take the plunge. Prices on everything from budget 4K sets to premium OLEDs have dropped sharply at Amazon, with some savings approaching 50%.

For creatives who spend all day pouring over visual work, looking for imperfections, a poor quality TV just isn't an option. Instead, even more than the average punter, we need accurate colour, deep blacks and high brightness to properly enjoy TV, movies and video games – and appreciate all these things when we have them.

To save you buying the wrong model, we've picked out three standout deals. The first is our top pick, balancing price and performance. The second is brilliant budget buy. And the third is a premium OLED for anyone who wants the very best picture. Of course, if you'd rather a smaller display, check out all the best Black Friday iPad deals.

We'll start with our top pick. Hisense's U8 Series is one of the best-value Mini-LED TVs around, and at 47% off, this deal is hard to ignore. Up to 5,600 local dimming zones and a peak brightness of up to 5,000 nits deliver bright highlights and deep shadows with minimal halos, while its QLED quantum dot colour is Pantone Validated, which matters if you care about accurate hues. Gamers get a native 165Hz panel with VRR and AMD FreeSync Premium Pro, and there's built-in 4.1.2-channel Dolby Atmos sound with up-firing speakers. Finally, an anti-reflection coating helps in bright rooms.

Our budget pick. If you just want a solid 4K TV without spending a fortune, Amazon's own Ember 4-Series is a great shout. You get 4K Ultra HD with HDR10+, Dolby Audio, Wi-Fi 6 and a new quad-core processor that keeps apps loading quickly. It runs the newest version of Fire TV, with Alexa+ voice search to find shows across your apps, and built-in Omnisense sensors wake the screen when you walk into the room to display artwork. It won't match the Hisense or LG for picture quality, but at this price, it's a brilliant buy.

If you can stretch to a grand, here's the one to buy, LG's C-Series OLEDs are perennial favourites: because each of its 8.3 million pixels produces its own light, you get perfect blacks and outstanding contrast, now boosted by LG's Brightness Booster and the new a11 AI Processor Gen3. Filmmaker Mode with Ambient Light Technology lets you see films as the director intended, and Dolby Vision and Atmos are both on board. Finally, gamers get a 0.1ms response time and VRR up to 165Hz, with G-Sync and FreeSync support.

It mostly comes down to how and where you watch. If picture quality is your priority, especially in a dimmer room, OLED is hard to beat. Because every pixel lights itself, blacks are truly black and contrast is superb, making the LG C6 is our premium pick. Mini-LED sets such as the Hisense U8 can't quite match that, but they get much brighter, making them a better fit for sunny living rooms, and they give you more screen for your money. If you just need a decent 4K TV for a spare room or studio, a budget set like the Amazon Ember will do the job nicely.

It's also worth thinking about size before you click buy. Measure your space and viewing distance, and remember that the price jump between sizes can be surprisingly small: on the Hisense deal, for instance, going from 55 to 65 inches costs just $150 more. Gamers should look for a high refresh rate and VRR support, which both the Hisense and LG offer. And if you'll use the TV to review your own photos or video, turn off any motion smoothing and switch to Filmmaker Mode or the most accurate picture preset.
