#9022. Ahead of Taiwan local elections, politicians crowd in at Art Taipei

This year's edition of Taiwan's 34-year-old fair Art Taipei (29 October to 2 November) and its third concurrent Taipei Art Week (TAW) fell, serendipitously, just before the alleged spying scandal that emerged around Taiwan's celebrated native son, the naturalised American Nvidia mogul Jensen Huang. This spared fair sales the ensuing worldwide tech stock dive. Rather, concerns during the fair focused more on the pending midterm elections on 28 November.

The fair's opening ceremony was thick with politicians. Prominent figures included incumbent Taipei mayor Chiang Wan-an, now in a close re-election race, who would days later face protests at the Taipei Pride parade and festival over his police department's aggressive raid of gay bar Commander D on 3 October. Taiwan's minister of culture Li Yuan heralded his department's successful efforts in September to get a pavilion at the Gwangju Biennale named for Taiwan rather than the sponsoring institution, which sparked a diplomatic row with mainland China, and pronounced that "AI will not replace artists!"

"The presence of political figures at art fairs is a familiar feature of Taiwan's cultural landscape," says Claudia Chen, director of Art Taipei, chair of its organiser, the Taipei Art Gallery Association (Taga), and cofounder of Taipei's Liang Gallery. She adds that it builds public visibility and engagement for the cultural sector. "We hope this attention can help deepen public understanding of the art market and highlight its close connections with cultural development, urban growth, and international exchange."

The question, she continues, "is whether this engagement with political leaders can translate into consistent policy support, particularly in areas such as arts education, international promotion, and incentives for private collecting and cultural patronage." Taiwan lags behind most East Asian governments in cultural investment. "We hope cultural development can become an important public issue and receive sustained support across political parties, allowing Taiwan to gradually translate its economic strength into a deeper and more far-reaching cultural influence."

Chen says that Taiwan's technology sector and the private wealth it fuels "provide an important foundation for its art market. However, translating economic growth into greater activity in the art market takes time," as well as innovation and outreach by galleries.

The 127 galleries that Art Taipei welcomed to the Taipei World Trade Center this year included the return of influential galleries such as Richard Koh Fine Art, from Kuala Lumpur and Singapore, for the first time post-pandemic, and Perrotin for a third consecutive year. Newcomers included Tokyo's Misako & Rosen. One of Taipei's leading platforms, Tina Keng Gallery (TKG+) and TKG+ Projects, joined for the first time in about five years. "In recent years, with Singapore, Seoul, Hong Kong, there is a lot happening, so we needed an opportunity to do a Taiwan show," says the gallery's assistant to the director, Alice Liang. With the suspension of the sleeker international fair Taipei Dangdai after 2025, Art Taipei has resumed its status as the main "hometown" option, she says.

Sales of a "museum-type" installation of works by artists including Sanyu, Kuo Tzumin and Michael Lin went "pretty well", says Liang. "People were surprised and curious," with "positive feedback" from collectors who skewed young and were both Taiwanese and foreign. She adds that the launch of the broader art week had little impact on sales, "but we can feel the difference, with the events, parties and open studios."

Fair organisers also report a generational shift among buyers, with 20.8% of those surveyed saying they were attending for the first or second time, double the figure for 2023. VIP collectors also declined from 77.5% to 54.2%, suggesting that the publicly accessible side of the art week is also providing outreach for the fair. Endeavours included five bus rounds, guided tours, digital art screenings at Taipei Lumitree and 30 public artworks displayed citywide, says Chen. For the art industry, a forum included speakers such as M+ Hong Kong curator Russell Storer and 2026 Venice Biennale Korea Pavilion curator Binna Choi.

The fair also featured an expanded presence of galleries from Korea and Japan, with 25 and 22 respectively, drawing on Taga's ongoing collaboration with those countries' gallery associations. Galleries from Japan, Taiwan's former coloniser, "have maintained a longstanding presence in the Taiwanese market, with many having established strong collector networks and brand recognition over the years," says Chen. The Korean presence "demonstrates the Korean art industry's capacity to expand into international markets through collaboration."

Tastes at the fair are also shifting towards Pop and contemporary art, says dealer Steven Chen (no relation). His Taipei gallery Yiyun Art has attended the fair for seven of the past ten years. It represents traditional Asian paintings, which remain a major sector at Art Taipei, if reduced from previous years. His dramatic maze of a booth, evoking a Chinese scholar's garden, saw steady crowds and sales, including of a painting by Yu Cheng Yao for $90,000. "With the young generation is coming more to the fair," says Chen, "we need a new language on ink art. It is the same culture with a new expression."

Claudia Chen says that Taiwan's collectors are maintaining "purchasing momentum" but have become increasingly deliberate, needing time and established relationships with galleries. Meanwhile, younger collectors are "gradually entering the market, bringing more diverse perspectives shaped by their own lifestyles and aesthetic preferences."

#9021. Should I Exercise with a Phlegmy Cough? What You Need to Know

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

You’re feeling a bit under the weather, but you don’t want to lose the momentum of your fitness routine. So, should you push through and hit the gym, or is it better to rest and let your body heal? Let’s break it down!

Sleep is the best way to help your body recover quickly when you’re sick. But if you’re determined to rise and grind, you could use the “neck check” to decide whether to lace up those sneakers or stay in bed.

Many sports doctors use this theory to say that if your symptoms are above the neck — sniffles, sore throat, or a mild headache — you’re generally good to go for a light workout. But if you’re dealing with chest congestion, a hacking or juicy cough, diarrhea, a fever, or an upset stomach, it’s better to take some time to catch up on your Netflix watchlist.

Big disclaimer: there’s little scientific evidence behind the “neck check,” so use your best judgment.

If you’re going with the above-the-neck rule, exercising with the following symptoms is probably okay.

Going super hard if you have a mild cold is not a good idea. But a light workout, like a walk or a chill Peloton sesh, can be a great way to stay active without overdoing it. Stretching or light yoga might also do the trick.

Stick to light activities like walking for most earaches. Avoid intense workouts like weightlifting, yoga, or pilates, as they can throw off your balance and put pressure on your sinuses, exacerbating the pain.

Light and short workouts are likely fine if your sore throat is mild and lacks fever, cough, or swallowing issues. Remember to stay hydrated — it can ease your sore throat and is beneficial during exercise.

Light activities like brisk walks or gentle bike rides can help for allergy-related stuffy noses. If your nose is blocked, stick to very light activities, focusing on breathing. Skip workouts if you have a fever, chest congestion, or a productive cough with phlegm until you’re symptom-free.

If you’re experiencing the following symptoms, the workout can wait.

Working out with a fever increases dehydration risk and can worsen the fever. Plus, fever saps your muscle strength and coordination, making you more prone to injuries. So, do yourself a favor and skip the workout until you’re back to normal.

An occasional cough is your body’s way of clearing out irritants, but a frequent or phlegmy cough could signal a respiratory infection like a cold, flu, or even pneumonia or asthma. While a tickle-induced cough isn’t a gym deal-breaker, a persistent one is.

Diarrhea and vomiting can dehydrate you, and physical activity only makes that dehydration worse. Feeling weak? That’s a recipe for injury. Plus, stomach bugs are highly contagious. If you feel antsy, stick to light stretching or yoga at home.

The flu hits your respiratory system hard, with symptoms like fever, chills, sore throat, body aches, fatigue, headache, cough, and congestion. If you’ve got the flu, take it easy and give your body some well-earned R&R.

Once symptom-free, ease back into exercise gradually. Start with less intense workouts to avoid overdoing it. As your symptoms fade, you can gradually return to normal activity.

Regular exercise may shorten recovery time, particularly for acute respiratory infections. Listen to your body’s signals to gauge your strength. If you’re still contagious, opt for home or outdoor workouts, so you don’t spread those germs to fellow gym-goers.

Human After All turned a 'drab B2B world' into a 'cultural kaleidoscope'.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Spotify is hardly known for being a dull brand. The streaming giant has made some bold visual choices in recent years, not least the controversial 'disco ball' that popped up on (or, depending on your viewpoint, plagued) home screens this May. But if there was one area of the brand that was missing out on the fun, it was Spotify Sessions.

No, that isn't the name of a series of live recordings, it's the title given to Spotify's webinars aimed at marketers. Spotify Sessions is designed to educate people about taking out ads on the platform. But this B2B virtual event series was, as you might expect, dry and jargon-heavy, with little of the vibrance Spotify is known for.

London based studio Human After All was tasked with helping Spotify Sessions rediscover its sense of fun – and fandom. "What should have been a cultural kaleidoscope had become a drab B2B world: a webinar that showed none of the fandom and culture that make Spotify unmistakable, the studio says. So we put culture on shuffle."

The maximalist identity is actually held together by a single typeface family, Spotify Mix. Meanwhile, a series of fun 3D icons are pulled straight from Spotify’s streaming data, from rhinestone cowboy hats to matcha boba and signet rings.

#9019. Does Creatine Increase DHT? What You Need to Know

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Ah, creatine! It’s a popular supplement promising muscle gains and enhanced performance. But as you’re hitting the gym harder and seeing results, there are some potential side effects to be aware of. Here’s the lowdown.

Creatine monohydrate is a naturally occurring substance found in muscle cells. It helps to produce adenosine triphosphate (ATP) — your muscles’ go-to fuel when working hard.

Although you can find creatine in foods like red meat and seafood, many gym enthusiasts and athletes boost their stores with supplements. Why? Because more creatine equals more ATP, which means more energy for high-intensity activities. More fuel means more mileage!

Now, here’s where things get hairy. You might dial up your body’s DHT (dihydrotestosterone) production when you uplevel creatine. DHT is a derivative of testosterone and plays a big-league role in developing male characteristics. But here’s the catch: while DHT might beef up your alpha vibe, it’s also notorious for thinning out hairlines in peeps predisposed to male pattern baldness.

So, do creatine supplements cause baldness? Maybe! The buzz mainly stems from a small 2009 study where college-aged rugby players loaded up on creatine and saw their DHT levels increase significantly.

Because DHT can shrink hair follicles and shorten the hair growth cycle, it may seem logical to blame creatine for contributing to hair thinning. However, it’s important to remember that these findings are a one-hit wonder — they haven’t been seen again in other studies. Plus, let’s not forget that intense workouts alone can pump up these hormones, too.

As a result, the jury’s still out, making the creatine-and-baldness saga a hot topic for gym gossip and scientists alike.

The same 2009 study found that after a week of taking high-dose creatinine at 25 grams per day, DHT levels rose by 56%. When the researchers dropped the dose to 5g daily for two more weeks, levels remained 40% higher than baseline. These findings contrasted with the control group participants who took a placebo.

Does this mean creatine could spell disaster for your do? Well, creatine boosts DHT, the usual suspect in male pattern baldness, also called androgenic alopecia. However, your disposition to hair loss and the effects of DHT is genetic, meaning that it’s inherited.

Some folks are more prone to DHT’s hair-ruffling effects because of how their androgen receptor gene is wired. Hormones like testosterone and DHT bind to androgen receptors, typically triggering normal hair growth. However, variations in the AR gene make the androgens extra effective, making you more likely to experience hair loss.

So, while there isn’t much evidence to say that creatine supplements cause hair loss, the connection to increased DHT levels is worth considering if your family reunions look like a convention for bald eagles.

Beyond the potential for a breezy scalp, creatine is actually solid in the safety department, with long-term studies giving it a thumbs up. However, although creatinine doesn’t pose a risk to healthy individuals, it might not be your best move if you have kidney, high blood pressure, or liver disease.

Another thing to keep in mind is that creatinine loves to hang onto water, so expect some extra bloat and weigh-in surprises as your body adjusts.

Thinking of starting a creatine kick? Chatting with your doctor first is always wise, especially if you have other health conditions or take medications. They can advise you and rule out any potential interactions.

If you’re taking creatinine and notice changes to your hair, a check-up is a good idea. Shedding a few strands is normal, but it’s a red flag if you start losing clumps of hair. Rapid hair loss can indicate underlying health issues that go beyond your hairstyle.

Furthermore, consult a doctor if hair loss is weighing on your mind. They can offer solutions or treatments to manage your hair loss and stress.

Creatine is celebrated for its muscle-building prowess, but rumors of a link with hair loss exist. The good news is there’s little conclusive evidence directly connecting creatine supplementation to permanent hair loss.

However, creatine loading may boost DHT levels, a hormone linked to male pattern baldness, especially in people genetically predisposed to hair thinning.

So, if you’re concerned about hair loss, it might be wise to talk with a doctor before adding creatine supplements to your muscle-building routine.

#9018. London Museum brings "back a bit of London's heritage" with Smithfield Market opening

Architecture studios Stanton Williams, Asif Khan and Julian Harrap Architects have completed their long-awaited transformation of the 1880s Smithfield General Market into the London Museum.

Opening to the public on Saturday, the former Victorian market hall now functions as a museum that tells the story of London’s history through exhibitions designed by German studio Atelier Brückner.

According to the London Museum, it is the largest dedicated city museum in the world.

Ten years in the making, the opening of Smithfield General Market marks the first phase of the London Museum’s relocation from the Barbican Estate’s former Museum of London, which is set to be demolished.

Stanton Williams, Asif Khan and Julian Harrap Architects have overhauled the General Market, which fell into disrepair after it closed in the 1990s, and will also convert the adjacent 1960s Poultry Market, which is expected to open in 2028.

“There’s an opportunity to represent London as it is now and in the future, and really take city museums to another level,” said London Museum’s New Museum Project director Alec Shaw.

“We’re bringing back a bit of London’s heritage – one building that has not been seen or encountered for at least 30 years, and the other one an amazing architectural gem that hasn’t been fully appreciated and will now be,” he told Dezeen.

The main entrance to the London Museum is marked by a covered street, West Poultry Avenue, which doubles as the Real Time gallery that stretches between the General Market and Poultry Market.

Entering the transformed Victorian market, visitors pass a museum shop and an auditorium before entering Our Time – an expansive gallery illuminated from above by an oculus.

Shops that once wrapped the perimeter of the market trading floor were removed to open up the space, but the restoration was designed to retain hints of the building fabric’s history.

“You can see pockets in the brickwork walls where joists of the first floor and little plaster columns were originally located,” said Julian Harrap Architects partner Lyall Thow.

“There was a second floor, represented by a darkened band where we didn’t overly clean the brickwork, and fireplaces in the upper offices were taken out, restored, and put back where they would have been originally.”

Stanton Williams, Asif Khan and Julian Harrap Architects overhauled 42 individual shops that formerly encircled the General Market into 12 multi-storey units.

Six units were kept to contain a restaurant, galleries and learning spaces, while the other six were left for the museum to invite partner institutions to occupy.

“What the ‘museum of tomorrow’ will be is not just a single institute, but a coral reef of small institutes that can plug in – Dezeen could have an office here, a leather upholsterer might have a craft workshop here, restaurants and pop-ups…” said Khan.

“This living ecosystem, which is reflective of the city, is possible because of this market building we’ve moved into,” he continued.

“What we’ve done is make openings, windows, and cuts through the floor and ceiling, which allow that energy to emanate out of the city and for the city’s energy to emanate inwards,” added Khan. “At the centre of it all is this enormous public space, the General Market ground floor, where anything can happen.”

A staircase takes visitors down to London’s Roman street level, to the museum’s permanent Past Time exhibition, which displays precious artefacts.

The restored brickwork walls in the subterranean space are interrupted by a six-metre window, revealing passing Thameslink trains.

A series of underground vaults that were discovered during the museum’s construction will open to visitors in spring 2027.

“This museum epitomises the idea of the primordial reflex in us to dig to find various treasures,” said Stanton Williams co-founder Paul Williams.

The architects aimed to make the qualities of the existing spaces work to the museum’s advantage, displaying delicate objects in the underground gallery and maintaining the communal feel of the market space on ground level.

“Decisions based on the building – like precious objects should be kept underground because it’s got a greater thermal inertia – loosen the straitjacket around the museum having to act like a museum in other spaces,” said Khan.

“It means some other spaces can be more market-like and have a more public-facing potential that a normal museum wouldn’t be able to do,” he continued. “The building has enabled the museum to become a different kind of museum.”

Unisex toilets were designed in a Victorian style, with decorative tiles depicting wildflowers that grew in London’s bombed-out sites.

Elsewhere in the museum is a 24-hour cafe where original interior tiles and a timber staircase were restored.

Shaw hopes the London Museum will be an inviting place that residents and tourists want to return to time and again.

“We want to be super welcoming – we don’t want to be intimidating as a museum,” said Shaw. “Some of the other museums are quite imposing buildings.”

“We want to be a destination, not just a museum, but a place for people to keep coming back to.”

Other museums recently completed in London include V&A East by O’Donnell + Tuomey and the V&A East Storehouse by Diller Scofidio + Renfro, which was given a Dezeen Award for its wayfinding design.

#9017. Vermeer expert casts doubt on authenticity of two paintings

The Love Letter: expert Adriaan Waiboer identifies “peculiar shadows and clashing colours, patterns and shapes” as indications that the painting is not by Vermeer Courtesy of Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam

Two of Johannes Vermeer’s rare paintings are not the real thing, according to Adriaan Waiboer, a former head of collections at Dublin’s National Gallery of Ireland. He is downgrading The Love Letter at Amsterdam’s Rijksmuseum and The Glass of Wine at Berlin’s Gemäldegalerie.

Although attributions are routinely questioned by art historians, what makes this case significant is that it is being done by a specialist with a deep knowledge of Vermeer. The Dutch-born art historian was responsible for caring for a Vermeer masterpiece in his own Dublin collection, Woman writing a Letter, with her Maid (around 1670-72). He was also the lead curator for the 2017-18 exhibition Vermeer and the Masters of Genre Painting at the Musée du Louvre in Paris, the National Gallery of Art in Washington, DC, and at the Dublin institution.

Waiboer has published his findings on the Rijksmuseum and Gemäldegalerie paintings in the latest issue of the Journal of Historians of Netherlandish Art.

Both The Love Letter and The Glass of Wine continue to be fully regarded as authentic Vermeers by their respective museums. The two paintings were exhibited in the pathbreaking Vermeer retrospective at the Rijksmuseum in 2023, which accepted that just 37 works are from the master’s hand.

Waiboer began his research by noting discrepancies between these two pictures and the rest of Vermeer’s oeuvre. “These initially took me by surprise but, over months of intensive analysis, grew in number and coalesced into coherent patterns,” he writes.

Relying on connoisseurship, Waiboer scrutinised the paint handling and stylistic features of the Rijksmuseum and Gemäldegalerie pictures with high-resolution images. He writes that “the human eye” may be more informative than technical research.

Waiboer says that, in The Glass of Wine, the man’s “passive demeanour towards his lover” does not mirror the suitor’s “assertive behaviour” seen in similar scenes in authentic Vermeer paintings Staatliche Museen zu Berlin, Gemäldegalerie/Christoph Schmidt

The Love Letter, which was dated 1669-70 in the Rijksmuseum exhibition, depicts a woman holding a cittern (similar to a lute). Her maid has just handed her a letter, which is apparently from a suitor. The painting lacks an early provenance, first appearing in 1892 in an Amsterdam auction. Waiboer points to its paint handling, which he describes as “marked by short, untidy brushstrokes and inelegant modelling of forms, materials and surface”. This departs from that of Vermeer’s paintings of the late 1660s and early 70s. This is particularly apparent in the facial highlights, the woman’s yellow jacket, the maid’s sleeves, the marble floor and the shadows cast by the two picture frames on the back wall.

Waiboer argues that “the crammed composition, anecdotal storytelling, peculiar shadows and clashing colours, patterns and shapes distinguish it from Vermeer’s work”. He concludes that The Love Letter is “an ambitious variation on several of Vermeer’s late works, reverberating a range of thematic, stylistic and compositional elements”. In addition, Waiboer sees ideas derived from works by Vermeer’s Dutch contemporaries, Samuel van Hoogstraten, Gerard ter Borch and Gabriel Metsu.

The Love Letter bears a purported Vermeer signature on the back wall, above the basket. Waiboer describes it as made with “conspicuously short, jerky strokes—possibly pointing toward an artist copying an example”. This suggests that the signature may have been added by another hand to mislead.

The other painting questioned by Waiboer is The Glass of Wine, which was also exhibited in the Rijksmuseum’s retrospective and is normally dated to 1659-61. It depicts a gallant young man about to offer a young woman another drink.

Waiboer argues that The Glass of Wine is simply “a pastiche”, created to imitate a Vermeer composition. He suggests the artist involved took elements from two authentic pictures: A Woman interrupted at her Music (1660-63, at the Frick Collection in New York) and A Woman with a Wineglass (1661-63, at the Herzog Anton Ulrich Museum in Braunschweig).

In The Glass of Wine, Waiboer points to differences with Vermeer’s authentic works: the carpet, compared with the more lifelike texture of that in A Woman Reading a Letter (1658-59, at the Staatliche Kunstsammlungen Dresden); the music book, compared with the more fastidiously depicted manuscript in A Woman Interrupted at Her Music; and the lion’s-head finials, again compared with the sparkling effect in the Frick painting.

Waiboer notes the man’s “passive demeanour towards his lover” in the Berlin painting does not mirror the suitor’s “assertive behaviour” in the Frick and Braunschweig works. He concludes that The Glass of Wine is “a skilful pastiche”, composed of elements derived from these two pictures, along with features from works by two other artists of the period, Ter Borch and Pieter de Hooch. However, the painter of The Glass of Wine did have a good knowledge of Vermeer’s work, so was probably someone in his studio.

In conclusion, Waiboer writes that The Love Letter and The Glass of Wine were made by different artists, who could have been active either inside or outside of Vermeer’s workshop. Whether Vermeer had studio assistants is the subject of another controversy. Until recently, it was almost universally assumed that he was a solitary artist, although the curator Marjorie Wieseman and her colleagues at the National Gallery of Art argued in 2022 that he did in fact run a studio.

The two museums that own the questioned Vermeers are taking Waiboer’s views seriously, although so far they are confident about their own attributions. Dagmar Hirschfelder, the director of the Gemäldegalerie, tells The Art Newspaper: “We will carefully examine the arguments put forward by Adriaan Waiboer.”

Hirschfelder points out that Waiboer’s assessment is based solely on a comparison of high-resolution images and a visual inspection of paintings behind glass. She adds: “No new, in-depth examination of the original picture has been carried out that takes into account technical findings and its condition. Rejecting the attribution of a work that has hitherto been regarded as securely attributed is problematic without a technically informed assessment of its condition, the development of the composition, and the techniques and materials used in its creation.” The catalogue of the 2023 exhibition is evidence of deep technical research undertaken a few years ago.

Pieter Roelofs, the head of the fine arts department at the Rijksmuseum, comments that it is “good to see continued interest in Vermeer and that his oeuvre is being questioned”. He adds that the Rijksmuseum, together with other collections, had conducted extensive research into nearly all of Vermeer’s paintings, including The Love Letter, in connection with the 2023 exhibition. “That research confirmed that The Love Letter is Vermeer’s own work,” Roelofs says.

Waiboer, now an independent scholar, is currently writing a book on Vermeer, for possible publication in 2028. The volume will examine the connections between the master’s work and two of his leading contemporaries, Ter Borch and Frans van Mieris.

#9015. 10 Signs You Might Not Really Be in Love: How to Tell the Difference

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Love can feel like navigating a choose-your-own-adventure book with half the pages missing. Are you truly in love or just caught in a wave of infatuation? Sometimes, what seems like a heart-thumping romance may be a fleeting crush.

Wondering how to tell the difference? We’ve got you! Here’s a rundown of the 10 signs you’re not really in love.

Feeling a bit puzzled about your feelings for boo? That’s pretty normal. But before you start planning your future or picking out matching Halloween costumes, you may wanna make sure it’s real love and not a case of a serious crush.

Here are some signs that you may not really be in love:

Caught up in the romance novel vibe? If you’re all about the feelings of being in love rather than who’s sharing your popcorn, it might just be that you’re smitten with the idea of love itself.

Time to check if your relationship is more about the fairy tale than the real person.

Chatting with your partner shouldn’t feel as shallow as a kiddie pool. If deep talks are tougher than pulling teeth and rarer than a unicorn, it’s a red flag.

Sticking to small talk about the weather and dinner plans suggests the emotional depth for a lasting bond might be missing.

When discussions about future plans feel as far-fetched as sci-fi adventures, they may reveal underlying doubts about the relationship’s viability.

If imagining a future together feels unrealistic or undesirable, it’s time to ask yourself why. Real love plans a future; infatuation lives for the weekend.

Remember when their sock on the floor was cute? If little quirks now make you more cranky than charmed, it might mean the love goggles are off, your feelings have shifted from affection to annoyance, and the reality check has bounced.

Love is seeing imperfections and adoring them anyway.

Feeling more at ease or more ‘yourself’ when your partner isn’t around is a telling sign. If you’re secretly throwing mini-parties when they leave the room, you need to stop and think. Real-deal love means missing their chaos when they’re gone, not celebrating the silence.

Shared values are the anchor of deep, lasting relationships. If your core values clash more than a polka dot and stripes ensemble, you’re in for a rough ride, as finding common ground could be challenging!

Lasting love grows from shared beliefs and mutual respect, not from opposing battle lines.

No respect? No future. Respect is as critical to love as air is to breathing. Without mutual respect, you might just be coexisting rather than genuinely connecting.

If you no longer admire or respect each other’s opinions and choices, sustaining a healthy relationship will be difficult.

If they’re out of sight and totally out of mind, that’s not just independence — it might be indifference. When love is real, you should long for their laugh or lame jokes when they’re away. Could it be that your emotional attachment isn’t as strong as it should be for a lasting relationship?

If your best moments are consistently away from your partner, your heart might not be in it to win it. Perhaps your relationship isn’t providing enough support or happiness.

True love enriches your life and doesn’t play second fiddle to your social circle. It’s time to evaluate where your emotional energy is invested.

Still window shopping while you’re supposedly locked down? It’s a sign you might not be all in. A love that lasts doesn’t keep a backup catalog — it’s too busy loving what it already has.

Knowing why you’re still scanning for alternatives can help you address what might be missing or unfulfilled in your relationship.

Are you genuinely in love or just in love with being in love? If you’re secretly thrilled when they’re not around, stuck in surface-level chit-chat, or dreading deep-future talks, these are cosmic signs that it’s rethink o’clock.

Don’t ignore the signals — tuning in now can save you heartache later and lead you toward a love that genuinely fulfills you.

Last medically reviewed on June 26, 2024

Picture this: you're standing at the gate for your Boston weekend trip, and the person next to you just swiped their credit card for $280 to book the exact same seat you're sitting in — a seat that cost you 7,500 Avios and maybe $5.60 in taxes. That's the British Airways Avios short-haul sweet spot in action, and once you see it, you can never unsee it. This is the redemption the ChooseFI community quietly uses to stretch their points further than almost any other domestic award. While everyone else is chasing first-class international awards (which are spectacular, don't get us wrong), this sweet spot lets you turn a modest points balance into a steady stream of nearly free regional flights — year-round, on American Airlines metal, with zero fuel surcharges. Here's the math that makes it click: A last-minute nonstop flight from New York (JFK/LGA) to Boston Logan or Los Angeles (LAX) to San Francisco typically runs anywhere from $150 to $300 in cash. You're paying that for roughly a one-hour flight — the kind of trip where by the time the flight attendant hands you a drink, you're already starting your descent. British Airways prices that same flight at a flat **7,500 Avios**. At a $200 cash fare, that's **2.67 cents per point (CPP)** — well above the standard valuation most programs offer for domestic economy. At a $300 last-minute fare, you're looking at **4 cents per point**, which is exceptional for any award program, let alone a simple domestic booking. The pricing inefficiency is hiding in plain sight: British Airways uses a **distance-based award chart**, which means short flights cost proportionally fewer points. The U.S. domestic short-haul zone (under 650 miles) sits at 7,500 Avios one-way — a price that hasn't ballooned with inflation the way cash fares have. Every time airfare spikes for a holiday weekend or a last-minute booking, your Avios redemption looks better and better. For the FI-minded traveler, this redemption is pure arbitrage: you're converting transferable points that cost you perhaps 1–1.5 cents each to earn into travel worth 2–4 cents each in real-world value. That's a 2–4x return, consistently, on routes you'd likely be flying anyway.

The magic here lives inside British Airways' distance-based award chart — and understanding why it's structured this way is the 'aha moment' that turns a confusing loyalty program into a tool you actually want to use.

Most U.S. airline programs (Delta, United, American) have largely abandoned distance-based pricing in favor of dynamic or zone-based awards that tend to price popular routes higher. British Airways never fully made that switch for partner awards. Their Avios chart still prices flights primarily by the number of miles flown between origin and destination. A flight under 650 miles costs 7,500 Avios one-way in economy — full stop. It doesn't matter if it's a Tuesday in February or the Sunday after Thanksgiving. The chart price holds.

The Partner Piece: Why You're Booking AA, Not BA

Here's the critical nuance that trips up new users: British Airways charges notoriously high fuel surcharges on its own operated flights. We're talking $300–800+ in carrier-imposed fees on top of the Avios. That would completely wipe out the value of this redemption. But when you book American Airlines-operated flights through British Airways Avios, those surcharges disappear entirely. AA does not pass fuel surcharges to partner award bookings. Your out-of-pocket cost is typically just the government taxes — often $5–15 each way.

This is the non-negotiable rule: always book AA metal through British Airways Avios, not BA-operated flights.

Avios are one of the most accessible award currencies in the ecosystem. You can transfer from four major transferable points programs at a 1:1 ratio:

Marriott Bonvoy® also transfers to Avios at a 3:1 ratio (3 Marriott points = 1 Avios), and Marriott throws in a 5,000 Avios bonus for every 60,000 Marriott points transferred. That's a less efficient path for this redemption, but worth knowing.

The 355-day booking window means you can transfer and book nearly a full year in advance — critical for holiday travel or high-demand routes.

British Airways allows open-jaw routing on Avios awards. That means you could theoretically fly into one city and out of a nearby city without paying for two separate awards — useful if you're exploring a region and want flexibility. For short domestic hops, this opens up creative itinerary options that pure point-to-point programs don't allow.

Before you touch your Avios balance, go to aa.com and run a standard flight search for your route. When the results load, look specifically for flights labeled 'Web Special' or filter by lowest MileSAAver awards. You're searching for American's own award inventory — the same inventory British Airways can see and book. If AA shows saver-level availability (the lowest award tier), British Airways will almost certainly be able to book it too.

This step saves you frustration. Don't transfer points until you've confirmed the flight you want is bookable at the saver level.

Double-check that your route qualifies for the 7,500 Avios tier by confirming it's under 650 miles. NYC to Boston is about 187 miles. LAX to SFO is about 337 miles. Both qualify easily. A quick Google search — '[City A] to [City B] flight distance miles' — gives you the straight-line distance. When in doubt, routes you'd describe as 'short regional hops' within the same metro corridor will almost always qualify.

Go to britishairways.com, log into (or create) your Executive Club account, and run an Avios award search for the same route and dates. You should see the American Airlines flight(s) appear at 7,500 Avios + a small tax amount — typically $5–$15. If the flight shows up here, you're ready to book.

Once you've confirmed availability, it's time to transfer. Here's what to do based on your points currency:

Important: Only transfer what you need. Points transferred to British Airways cannot be moved back.

Return to BA's award search (refresh if needed), select your American Airlines flight, and complete the booking. You'll pay the Avios from your balance plus the small tax amount with a credit card. You'll receive an American Airlines confirmation number, which you can use at aa.com to manage your reservation, select seats, and add TSA PreCheck or Known Traveler Numbers.

If your ideal date shows no saver inventory, try:

Let's make this concrete. It's mid-October and you want to visit a college friend in Boston for the weekend — flying out of New York's JFK on a Friday evening, returning Sunday afternoon.

You pull up Google Flights. Friday evening nonstops from JFK to BOS? The cheapest is $189. The convenient 6:30 PM departure on American Airlines is $229. Sunday afternoon return is another $199. Round-trip cash cost: $428.

You check aa.com and confirm both flights show saver-level award availability. You open British Airways' site and find:

You transfer 15,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards points to British Airways — it arrives instantly. You book both flights through BA, receive your AA confirmation numbers, and log into aa.com to select your seats.

If those flights had crept up to $300 each (not unusual around Columbus Day weekend), you'd be looking at 4 cents per point — outstanding for a domestic economy booking.

You're on a standard American Airlines narrow-body — likely a Boeing 737 or Airbus A319. It's economy, which for a 45-minute flight is entirely appropriate. You'll get a beverage service, overhead bin space, and you land at the same gate, use the same terminal, and have the same on-time performance as any other passenger on that plane. The difference is that they paid $229 and you paid $5.60 plus some points that cost you roughly $150 to earn through everyday spending.

That's the FI mindset applied to travel: same experience, radically different cost.

Do This: Book Up to 355 Days Out for Holiday Travel BA's booking window opens 355 days in advance, and American releases its best saver space early. If you're targeting Thanksgiving weekend, Christmas, or a peak summer Friday, set a calendar reminder to search at the 355-day mark. Award seats on popular routes at peak times go fast.

Do This: Use the Open-Jaw Rule Creatively BA allows open-jaw routing on Avios awards. If you're flying into NYC but want to return from a different airport — say JFK inbound and EWR outbound — you may be able to structure this as a single open-jaw award rather than two separate bookings. Worth exploring for multi-city weekend trips.

Avoid This: Booking BA-Operated Flights with This Strategy This cannot be overstated — BA's own flights carry $300–800+ in carrier-imposed surcharges. If you accidentally book a British Airways codeshare or BA-metal flight instead of an American Airlines-operated flight, you'll owe hundreds in fees. Always verify the operating carrier before confirming. Look for 'Operated by American Airlines' in the booking details.

Avoid This: Transferring Points Before Confirming Availability Points transferred to British Airways are one-way and permanent. Never transfer until you have eyes on the specific flight, date, and saver availability you want. The 30-second search on BA's site before transferring is non-negotiable.

Do This: Keep Your Account Active Avios expire after 36 months of account inactivity. If you accumulate Avios for a future trip, make sure to earn or redeem at least a small amount every three years. Even a small shopping portal purchase through the BA Executive Club keeps your balance alive.

Do This: Stack with Other Short Hops Think about recurring trips in your life — quarterly visits to family, annual conferences, weekend trips to a nearby city. This sweet spot isn't just for one redemption; it's a repeatable system. A modest Avios balance of 30,000–45,000 points could cover three to six regional roundtrips per year.

Why distance-based pricing changes the domestic flying equation

Most U.S. airline loyalty programs use region-based or dynamic pricing for award flights, charging the same number of miles whether you fly 200 miles or 2,000. British Airways uses distance-based pricing instead, which means shorter flights cost dramatically fewer Avios. Since BA is a Oneworld partner with American Airlines, you can use Avios to book AA-operated nonstop domestic flights. The result: a flight that AA might price at 12,500-25,000 miles can be booked for just 7,500 Avios through BA. This is one of the most reliable and repeatable sweet spots in travel rewards.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Sign up for a free BA Executive Club account at ba.com. This is where your Avios balance lives and where you will search and book award flights on American Airlines.

Transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards, Amex Membership Rewards, Capital One Miles, or Citi ThankYou Points to your BA Executive Club account. Transfers are typically instant. Only transfer what you need for a specific booking.

On the BA website, search for your route using the "Book with Avios" option. Look for American Airlines-operated nonstop flights. Filter results to find flights coded as AA with available Avios seats.

Confirm the flight is pricing at 7,500 Avios (under 1,151 miles) or 10,000 Avios (1,151-2,000 miles). Check that taxes and fees are the expected $5.60. If prices seem high, try different dates or check that you selected a nonstop flight.

Book the flight and add your AAdvantage number to the reservation so you receive any applicable elite benefits. You will receive a confirmation from British Airways, and the ticket will also appear in your AA account.

Yes. British Airways and American Airlines are both Oneworld alliance members, so you can use BA Avios to book award seats on AA-operated flights. You book directly through the British Airways website (ba.com) and search for AA flight numbers.

Flights under 1,151 miles cost 7,500 Avios each way in economy. Flights between 1,151-2,000 miles cost 10,000 Avios. Flights between 2,001-3,000 miles cost 12,500 Avios. The value proposition is strongest on the shortest flights where the Avios cost is lowest.

Not on domestic American Airlines flights. The typical fee is just $5.60 each way. High fuel surcharges only apply when booking British Airways-operated long-haul flights, not when using Avios on partner airlines like AA domestically.

Chase Ultimate Rewards, Amex Membership Rewards, Capital One Miles, and Citi ThankYou Points all transfer to British Airways Avios. Transfer ratios are 1:1 from Chase, Amex, and Capital One. Transfers are typically instant or within 24 hours.

This sweet spot was practically designed for the ChooseFI beginner — someone who has their first transferable points card (a Chase Sapphire Preferred, an Amex Gold, or a Bilt card) and wants to make a real, tangible redemption without navigating complex routing rules or praying for elusive premium cabin availability.

Minimum to get started: You need at least 7,500 Avios (or transferable points to convert) for a one-way. For a round-trip, 15,000. Most sign-up bonuses — even modest ones — cover multiple round-trips with this sweet spot.

Who this is NOT for: If you're flying coast-to-coast (NYC to LAX is over 2,400 miles — a different, higher Avios tier), this specific pricing won't apply. This sweet spot is purpose-built for short hops under 650 miles. It's also not the move if you already have AA elite status and can snag cheap upgrades — but for the rest of us, it's perfect.

This redemption earns a **5/5 for beginner friendliness** — and that rating is fully deserved. Let's be specific about why. The hardest part of most award bookings is finding available seats and navigating confusing partner systems. This one simplifies both: you're searching a major U.S. airline's (AA) domestic saver inventory, which is widely available on popular short-haul routes year-round. You're not hunting for a specific aircraft with lie-flat seats or hoping a single partner releases one business class seat. Domestic economy saver space is genuinely accessible. The booking process itself is two websites: aa.com to check availability, britishairways.com to book. Neither requires a phone call, neither has complicated routing rules for simple one-way or round-trip domestic bookings, and the transfer from Chase or Amex is instant. **The three things to get right:** 1. **Confirm saver availability on AA before transferring** — This habit protects you from the only real risk (irreversible point transfers). 2. **Verify the operating carrier is American Airlines, not British Airways** — One glance at 'Operated by' in the booking details handles this. 3. **Keep your BA Executive Club account active** — Set a reminder to log in or earn at least once every 36 months so your Avios don't expire. That's genuinely the whole checklist. If you've never booked an award flight before, this is the redemption to start with. You'll build the muscle memory — search, confirm, transfer, book — in about 20 minutes, and you'll have a nearly free flight to show for it. Welcome to travel rewards.

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

Using British Airways Avios for short domestic nonstop flights on American Airlines is one of the most practical and repeatable sweet spots in travel rewards. At just 7,500 Avios each way with $5.60 in fees, it dramatically undercuts what AA charges through its own program. With four major transfer partners feeding BA Avios, this sweet spot is accessible from virtually any points-earning strategy. Whether you are booking a quick NYC-Chicago hop or an LA-San Francisco shuttle, BA Avios should be your first look for short-haul domestic flights.

#9013. Five key projects by Dezeen Awards emerging architect of the year Kuma&Elsa

This year Kuma&Elsa was named emerging architect of the year at the Dezeen Awards. Here, they select five projects that demonstrate the ethos of the studio.

Led by Japanese architect Shohei Kuma and French-Spanish urban designer Elsa Escobedo, Kuma&Elsa has completed a wide variety of projects from their bases in France and Japan.

“We believe it is important not to impose a common consistency across our projects,” Kuma told Dezeen.

“Every project is unique, shaped by a one-off combination of site and client. Preserving that uniqueness requires an open mind. Personally, I quickly lose interest when things are planned in advance.”

“That said, there are certain topics, many of which are shared by our generation, such as feminism, the care for natural resources and a shared public space, that interest us on a personal level, and I imagine they find their way into our work,” added Escobedo.

“We try to approach them with a sense of joy.”

Although they have already designed a wide range of projects, from installations to houses and public toilets, the duo would like to work on more varied schemes and unusual projects, along with completing their own, long-running renovation.

“It would be nice to actually finish this self-renovation project at some point…” said Escobedo.

“More seriously, I’d love to experiment with the reuse of materials on a larger scale, or in a European context, working with European craftspeople.”

“I would love to work on overlooked building types and uses, especially those that have little place in architectural history and attract few expectations,” added Kuma. “Designing a toilet pavilion for the Expo, a building type that nobody expects to become architecture, is one example.”

Along with the variety in projects, both architects agreed that the wide range of daily activities is what they most enjoy about being an architect.

“The variety, the diversity,” said Escobedo, when asked about her favourite part about being an architect.

“One day you’re on a construction site with incredible Japanese carpenters, the next you’re discussing a detail with your favourite thermal engineer, the following week you’re taking part in a conversation with colleagues you admire, before finding yourself struggling to install the plumbing and tiles in a shower because you had the brilliant idea of taking on a self-build project.”

Kuma also added that he enjoys the intensity of working on site.

“The construction site,” he said. “Nothing is more stressful or demanding, with all the struggles involving people and money. Yet every time I see a building taking shape, I feel glad I chose architecture. There is something addictive about it.”

Read on to find out five key projects by Dezeen Award-winning studio Kuma&Elsa, as described by the duo:

“The client’s childhood home, a traditional Japanese house, has an engawa gallery open to the garden. The new residence occupies the top two floors of a building owned by the client. She, along with her two sons and their families, will move into three apartments located on the sixth and seventh floors.

“At the centre of each apartment, we inserted a hut-like volume that gathers the quieter rooms: a small living room and the bedrooms. In the space carved out around it emerges an intermediate zone – an engawa that serves both as a place to stay and as a passage.

“Balcony, engawa, and hut thus form three spatial layers that resonate with the childhood home. The structure consists of Y-shaped modules made of lightweight steel sections and bracing cables, typically used in shelving systems.

“These modules are arranged two by two in mirrored pairs along a regular grid, with occasional inversions. From these new dwellings, one can look down across the street at the engawa of the childhood home. This project does not seek to nostalgically replicate that memory-laden place, but rather to build a new home nourished by the memories of the old one.”

“One water is a bathing and rest pavilion for the Osaka World Expo 2025. Toilets are at first glance a pragmatic facility, dedicated to human physiology. But they are also intimately linked to contemporary issues such as the use of natural resources and gender.

“One water uses the path of rainfall on the accessible roof and its subsequent accumulation to create encounters between water and the public, and contribute to the supply of the toilets.

“The design of the pavilion allows for the reuse of materials and structural components, and makes no gender distinction in the toilets, because, after all, ‘we are all fish in one water’.”

House by the temple, Saitama Prefecture, Japan, 2024

“The house is opposite the entrance of a temple that is surrounded by a park of ancient trees and a wall, as if it belongs to another world. Reflecting this closed composition, we designed the house as an everyday world for a family.

“The main building is located at the back of the plot and has a quarter-circle plan to reduce its own shadow. The street facade is a single-storey hut, which creates a continuity between the open space of the park and the garden of the house.

“On the ground floor, the park is the backdrop to the house. On the first floor, each room offers distant views of the temple, like an observatory.”

“A daily public space in a residential area. We create a plaza in a small residential area where human life is still at human scale.

“The house is like the background that forms the square. The composition consists of various couples: the smooth black mortar of the outer wall and the rough crushed black basalt ground, the emerald entrance hut and the crape myrtle tree with white flowers, the interior spaces and the outside square.”

Water Flower Courtyard, Montpellier, France, 2019

“The life of a flower is short: we wanted to express the fragility of a concentrated life from flowering to dispersal. This project was open to the public for a week during the Montpellier architecture festival Festival des Architectures Vives in June 2019.

“Eighteen lightweight units made of two-millimetre-thick aluminium sheets are laid out together as a forest.

“The tube is a vase that contains water and peony flowers, the bowl contains water and slate stones. All structures are self-supporting and their stability works as in a roly-poly toy. After a few days, petals start falling on the surface of the water.”

Visa has refreshed its global identity for the first time since 2021, debuting a new flexible system that spotlights progress. From life's intimate moments to its grand celebrations, Visa has been a companion to many, but how do you distil that into an identity already so iconic?

The best rebrands aren't always about extreme metamorphoses; sometimes it's about capturing your brand essence to reinforce what the audience already knows. Unpretentious and wonderfully simple, Vias's new refresh is a prime example of how scaled-back branding can build authentic heart.

Created by Base Design, Visa's new strategy was shaped by people and the notion that progress looks different for everyone. Whether it's buying a coffee for the commute or scoring tickets for a once-in-a-lifetime gig, Visa is the quiet companion to these slice-of-life moments.

“When you’re working with a brand as iconic as Visa, the challenge isn’t recognition. It’s relevance,” says Min Lew, managing partner and executive creative director at Base Design. “Our ambition was to build on Visa’s extraordinary equity while giving it a renewed sense of energy and expression, one that feels as relevant to the next generation as it does to the generations who have grown up with it.”

The refreshed branding centres around three visual elements – a new symbol, a signature graphic device, and a bespoke typeface. Derived from Visa's iconic wordmark, the new “V” brand symbol serves as a shorthand identifier and features Visa's slick wingtip design. A contemporary development, it modernises the brand without replacing its already strong identity.

A new hero graphic device derived from the bands of the original Visa logo brings a sense of dynamism to the identity, signalling momentum and progress. “The most powerful identities are built on simple ideas with extraordinary depth,” says Min.

"With Visa, we translated their role of championing everyday progress into a distinctive graphic expression. More than a framing device, the hero graphic device brings movement, direction, and possibility to the identity. This simple gesture becomes the foundation for a visual language that can be energetic at a global sporting event, confident and bold in a B2B environment, or vibrant and elevated for affluent audiences. Each expression is distinct, yet unmistakably Visa.”

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

Finally, there's the addition of Visa Sans, a new typeface created in collaboration with Displaay Type Foundry. Taking direct influence from the Visa wordmark, the new typeface expands the brand's heritage into a concise, modern font, with authoritative geometric letterforms for legibility at scale and rounded forms to add a distinctly human warmth.

The identity also spreads into sonic branding, motion, and iconography, along with dedicated sub-identities such as Visa Infinite. To encourage playfulness while maintaining a sense of consistency, Base Design created three levels of expression. "A core identity for everyday communications, an extended version for more expressive storytelling, and bespoke “stretched” treatments that push the visual language further for highly visible experiential applications and marquee cultural activations."

In everyday life, Visa is often a subtle player. This flexible new identity doesn't scream for attention; it radiates authority and soul, shining in its unpretentious simplicity. “We have deep trust and recognition as a brand," says Visa’s chief marketing officer, Frank Cooper III. "This refresh gives us an opportunity to build on that, making Visa feel fresh and relevant for the next generation while staying true to what people know and value about us.”

#9011. Say What? 7 Tips to Unclog Your Blocked Ears

Earwax buildup, allergies, infections, or changes in air pressure might be behind your clogged ears. There are many easy ways to get relief at home.

Whether it’s from a cold, allergies, or changes in air pressure, blocked ears can disrupt your day-to-day activities and even cause discomfort. Thankfully, there are several effective methods to help unclog your ears and restore your hearing. Listen up!

Why are my ears clogged?

Clogging can happen either on the inside or the outside of your eardrum. Here are the most common ways your ears can get blocked:

  • Earwax in the outer ear helps prevent particles and excess water from entering the middle ear. However, if earwax builds up too much outside the eardrum, it can cause a blockage.
  • If you’ve been swimming recently, some water might be stuck in your ear canal, pushing against your eardrum. When that water hangs around too long, it can lead to a swimmer’s ear, an outer ear infection.
  • Sinus infections, ear infections, and Eustachian tube dysfunction can pressure your eardrum’s inner side.
  • Allergies can cause uncomfortable inflammation and congestion in your ears. Your sinuses, throat, and ears are connected, so when you feel stuffed up and sniffly, your inner ear feels the pain too.
  • Changes in air pressure, like when you fly, can cause uncomfortable ear pressure.

Best clogged ear remedies

1. Pop and unclog

The easiest way to unclog your ears is by “popping” them. Just pinch your nose shut, seal your lips, and gently blow. This simple technique, known as the Valsalva maneuver, won’t clear earwax or fluid but is a common trick people use on planes.

2. Swallow, yawn, or chew

The Eustachian tubes connect your middle ear to the back of your throat. They briefly open when you swallow, yawn, or chew. Altitude changes can cause these tubes to close, but chewing gum or yawning can help reopen them. Alternatively, you can try the Toynbee maneuver, where you hold your nose and swallow.

3. Ear drops

Over-the-counter (OTC) ear drops can soften and dissolve excess earwax. If you prefer a DIY approach, warm a small amount of mineral oil and use an eye dropper to apply a few drops into your ear for a few minutes.

Pro tip: Baby oil or olive oil can also be used, but make sure it’s not too hot. Additionally, diluted hydrogen peroxide drops can be helpful.

4. Warmth and gravity

To loosen up clogged earwax, use a warm, damp washcloth as a compress. Lie down with the clogged ear facing down against the heated washcloth. Gravity and heat will help the earwax move along more easily.

5. Hit the steam room

Steam can help drain sinuses and alleviate pressure in your inner ear. Close the bathroom door, let the hot shower run for a while, and then luxuriate with deep, cleansing breaths. 

6. Take allergy medication

Because your throat, sinuses, and ears are interconnected, any sickness affecting your sinuses or throat can also impact your ears.

Over-the-counter antihistamines, decongestants, or nasal sprays can relieve sniffles, coughs, and ear discomfort.

7. Rinse away the gunk

Rinsing your nasal passages with a medication-free saline solution can help reduce congestion and clear out mucus that might be causing ear blockage. You can also consider investing in a nasal irrigation system for more thorough mucus clearing.

When to see your doctor

Have you been unable to unclog your ears for a few days, or are you experiencing severe pain, fever, dizziness, hearing loss, fluid discharge, or unusual odor? If so, it’s crucial to contact your healthcare provider promptly. These symptoms may indicate an infection that needs medical attention.

What not to do when you have clogged ears

  • Cotton swabs: Q-tips and other cotton swabs to remove earwax can push it further into your ear canal, so don’t do it. 
  • Candling: Ear candles might seem like a fun party trick, but there’s no science to prove they work, and they’ve been shown to cause injuries.
  • Sprays: Decongestant nasal sprays can be helpful, but using them too long can lead to rebound congestion.
  • Drying solutions: A few drops of rubbing alcohol or a mixture of one part vinegar and one part alcohol can help dry out the ears when you have a swimmer’s ear. However, doing this regularly can lead to irritation.

Takeaway

Clogged ears are often caused by earwax buildup, allergies, infections, or changes in air pressure. You can use over-the-counter or DIY ear drops, irrigation kits, or warm compresses to unblock your ears. Antihistamines or nasal sprays can also help relieve clogs caused by allergies.

PSA: Consult a healthcare provider if your blocked ears are painful or at-home remedies don’t work.

#9010. Rare Marie Antoinette ‘Breast Bowl’ Hammers for $2.47 M. in Paris, Surpassing Top Estimate

One of the last known “Breast Bowls” still in private hands that once belonged to Queen Marie Antoinette has just hammered for €2.25 million ($2.47 million), or €2,945 million with fees ($3.23 million), at the Coutau-Begarie & Associés evening auction in Paris’s Hôtel Drouot, beating its high estimate of €2 million ($2.19 million).

Legend has it that this series of 18th-century porcelain bowls, made by the Royal Sèvres manufacturers, was modeled after the ill-fated French queen’s real breasts. While no documented proof of such a legend exists, the so-called “jatte-téton” or “nipple bowls,” painted in fleshy light pink with an areola and nipple at the tip, do have a surrealistic, convincingly realistic quality, despite a too-perfectly circular shape. Related Articles Auction of Nazi-Looted Torah Fragment Canceled After Outcry and Israeli Government Intervention Can AI Help Identify the Sitters in Historical Portraits?

Made in 1787, the bowl in question was in fact inspired by ancient Greek mastos, or breast-shaped drinking cups used at banquets dating back to the 6th century BC. It is one of four highly prized jatte-tétons delivered that year and in 1788, destined for the royal “pleasure dairy” in Rambouillet, near Versailles, that King Louis XVI gifted to Marie Antoinette. There, per the fashion of the time, nobility would gather to socialize and taste an assortment of fine milk, cream, and cheese delicacies prepared for them.

The rare breast bowl comes from the collection of French dealer Claude Meyer, who passed away in November 2025. His children happened upon it while going through boxes of storage, and learned that their late father, whose Paris gallery closed in the 1990s, had never offered it for sale. It is unclear how Meyer acquired the piece, which is known to have once belonged to the French Marquise de Chanaleilles.

Three of the four breast bowls made in 1787 and 1788 for the queen’s royal dairy dishes are housed in public collections today, including two at the Musée de Sèvres and one at the Museo Duca di Martina in Naples. The bowl that sold tonight is the last of that specific series. They are “the most celebrated and the most extravagant shape of the porcelain service,” by the royal Sèvres manufactory for the queen’s dairy, notes the auction house in its description.

With the bowl comes an intricately carved tripod stand decorated with goat heads in relief, as seen above. Indeed, the breast bowls require a pedestal to hold them upside down, as it were, so as to contain the milk and cream they were meant to serve.

Speaking to Le Journal des Arts about the bowl, auctioneer Alexandre de La Forest Divonne observed: “It has become something of a symbol of the queen; it is truly a totem.”

Senior vice president Karen Robinson discusses the value of open conversation about AI.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Since its debut in December 1982, Adobe has seen a multitude of evolutions, but at its core, it remains a brand committed to empowering everyone to create. But with the increasing presence of AI in Adobe's products, some users are anxious that their original artwork is at risk of AI theft.

To dissect these growing anxieties, I sat down with Karen Robinson, Senior Vice President and Deputy General Counsel, Intellectual Property and Litigation at Adobe. Together, we discussed how Adobe is protecting its creatives and the importance of open discussion when it comes to AI.

I think there are two aspects to this that we've been trying to focus on. There's the input, which is the training part – what kind of data AI needs in order to be able to generate images. And then there's the output. In the United States in particular, these decisions on input are being decided in court, and it's very difficult for any individual company to influence how they decide the law.

What we're hearing from creatives is they're concerned about being pushed out of their own market, so we've tried to lean in on the output side. There's nothing that protects a visual artist who has a distinctive style from having somebody knock it off and profit off of their work.

You don't have to wait to figure out where AI is developing to know that creatives need to be protected

That's why we have Content Credentials. This is a standard that we helped create; it's open source and free to the world so other companies can incorporate it into their products. There are 5,000 companies now and counting that do, and it covers everything from platforms to cameras. It allows a creative to have more control. They can mark their stuff as "do not train", something that Adobe voluntarily acknowledges and respects.

There's an opportunity for governments to step in and make that mandatory across the board, because it doesn't matter if one or two companies do it; if there are 3,000 companies that don't do it. What you really want to make sure is that when a creative says, "This is my art, this is mine," and labels whether you're okay training on it or not, they control that, and it carries from platform to platform. Right now, a platform can choose to just strip it out, and it doesn't matter what you've indicated as a creator about how you want your art to be treated. Content Credentials is one way we've been trying to prevent that.

We're sensitive to the concerns around the First Amendment and the idea of free speech. We should have the ability to train, and I don't mean AI training; I mean as an artist. I took studio arts, and I had to practice Pointillism. I'm not trying to become Seurat, so I should be able to imitate that style in certain settings and not have to worry about liability.

But if I'm imitating it, putting it out on the market and knocking out an actual artist, that's a very different thing. If I'm commercialising and profiting off of their work that I have copied, even if it's AI-generated, there should be protection for those artists. You don't have to wait to figure out where AI is developing to know that creatives need to be protected from output.

The way that we look at AI is very different at Adobe. We're looking at it as a tool. Yes, of course, you could go to Firefly and put "unicorn jumping over a rainbow," and you're going to get a result. I don't think that level of interaction is going to give rise to art. That's not me being an artist. I can't claim copyright over that, nor should I. We just see AI as a natural extension of the tools that we are offering.

I often think it's the exact same argument that people made about cameras. When photography first came out, people were like, "Oh, you're not doing anything special, you're just clicking a button." We think of AI as a tool in the hands of artists, not as a thing in and of itself. That is how we look at it and incorporate it into our products.

When we think about our creatives, there is a spectrum. There are, of course, some people who are like, "I'm an artist, and I don't want to touch AI." You can use Photoshop or Illustrator and never have to worry about that. Then we have a spectrum where people say, "I want to use it for ideation," all the way to, "I want to partner with AI to create something that I have in my mind that I might not have otherwise been able to do." We really want to empower everybody in that spectrum, and then make sure that in using those tools, they are not losing the right to get the kind of protection that their art should be entitled to.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

At the end of the day, Adobe has been around for 45 years, in large part because we continue to innovate and we offer a product that people value and trust. Anytime you are talking about open source, you have to start worrying about security issues. That is certainly the case with ArtCraft and other open source offerings.

I won't say that anybody is excited about the fact that someone is trying to profit off of the hundreds of millions or billions of dollars over 45 years that Adobe has invested in its products and employees. But we also know that at our core, there are a lot of other products that people could use. We have faced competition in the past and will continue to do so. The way that we have typically responded to that is to just continue innovating. But that doesn't mean that we ignore that we have intellectual property and rights that come with that.

I would invite people to engage with it. I'm not saying this isn't already the case, but I wonder if the folks who are particularly resistant to it have taken the time to fully engage with it and view it as an extension of their creativity. You may have people who say, "Absolutely, I played around with it, and I hate it." That's fair. But I think there are an awful lot of people who haven't actually really engaged with it to get a sense of what it is.

The reality is that AI is here. It just is. What we've been trying to do is hear from communities: what are the issues, challenges, or problems they see? The only way that we're going to be able to actually engage and maybe even address some of those challenges is through dialogue, rather than just saying, "I don't want AI ever." AI is here, and I think all of us recognise that it is not going away.

Art is fundamentally tied to humanity in a way that we just can't separate.

We want to engage. Whether it's Congress or Parliament, we're walking into spaces and trying to represent what we're hearing from our creatives. The more we hear, the more we can be a voice, because otherwise you can just be seen as "another company." But as a company that has been built on creatives for the last 45 years, it is meaningful to us.

Firstly, a universe in which AI replaces folks? I just don't see it. Art is fundamentally tied to humanity in a way that we just can't separate. Secondly, how does that benefit anybody? It doesn't benefit society as a whole, and certainly doesn't benefit companies like Adobe, who are so tied to their creatives.

Summing it up, I would say: play with it a little bit more, and also share. Come and have the conversations around it and see if there isn't an opportunity for guidance, guardrails, and help. Heck, you don't have to talk to us about it – talk to your regulators, talk to your legislators, let them hear your voice, because your voice needs to be part of the discussion. Right now, I feel like the folks who are so anti-AI often just aren't engaging in the discussion, and I think it would be a shame for people who have legitimate concerns and issues to not be heard as part of this conversation.

#9008. Are Tangerines Good for You? 5 Health Benefits You Might Love

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Tangerines are not just tasty — they’re a powerhouse of nutrients. Packed with tangy flavor and vibrant orange color, these citrus delights offer a host of health benefits. From boosting your immune system to rejuvenating your skin, tangerines are nutrient-rich allies for your well-being. Let’s delve into their nutritional profile and discover why they’re a smart addition to your diet.

Tangerines are nutritional powerhouses. Here’s what each of these little champs pack under their orange belts:

Tangerines are teeny cousins of the orange but with a thinner, easier-to-peel skin. They boast a sweet and juicy flavor and pack a ton of vitamins, particularly vitamin C, as well as minerals like potassium, antioxidants, and dietary fiber.

These tiny bursts of sunshine have many benefits that can significantly enhance your health. Here’s why you might want to make tangerines a regular part of your diet:

Tangerines are loaded with vitamin C, turning them into tiny, tasty guardians for your health. This crucial vitamin supercharges your immune system by enhancing the function and effectiveness of white blood cells, which are essential for fighting off pathogens and infections. By improving the activity and response of these cells, vitamin C helps your body combat a wide range of infections more effectively.

Therefore, regular consumption of these mini-oranges satisfies your taste buds and boosts your body’s defense mechanisms — a win-win!

Want that glow? Tangerines have got you covered. They’re high in potassium, a real game-changer for regulating hydration and balancing fluid levels in your skin cells. This essential mineral keeps your skin cells plump and hydrated, warding off pesky, dry, dull patches.

Plus, potassium supports the removal of toxins and wastes, which means clearer, more radiant skin.

Tangerines are also a fantastic source of vitamin A, which strengthens the outer layer of your skin, smoothing out wrinkles and reducing fine lines. Along with vitamin C, it’s a potent antioxidant, protecting your skin from the damaging and aging effects of free radicals.

Are you having tummy troubles? Tangerines can help with a fiber boost that keeps things moving smoothly along your digestive tract.

These zesty little superheroes are your gut’s new best friends. They’re loaded with fiber that bulks up and softens things down there, making your bathroom visits smooth and speedy. This fruity fix helps manage everything from irregular pit stops to those bloated bleurgh days.

Fiber also balances your gut flora, promoting a healthy microbial environment in your intestines. This balance is crucial for optimal digestion, nutrient absorption, and immune function.

So, grab a tangerine to remedy your belly blues next time your gut feels out of whack.

Tangerines are a dynamo when it comes to battling serious health baddies like cancer and heart disease. These little orange wonders are loaded with flavonoids, natural compounds that help with heart health and cancer prevention.

Flavonoids help relax the blood vessels, lowering blood pressure levels and reducing the strain on your heart. This helps keep your ticker ticking smoothly and reduces the risk of cardiovascular diseases like heart attacks and strokes.

But wait, there’s more! When it comes to cancer, flavonoids mess with the bad guys — cancer cells — stopping them from multiplying and spreading their nonsense around your body.

Keep your peepers sharp with a dose of vitamin A from tangerines. This essential nutrient and compounds like beta-carotene shield your eyes from age-related issues and support healthy vision. It plays a key role in creating rhodopsin, a protein in your eyes that allows you to see in low-light conditions.

Munching on tangerines helps keep your night vision in superhero shape and supports overall eye function, keeping your peepers sharp and responsive.

Furthermore, tangerines contain other essential eye health nutrients, like lutein and zeaxanthin. These antioxidants are found in high concentrations in the retina, where they help filter blue light and prevent oxidative damage, further protecting the eyes from conditions like cataracts.

Sure, tangerines are delish and make your taste buds do a happy dance, but they’re also packed with nutrients that can seriously amp up your well-being.

From giving your immune system a high-five to keeping your heart beating like a healthy drum, tangerines are basically wellness wrapped in a bright orange peel. So, go grab one and make it your main squeeze!
