#9007. Biscuit-tin lids, horse brasses and scrap metal form sculptural V&A Christmas tree by Burberry

Fashion brand Burberry‘s chief creative officer Daniel Lee worked with artist Ann Carrington to create a Christmas tree sculpture for the Victoria & Albert Museum, made from “memories, traditions and little treasures.”

The 16-foot (4.8-metre) tree, which was unveiled this week, sits in the entrance hall of the Victoria & Albert Museum (VA’s) South Kensington location and was designed to celebrate craft and creativity.

“This collaboration with Ann is a celebration of creativity and what better place to showcase this than the V&A?” Lee said. “It’s one of my favourite museums and a constant source of inspiration to me.”

Lee and Carrington made the tree from old money boxes, biscuit and sweet-tin lids, trinket dishes, silver trays, horse brasses and embossed plates, which were turned into rosettes and ribbons and attached to a metal frame.

The tree, which was made as part of Burberry‘s 170th anniversary celebrations, also features ribbons and bows made of scrap metal.

According to Lee, he and Carrington made the sculpture from “memories, traditions and little treasures. Objects and materials that most people would overlook.”

Carrington added that the design was inspired by the ritual of getting old Christmas decorations out of storage in time for the festive season.

“We wanted to capture that magical moment when you retrieve the battered old box of Christmas decorations from the loft, sift through the faded party bows and tattered tinsel accumulated through the generations and begin the joyful ritual of dressing the tree,” she said.

“I’m always drawn to work that’s handmade, and Ann is a master of her craft,” Lee said of the collaboration.

As well as the tree, the V&A will also be showing The Burberry Trench: Crafting an Icon, a display that traces the history of the trench coat. Burberry has a multi-year partnership with the museum and is set to open The Burberry Gallery at the South Kensington location in 2028.

Lee has previously unveiled an archive-inspired logo for Burberry, and a few years ago, the brand revealed its redesigned London flagship store.

#9006. Batima Zaurbekova’s Textiles Meld Traditional Kazakh Techniques with Modernist Influences, Defying Easy Categorization

How does an artist sustain five decades of artistic production while remaining faithful to her cultural heritage? For Batima Zaurbekova, one of Kazakhstan’s most respected artists, the answer seems to be an unrelenting commitment to her craft. “You can’t be lazy,” the 80-year-old artist told me during a recent conversation.

That maxim is borne out in “Threads of Heritage,” a retrospective of more than 80 works at the Abylkhan Kasteyev National Museum of Arts in Almaty, Kazakhstan. Her largest exhibition to date, it features the textiles she is known for as well as drawings and paintings. Curated by Alina Fedorovich, a curator at the Museum of Moscow, the exhibition traces a career in which tapestry becomes both a repository of cultural memory and a vehicle for artistic reinvention. Related Articles 3,600-Year-Old Bronze Age City Discovered in Northeast Kazakhstan Keira Knightley's Emerald-Green 'Atonement' Gown Heads to Christie's

Rooted in traditional Kazakh textiles, her practice is also shaped by the influences of modernist painting and music, moving fluidly between abstraction and figuration and in turn, defying easy categorization. Her tapestries hold seemingly disparate influences, transforming traditional motifs into a distinct visual language. Ornamental Rug (1969), for example, revives motifs associated with horses, spiritual symbolism, and petroglyphs depicting mountain goats. Completed just after her graduation and the earliest work in the exhibition, Ornamental Rug provides a recognizable reference to the country’s landscape via the distinctive horns of the wild argali, a local mountain goat, while distilling these forms into rhythmic, stylized arrangements. The work’s title foregrounds the relationship between ornament and abstraction, suggesting how decorative forms can become a vehicle for modernist experimentation.

Zaurbekova grew up in the mountainous Zhambyl region of Kazakhstan, where textile-making was part of everyday life. She remembers watching older women create syrmak, traditional felt rugs, and kurak-korpe, patchwork quilts meaning “stitched from scraps.” Neighbors gathered to work, sing, cook, and share food, embodying the Kazakh tradition of asar, in which a community joins forces to help a household undertake a task, be it making a carpet or building a home.

Textile-making was as much a social practice as a technical one, transmitting skills and cultural knowledge across generations. This collective spirit is evoked in In the Yurt (1985), a weaving in which a maternal figure presides over the dastarkhan, the table prepared for guests. The yurt, a traditional felt dwelling associated with Kazakh nomadic life, becomes a symbol of hospitality, family, and belonging. Its ornaments merge with the surrounding figures, establishing a visual language equally rooted in the formal and the domestic.

In her youth, Zaurbekova had alternative ambitions for herself. “I really loved music, so I wanted to become a musician,” she recalled. However, her seamstress mother encouraged her to pursue painting instead. She is equally accomplished in oil painting and tapestry, and occasionally the same image is translated in both mediums.

Nevertheless, music has remained central to Zaurbekova’s life and practice, in which her visual compositions are animated by repetition, variation, and rhythm—the basic structure of music. This way of working is best observed in one gallery showing three works, each titled Composition and made in 1980, 2019, and 2024. Their stained-glass aesthetic, contrasting color planes, and rhythmic linear forms evoke Henri Matisse’s celebrated “Jazz” series. Undulating figures and vegetal motifs merge within an ornamental field, dissolving the distinction between figure and ground.

“Threads of Heritage” is being exhibited in dialogue with the museum’s collection of Kazakh decorative and applied art. Traditional felt objects, carpets, and ornaments establish the historical context out which Zaurbekova’s work emerges, while the installation reinforces the relationship between inherited forms and contemporary expression. Here, custom-built walls reference the architecture of the Khoja Ahmed Yasawi Mausoleum, an important historical monument whose forms recur in the artist’s imagery, like the monumental Antiquity (1993). The display also evokes the balbal, ancient stone monuments that connect contemporary life with earlier cultures.

The exhibition’s largest gallery showcases Zaurbekova’s technical mastery and evolving visual language. Each tapestry offers a dazzling array of color that boggles the mind. How, exactly, does she coax such subtle gradations from a seemingly limited collection of threads? “Selecting the right colors is a big part of the work—and it takes me a long time,” Zaurbekova explained. During the Soviet period, artists often dyed threads by hand, painstakingly creating transitions from darker to lighter shades. Although commercially produced threads from Belarus expanded her palette in the 1990s, Zaurbekova has continued to experiment, combining those threads and ones she has dyed to create colors all her own. “Kazakhstan, our land, is very rich, and this is represented in the rich colors of my work,” she told me.

Zaurbekova’s textiles are woven over several weeks to multiple months, and the artist still works for up to 18 hours a day. The vertical threads form the foundation of a given work, she explained, while horizontal threads of different colors construct the image. Through subtle variations in their combinations, Zaurbekova achieves tonal effects that can make woven surfaces appear almost painted. She is also deft at making alasha, a traditional yet simple Kazakh carpet.

Rather than presenting national identity as a fixed collection of symbols, her compositions transform familiar motifs through color and pattern. In keeping these traditions alive, Zaurbekova said she thinks “all of my work reflects our nationality and national pride.” Kazakhstan (1977) depicts themes of agriculture and collective labor. To make it, Zaurbekova used threads sourced from a Kazakh carpet manufacturer, working within the limitations of an existing palette to achieve subtle distinctions of tone. Her exacting yet delicate manipulation of the threads’ colors gives the woven surface a gentle vibration and shimmering quality. A work like this makes visible the precision and patience necessitated by such a craft.

A centerpiece of the exhibition is Vastness (1975), a large tapestry from the museum’s collection showing a bride associated with spring and Nauryz, the celebration of the spring equinox and new year. Around her, women gather at tables and a young man on horseback appears among the birds. Elsewhere, figures emerge from the surrounding forest, creating a dense tableau that feels as abstract as it is narrative. The exhibition’s final gallery focuses on the shanyrak, the circular wooden crown at the top of a traditional Kazakh yurt. A symbol of home and family, it serves an architectural motif representing womanhood. In Mother Earth (1984), connections between generations of women evoke the continuity of life and inherited knowledge. Zauberkova’s achievement lies not only in her sheer technical mastery, but in her ability to reinterpret Kazakh textile traditions through a vision that is unmistakably her own, creating work that is deeply rooted in its cultural origins while remaining formally inventive and alive.

#9005. Carroll Dunham Calls His Filthy Formalism “Abstraction with a Hard-On”

I thought it best to confess up front that I was still forming an opinion about his work. Carroll Dunham took that like a gentleman. He is familiar, he made clear to me during ourranginginterview, with the two main camps of interpretation about his potty-mouthed paintings and drawings: 1) that he is a high formalist with an ear for the unconscious seldom rivaled since Surrealism, and 2) that he is a simple vulgarian.

“I’m lucky people even want to write about my work,” Dunham said. “I made the paintings. They can say whatever they want.” At 76, Dunham is thin, likable, and frank. He has a sharp, deadpan face framed by transition lenses and Beckettian white hair. When we spoke in his studio in Connecticut, he wore a silk suit in the shade of gray-green the French call caca d’oie, the shirt buttoned only in the top half, cholo style, with chunky sneakers in the same shade. Related Articles Some Collectors Feel 'Energized,' Some 'Burned': As the Curtain Rises on the New York Fall Season, Mixed Signals from Market Insiders Dealer Matthew Brown More Than Doubles His Los Angeles Space with Move to Hollywood Media District: 'I Really Believe in LA'

The spacious upstairs had been given over to small abstract sculptures he was making out of aluminum sheeting with assistants. It was July, and Dunham was between two capstone surveys of a long career. A show of his drawings spanning 1974 to 2024 had recently come down at the Art Institute of Chicago, while curators at the Institute of Contemporary Art, Miami, were finalizing a survey of his paintings from 1983 to the present for December. It was the kind of summary moment an artist is lucky to be alive for.

Since the ’90s, Dunham’s best-known pictures have starred carefully framed cartoon penises, vaginas, and anuses in varying states of specificity, usually attached to the bodies or the faces of humanoids engaged in sex or violence. This scenery belongs to a tradition of ridiculous bodily extremes, from Greek vases to Thomas Rowlandson to Gustave Courbet to Nicole Eisenman. His style, meanwhile, belongs to the black outlines and dropped-in colors of cartoons. That graphic clarity seems to ask us to read his bodily subjects loud and clear, without any of the technical seduction of peers like Lisa Yuskavage or John Currin.

Although his loud and lusty scenarios committed no real transgression (Peter Saul took care of that in the ’60s, then Robert Mapplethorpe in the ’80s), what may genuinely surprise the uninitiated is the academic remove that characterizes the writing about Dunham. His work is discussed—and discussed primarily by those born before 1975—almost exclusively in the specialist language of form or space or paint application, with little reference to the subject matter. It seems that the writers in Camp 1 understand the shock factor that attends men dildoing their rectums with pistols, or angrily ejaculating on each other from enormous penis-noses, as ammunition against the claim that subject should dictate one’s opinion of a painting. As if to deny the charge of prudery, some of them describe moments of rapture. On a Dunham painting made between 2006 and 2012, of a giant woman spreading her anus and vagina above a landscape like a parade float, the artist Paul Chan wrote of feeling transported: “When I entered the room where it hung [at the Whitney], I gasped. The painting was at once exuberant, provocative, and entrancing. It literally took my breath. I quickly glanced at the other people in the room. Was anyone else having an asthma attack looking at this?”

Representing Camp 2 are John Yau (The Brooklyn Rail, 2007: “Saul is an iconoclast and Dunham is a wannabe.”) and a young man in a basketball jersey I met at the Chicago show. This man was examining a pencil scribble from 2020 of a fist clasping an erection, the balls parted and meatus shaped like a teardrop. I asked him what he thought, and he said, “I feel like I’m being pranked.”

Dunham walked me to the “other studio,” a smaller room reserved for painting, where acrylic tubes lay neatly on a table in gradients, labels down. A canvas he had just finishedstood on sawhorses. It showed a man with long black hair down on all fours in a sculpture studio. The painting is called Looking for Something, and its protagonist’s pants are on the floor. His skin is white, and a woman, who is purple, kneels behind him, her head thrown back in a wail or moan. With her hand, she does something to the man’s ass that is not visible to us. In the foreground, another purple person, a Peeping Tom, watches them through a window. Nine of these most recent “Sculptor” paintings, from about Covid to now, were to go up at the Matthew Brown gallery in Manhattan in September as a sort of appetizer for the Miami show.

I asked where these recent purple/white folks come from. “They come from my work,” Dunham explained. “And I don’t mean that to be glib. They really do. So to even answer that question, I would have to go, ‘Before I was doing these paintings, I was doing these paintings, then these paintings,’” he continued, miming with his hands successive leaps into the past.

BORN THE FIFTH IN A line of Carrolls to a Connecticut poultry farmer who turned to real estate, Dunham went to Phillips Academy (Andover), class of 1967. The sculptor Mel Kendrick was his roommate. “Tip was doing Rapidograph drawings,” Kendrick recalled as we spoke by phone, using Dunham’s nickname. “Almost hippie drawings, very fine sketches.” (Of “Tip,” Dunham said, “It’s a WASP thing.”) Kendrick also recalls Dunham’s appetite for science fiction. (Face-down on his studio table, I spotted James L. Cambias’s Darkling Sea.) Dunham took darkroom classes. In the school’s literary magazine, his finely exposed photograph of a pouting and rotund lady in a playground swing illustrates a poem by Anthony Grafton, the historian-to-be. “Anything he did, he always had a touch,” Kendrick said. “Tip is very specific. And that’s something I don’t know if people know about his paintings, even now.”

After a year at the University of Rochester, Dunham followed Kendrick to Trinity College, in Hartford, where they worked in a small studio art department. “That meant smoking a lot of dope and reading Artforum,” said Dunham. On weekends, Dunham and Kendrick would drive down from Connecticut in Dad’s (Carroll IV’s) pickup truck, Kendrick recalled, to sample the new galleries in Soho—Bykert, Paula Cooper, Sonnabend, OK Harris—and to feast on spaghetti and jug wine at the apartment of their Trinity teacher Terence LaNoue.

LaNoue made almost three-dimensional combine paintings with poured latex and molds. He “was a great teacher, but I always had a kind of resistance to what he was making,” Dunham said. “And I’ve been that guy. I know that I’ve had good experiences between students and me where it really didn’t have to do with them being that turned on about my work.” Dunham never followed, either, in the footsteps of the artist with whom LaNoue installed him for a formative internship. Dorothea Rockburne produced—and still does, at 97—large, clean panes of paper or vellum, lined geometrically or coated in graphite. But the two got on, and still do. “Brighter than almost anybody around,” Rockburne said of him by phone.

What attracted Dunham was the planning implied by Rockburne’s planes—she taught him and Kendrick “how to handle a T-square and other basic things,” she said. He was also drawn to the repetitious text paintings of Mel Bochner (who lived with Rockburne), and to the heaps of raw material arranged by Barry Le Va and by Richard Serra. On graduating, he moved into a loft on Thomas Street shared with Kendrick and Peter Wheelwright, the architect. His 1970s and ’80s in New York were “isolation lite,” he told me. Dunham was part of no scene, he said, but befriended the photographers of the so-called Pictures Generation, and married one: Laurie Simmons. For seven years he worked in a frame shop, then for another seven at Time magazine, as a layout artist, all the while plotting his entrance into the art world.

DUNHAM’S ’70s ART BEGAN with single-line squiggles on canvas or paper. Some are elegantly coiled springs, while others resemble long strings dropped to the floor, their loops filled with ground colors of fast-drying casein or acrylic. He debuted with them at Artists Space in 1981, the Chicago survey was their first time on view since. Rockburne sees little of herself in Dunham’s famous later work. “It had that kind of [Sol] LeWittian, instructional aspect,” said the artist John Newman, another Dunham confederate from those days, by phone. “In the ’70s, drawing was sort of raised to a new place,” Newman explained, “as a much more immediate and idea-oriented kind of territory that wasn’t so laden with the history of painting and sculpture.”

The string-loops soon became blobs. When Dunham found the lid of a shipping crate on the street, around 1980, and used that for his surface, the almost sculptural grains and knots of the plywood veneer became guidelines for even more specific and conflicting blobs all mashed together—amoebas, geysers, wilting donuts, kinked tubes, beans, ripples, Froot Loops—in palettes ranging from medical textbook to clown paint. It is with these plywood paintings that the Miami survey begins. From 1984 to ’88, they appeared in three shows at the Baskerville + Watson gallery, with the middle show limited to monochromes.

“When the veneer things came out,” Newman recalled, it was amazing. “Think about the first time you ever read James Joyce. You really had to step up to it, participate in it. It was new information.” The art dealer David Nolan “hated them” at first, he said by phone: “I thought these garish, psychedelic colors were just there to shock me, and I just wasn’t interested.” But after a while, he began “to peel away the layers and see how they’re put together. And once I understood that, I thought, Oh God.”

The third show sold out before even opening, scoring acquisitions by the Museum of Modern Art, the Whitney, and the Brooklyn Museum. Dunham quit his magazine job. Gestural painting had been deemed safe again by young galleries, and although Dunham used a brand of biomorphism that didn’t quite fit with the headliners—Basquiat, Baselitz, Schnabel—he was made. Instead of buying up pallets of plywood and sticking safely to what worked, however, Dunham pivoted again. By the ’90s, his veneer paintings migrated to stretched linen, this time as single forms. They began to elongate into screaming fish-lipped mouths, nugget bodies, wincing faces, and undeniable penises. “They weren’t until they were,” Kendrick said of these organs. Nolan noticed them, too. But since they were untitled, Nolan said, “I thought he was avoiding what was right in front of our noses. They are bodily explosions. Come on.”

DUNHAM HAD BEEN PLENTY aware. He described the ’90s work to me as “abstraction with a hard-on.” But he seemed as bewildered as I about its origin. He spoke with plainness about sex and aggression as if he were a social worker, treating his own work as a sort of passive conduit for those realities. This tone did not seem to me like an act. I asked if he had tried to be provocative with his art, then or now. He said no: “It doesn’t interest me very much … The entire enterprise was provocative.” He spoke of Duchamp’s urinal.

Into the new century and his large survey at the New Museum in New York from 2002 to 2003, which was his last show of that scale until this year, his canvases begin to carry entire buildings and shiploads, colonies and planets full of hateful little nugget people with their penises, guns, and hideous gourd breasts. The exceptions from sex—lumpy tree scenes and landscapes—became the transgression. From there, he went more humanoid. In the past 20 years, his nuggets have grown up, first into suited G-men with fedoras and angular suits, then into cleanly clarified cartoon nudes, their globe buttocks outlined in elegant black and set in plain landscapes or rooms. They wrestle, fight, bathe, masturbate, copulate, and blind each other. They examine their gaping anuses, their big labia like bike tubes, and their nipples like air-hockey pushers.

These characters occupy about half the Miami paintings. In one, Horse and Rider (My X), 2013–15, a woman holds her arms up in a “Why me?” pose on the back of a horse. The lines of her reach continue south into a stand of flowers and a broken tree branch, dividing the canvas into a perfect X, which Dunham has left visible in pencil beneath the paint. At the geometric center is the woman’s anus, as if to say “Look here.” Just beneath, the horse’s anus gapes, too. He turns back at us with a look like “Excuse you.” (No human or humanoid, however, has eyes in a Dunham work.)

Dunham said of this X composition, “I was very excited when I figured out that that would work.” He explained: “It’s two layers of truth. There’s the subject and whatever that requires to be plausibly rendered.” (He counted “breasts, genitalia, asshole, some notion of limbs, and hair.”) “Then the geometry of the canvas has this other kind of truth, and the two things have to become one thing.” And the woman? “I honestly do not remember why I thought it would be interesting to put a woman on a horse in the paintings.” He thought. “It’s nice to have a black dot in the center of a painting. And it’s even nicer when that black dot is a woman’s ass, you know?”

Nolan was the only one I spoke to who saw strategy in Dunham’s turn to hyper-figuration. He saw the artist “dealing with his own demons or faults about the world.” But he described the work as Dunham did, composition-first. “If you try to forget there’s a face in there, the compositions are very strong.” He advised me to view the paintings upside down, pointing out convincing similarities to Aztecan decoration and adding that recently he, Nolan, had refused to sell one—for a lot of money—until the potential buyer flew to New York to see the shapes in person. “That is a problem with the younger generation. They will lose all of the subtleties.”

WHAT DOES THE YOUNGER generation think? The Miami show this winter (and the Chicago catalog forever) will give them the chance to see Dunham’s career as a single entity and to decide if the evolution of blob to aggression to anus stands up to the hindsight of a more literally minded era. In the purple alien characters on view at Matthew Brown this fall, from the series Dunham calls “Studio on Another Planet” (2022–26), one was hard-pressed not to read a narrative about artists at work in a culture that will misunderstand them: a solitary white male surrounded by voyeurs (critics? dealers? posterity?) as he quietly molds his clay on their land, incurring their sinister attentions. In the last of those canvases, Finished (2019–2025), the aliens have had enough. They’ve dragged the artist outside and are now quartering him to death.

“You’re not supposed to get it,” Newman said of Dunham’s pictures. “Art is about having an experience.” Newman speaks, Darwin-like, of Dunham’s characters emerging from the primordial soup of the plywood paintings. “Younger people probably don’t know the early work. And I actually think if they did, it would help them understand his later work better.” In my conversations with Camp 1, I began to wonder if there has ever been a generation more permissive, more game, than the one that had Dunham as a sort of living symbol of egress: out of the hermetic tasks of Minimalism, through pure shape, into a future where human fictions of any extreme can live without excuse or embarrassment. And I began to envy them.

I asked Dunham if he believed pure abstraction existed. He said yes, adding, “And I think that when I started my work, I was doing it. And then I think at a certain point I realized that it fascinated me to try to add some really literal aspects of just being a human being incarnated, or incarcerated, however you think about it, in a body.”

But I didn’t fully buy Dunham’s hermetic account of his own work as “always in some way self-referential.” There seems to be plenty of lived Artist v. World in his pictures and posture, and plenty of visual breadcrumbs leading to the culture at large. I asked, for instance, which cartoons he watched with his two children, who were born in 1986 and ’92. His eyes widened. “Ren & Stimpy was good,” he said of John Kricfalusi’s unhinged and influential program. “But the masterpiece of ’90s cartooning as far as I’m concerned was Angry Beavers,” which he watched with his son. I was fishing. The affinities between Dunham’s ’90s work and the prevailing depravities of Nickelodeon and Cartoon Network are inarguable; and in those affinities, a new generation may see homage to the last golden age of a truly transgressive child-absurd.

Speaking of his younger child, Dunham flashed back: “He came into my studio a lot. He would pick up on things I was drawing and then he would draw stuff of his own that was kind of like that. So I got a lot of, you know, 6- and 7-year-old energy coming back at me about my own work.” Dunham smiled. “It definitely encouraged a certain kind of energy. It’s very sweet to think about actually.”

#9004. What's Love Got to Do With It? The Relationship Cycle Explained

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Relationships aren’t just about candlelit dinners and cozy sofa nights — they’re complex AF, filled with ups, downs, twists, and turns. From the first flush of love to the settled comfort of commitment, relationships have stages that evolve with time.

Each relationship phase serves a unique purpose, helping you learn more about each other, yourself, and the kind of relationship you want to build. Understanding the dynamics of these stages is crucial for any couple (or throuple!) aiming to develop a lasting bond.

Whether you’re in the throes of a new romance or navigating the challenges of a long-term commitment, continue reading to learn how to rock each phase like a pro.

From those “can’t eat, can’t sleep” early days to the “let’s build an empire” moments, each relationship stage is like a season of your fave drama binge. But, like any good drama, the plot thickens as time passes and things change. Here’s what to expect, month by month:

Welcome to the love bubble, where everything about your significant other seems nothing short of magical. The positives overshadow any negatives, creating a blissfully skewed balance sheet of love. It lasts from about 6 months to 2 years for most peeps, but many folks say they are still madly in love even after 20 years together!

Research shows that during this stage, the prefrontal cortex, which is crucial for critically judging others, shows decreased activity. In other words, you’re less likely to focus on your partner’s faults and more likely to overlook their flaws.

Lurve also activates specific areas in the brain that are driven by goals and rewards. These areas are rich in dopamine and oxytocin receptors, chemicals that make you feel good and bonded to others. They encourage you to pursue and maintain a relationship because it feels rewarding and fulfilling.

If the euphoric stage is the wild, pulse-racing party of love, the early attachment stage is the cozy after-party where things get real comfortable. In the thrilling initial phase, your brain is doped up on dopamine, but as this initial buzz begins to mellow, a more sophisticated part of the brain starts to step up — the ventral pallidum.

Now, after the first year or so, deeper bonds are formed, helped along by attachment hormones like vasopressin and oxytocin, also fondly known as “the love hormone.” These hormones help transform the electric excitement of new love into a warm, enduring attachment.

Hold tight because the crisis stage hits around 5 to 7 years, and it’s a true test of your relationship’s resilience. This phase often feels like a rollercoaster, where life’s challenges can either pull you apart or push you closer together. Many couples experience a drift during this time, and how you handle it — either by addressing the issues head-on or continuing to drift — can define your future together.

Significant life events, like becoming parents, often occur during this stage and can intensify the pressure. These events can either strengthen your bond through shared responsibilities and mutual love or strain it to the breaking point. Successfully navigating this stage means moving beyond mere survival to fostering a deeper, more meaningful connection.

If you’ve made it this far, congrats, you’re in the deep attachment stage! Post-crisis, you’re looking at 7 years and beyond where you settle into that deep, comfy love. No more daily fireworks — now it’s about a slow-burning ember that warms the house.

You know each other inside and out, warts and all. It’s about unconditional support, knowing looks across crowded rooms, and being each other’s rock. Welcome to the good life!

Every relationship is a blend of sweet and sour and everything in between. Understanding the stages, from the initial euphoria to the deep attachment stage, helps you embrace the journey, keep your bond strong, and prepare your heart for whatever comes next. So buckle up and enjoy the ride — it’ll be worth it!

#9002. Rachel Whiteread Has Designed the 2027 Brit Awards Trophy

Dame Rachel Whiteread, who was the first woman artist to win the Turner Prize in 1993, has been selected to design the 2027 Brit Awards trophy. The trophy has previously been designed by the likes of Damien Hirst, Zaha Hadid, Es Devlin and Anish Kapoor.

The trophy will be bestowed upon musicians nominated for the prestigious award ceremony taking place on February 27, 2027. Each trophy takes inspiration from the image of Britannia, a tall, elegant female figure that personifies Britain. For her design, Whiteread has inverted the statue, exposing its silver lining with punched holes throughout. “I exposed the interior of the statue—as an artist would do with their music,” said the artist in a statement. “I accepted the invitation to design next year’s Brit Award trophy, as I saw this as a natural extension of my work—to continue to celebrate and recognize British art and creativity, and to have an opportunity to apply my own perspective within such an iconic British cultural institution.” Related Articles Nnena Kalu Wins Turner Prize, Becoming First Learning-Disabled Artist to Take UK's Top Art Award Rachel Whiteread's Collaboration with French Silversmith Company Inspired by Corrugated Cardboard

Whiteread said she also agreed to design the statue in an effort to safeguard arts and culture, which she described as being “under very real threat.” “The Brits have celebrated musical creativity and artistry for decades now. We have some fantastically creative musicians who have produced music that lays their souls bare, provides hope in times of darkness, or speaks directly about a moment in time,” she added.

In designing the trophy, Whiteread joins a prestigious list of other artists who have given the statue new life: Dame Peter Blake, Tracey Emin, Vivienne Westwood and Yinka Ilori. In 1997, Whiteread became the first woman to represent Britain at the Venice Biennale, and in 2001, she became the third artist to have her work placed on the Fourth Plinth in Trafalgar Square, which took the form of an inverted resin recreation of the plinth.

#9001. Meet Courage Dzidula Kpodo, Lesley Lokko's pick for the most influential architect of the next 20 years

Photography by Cyril Marcilhacy. unless stated

Ghanaian-Scottish architect Lesley Lokko has nominated Courage Dzidula Kpodo as a key name to watch over the next two decades for Dezeen’s 20×20 project, sponsored by Kohler.

In this interview he explains why despite growing global attention, his ambitions remain resolutely local.

Having only graduated in 2025 from a master’s in architecture at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) – for which he was awarded the Arthur Rotch Prize for highest overall mark – Kpodo is already someone Lokko believes will “help shape the next chapter of African architecture”.

Kpodo’s work, which sees him blur the roles of architect, artist and archivist, is focused on revealing what he calls the “silences” in prevailing narratives about Ghanaian architecture, and challenging the idea that Ghana’s future development must be a “linear prescription of urbanisation”.

If this sounds theoretical or speculative, Kpodo’s approach is anything but: the site of his MIT thesis was an almost five-acre stretch of farmland in Ghana to which he purchased a 99-year lease in 2022, and is currently using as a live site to consider alternative forms of development in the region.

Stating how, if nothing else, the purchase would “preserve the value of the money I had in my savings account,” Kpodo sees the site becoming an alternative institution of sorts, constructed using materials he has salvaged from vernacular buildings that would otherwise be demolished.

“The committee at MIT was a bit shocked, because they weren’t used to the idea of a thesis project existing in the real world,” Kpodo told Dezeen. “But I still thought of it as almost as a sort of sketch, just at 1:1 scale.”

“Doing that gives you something to test – people are going to interface with it; you can test out its failures and success very quickly.”

Growing up in Kumasi, Kpodo initially focused on visual art in school before pursuing a course in architecture at the Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST), and subsequently MIT.

At KNUST he was quickly exposed to narratives around both architectural success and Ghana’s own architectural history that left him seeking something more “homegrown”.

“We had a lecture from Francis Kéré in which he spoke about his Serpentine Pavilion, and how taking on commissions from big institutions or big clients can become critical for defining your practice,” said Kpodo.

I thought: okay, what can I do now that is within my means instead of waiting for the big commissions to come?

“At the time, I couldn’t imagine any of these commissions coming to those of us working in the South. I couldn’t see any architects who were operating on that scale, or even at a kind of global scale,” he continued.

“It almost had the opposite effect on me. I thought: okay, what can I do now that is within my means instead of waiting for the big commissions to come? I think it’s by being local that I can have something to offer to the world.”

Kpodo became interested in local architectural archives, initially those of the KNUST Development Office, but also the less formalised collections of images and drawings that he encountered online.

He soon helped establish Postbox Ghana, a research collective initiated by artist Manuela Nebuloni to create an alternative architectural archive using postcards and stamps from the 1950s to the 1980s, which often depicted examples of Tropical Modernism and state infrastructure constructed following Ghana’s independence.

However, Kpodo still felt that these archival materials did not speak to his own understanding of Ghanaian architecture, having grown up in a “not-so-well-to-do context” in Kumasi and only really encountering modernist architecture when first entering the KNUST campus.

“The whole archive that I was exposed to, whether it was in the Development Office or in the postcards, had a huge, significant gap in it,” he said. “I remember stories my dad would tell me about building practices and cultures that just didn’t make it into this archive or our training in architecture school.”

“As a newly independent country, Ghana wanted to break away from any kind of ethnographic notion of what the ‘Gold Coast’ – to use its colonial name – was. So those ‘traditional’ buildings and other forms of practices did not make it into the framework of thinking about what our future meant,” he continued.

“But even though these buildings are far removed from the city centres and from the archive, they were foundational in the sense that they enabled the cocoa industry, and brought in the money that built the institutions and structures that are enshrined in postcards.”

Kpodo began to photograph these vernacular buildings himself, many of them farm structures made using laterite, a type of local red earth that is formed into air and sun-dried blocks for construction

When I talk about rebuilding them, it usually lands. People get it, and then they begin asking, ‘okay, but what can it be?’

Upon finding many of these buildings slated for demolition, Kpodo has more recently begun to purchase them, before carefully deconstructing their laterite structures to become the raw material for new structures on his land.

The idea was initially met locally with some confusion. “I remember one man said, ‘oh, are you going to extract gold from the walls?’ because laterite can contain gold,” he recalled.

“But when I talk about rebuilding them, it usually lands. People get it, and then they begin asking, ‘okay, but what can it be?’ And then some kids would even begin making their own proposals. For me, just creating that imagination is worth it.”

The land that Kpodo purchased in 2022 is in Ghana’s eastern region, and was at the frontier of cocoa production in the early 1900s. Some descendants of the first farmers on the land are still based there, and were among those Kpodo interviewed to understand the history of the landscape.

Alongside the widening of a communal path – the focus of his MIT thesis – and the moving of vernacular building materials there, he has also constructed a simple timber deck, both as a rest point for the farmers and an observation point for watching future changes unfold on the site.

If I were asked to design a Serpentine Pavilion, I’d probably make a replica in Ghana, too. You can only do so much in an exhibition setting

Kpodo envisions that this future will include both new agricultural processing facilities for the farmers on the land, as well as community spaces that enable further discussions around its ongoing development.

This work also forms the basis of Kpodo’s educational and curatorial work. He is keen to continue “speaking both languages” – the more practical with the conceptual – but he feels the latter should always be grounded in a “local base” rather than detached from it.

In 2023, his work with Postbox Ghana was exhibited at both Vantage Point Sharjah and the Venice Architecture Biennale. In 2025, he curated the LagosPhoto Biennial alongside Maria Pia Bernardoni and Robin Beth Riskin, with the theme of Incarceration.

Kpodo also taught on the one-month Nomadic African Studio at the African Futures Institute, founded by Lokko as a space “dedicated to rethinking education, culture, and practice from the African continent outward.”

Most recently, he orchestrated the transportation of the wall of a laterite farmhouse a little further afield to the Fondation Cartier in Paris, as part of the exhibition Ibrahim Mahama: Harvest Season, where it is accompanied by images from the Postbox Ghana archives.

“If I were asked to design a Serpentine Pavilion, I’d probably make a replica in Ghana, too,” he said. “You can only do so much in an exhibition setting. You can only talk so much. If the work has no ground and no local base, then I think it becomes very difficult for you to bridge what it is that you’re presenting versus the work that it proposes to be doing.”

“We need to cultivate other sites that do the real work, sites that translate it into something which is not necessarily concerned with an educated audience,” he continued.

“My sense is that we’re increasingly going to see the most ‘powerful’ institutions seek out these hyper-local narratives and projects as a way to really understand the world.”

To celebrate Dezeen’s 20th birthday, we asked 20 of the most influential architects and designers of the last 20 years to identify someone they think will have a major impact in the next 20 years. Over the next four weeks, we’ll reveal their picks in a series of profile interviews. The series is presented in partnership with Kohler.

#9000. Vibration Plate Benefits, According to a Weightlifting Coach

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Vibration plates are like mini surfboards that give you a good shimmy while you’re exercising. Though you won’t find a mountain of extensive research behind them, you may be impressed by their possible benefits.

We asked a weightlifting coach to explain and show us how to add good vibrations to our workout routine.

These machines, which look like platforms or scales, are designed to activate something called whole-body vibration (WBV). WBV makes the body work harder by forcing it to contract muscles automatically.

Fans of WBV like to perform classic exercises on top of these machines, including:

Research points to WBV’s ability to boost blood flow.

Weightlifting coach Jarrod Nobbe explains that vibration plates help move blood by stimulating muscle contractions through rapid vibrations.

“The rhythmic contraction and relaxation of muscles help pump blood more efficiently throughout the body,” he says.

As Nobbe adds, movement generally increases blood flow and core temperature, preparing the body for activity. This means vibration plates may be an excellent warm-up activity.

A 2021 study showed that WBV can be an alternative exercise for older adults, boosting the effects of strengthening exercise.

Nobbe says this is because WBV engages muscles in a way that mimics resistance training.

“The vibrations activate and force muscles to contract and relax multiple times per second, which can lead to gains in muscle strength and endurance over time, especially when combined with specific exercises,” he says.

Nobbe points to some anecdotal evidence suggesting that regular use of vibration plates may help boost energy levels, possibly thanks to increased blood circulation and enhanced muscle activation.

“Ultimately, I stand by the idea that movement is medicine,” Nobbe says. “Tons of research already proves that regular physical activity boosts mood, mental health, and promotes energy levels.”

Nobbe says WBV may reduce muscle soreness, stiffness, and inflammation by encouraging blood flow to the muscles. This, he explains, aids in faster recovery post-exercise or injury.

WBV has been shown to improve bone mineral density, which Nobbe points out may positively affect those at risk of osteoporosis.

“The mechanical vibrations stimulate bone cells, potentially leading to increased bone density and strength, delivering the same positive bone health benefits of resistance training,” he says.

“Unfortunately, vibration plates aren’t a one-stop shop for weight loss,” Nobbe says.

He explains that vibration plates alone are unlikely to significantly reduce belly fat without dietary changes and additional exercise.

“While vibration plates can contribute to overall calorie expenditure and muscle activation, targeted fat loss requires a comprehensive approach including diet, cardio exercise, and resistance training,” he says.

These tips will help you stand on your vibration plate with a slight bend at your knee or perform exercises on top of it.

More research is needed around WBV — AKA what happens when you use a vibration plate — but existing smaller research is promising.

Use your machine carefully, and remember to maintain a healthy lifestyle and workout routine.

Last medically reviewed on June 27, 2024

#8999. Final Report Details Minor, But Visible Damage to the Bayeux Tapestry Following Trip to the British Museum

A final report released by France’s ministry of culture yesterday details where the Bayeux Tapestry sustained some minor damage following its transfer from Normandy to the British Museum, reports Le Figaro.

While the overall state of the nearly 1000-year-old tapestry was deemed “satisfactory” by the eight conservationists and experts working in France and England, who co-authored the report, they found there were “two zones of fiber breakage,” new folds and tensions, as well as “very small” damage that appeared in areas that were already weakened, prior to the voyage. News of an initial condition report about the tapestry showing some damage made headlines in September, but this is the first time a final copy has been seen by the media. Related Articles British Museums Are Experiencing a 'Bayeux Bounce' in Attendance, Thanks to Replicas of the Tapestry Scientists Say They've Rediscovered How the Romans Made the British Museum's Color-Shifting Lycurgus Cup

ARTnews has reached out to France’s Ministry of Culture for a copy of the report, which was not shared via press release or posted on its website, as is customary with public announcements.

In other details, translated from the French news story, experts reportedly observed that “a red wool thread in an embroidered area and another from the linen background cloth have undergone a slight progression.” Additionally, they spotted “slight folds and pockets,” as well as areas of tension in the embroidery and its linen support. For the latter, the tapestry’s horizontal display, in contrast with its previous vertical hang, should help fix the stretching issue. The report also warns of areas to watch closely, particularly on the tapestry’s return trip to France in July 2027. These include several more pronounced folds, areas of wear, and a broken thread.

The authors, who conducted their report in July and August, added that it’s not possible to know precisely when the changes occurred within the time span of the tapestry’s transfer from Bayeux to its current display in London. Additionally, they noted that this last check, including additional, highly detailed photographs of the artifact, is the most complete review of the tapestry to date. It was compared with two less thorough assessments made in 2020 and 2025.

“We now know the condition of the tapestry as never before, which will be useful later on,” said Delphine Christophe, general director of heritage in France, speaking to Le Figaro. She added that the overall assessment, despite the noted damage, proved “exceptional,” given the fragile tapestry’s roughly 230-foot length and 20-inch height.

The loan of the tapestry was heavily criticized in the months leading up to the handoff, due to risks of harming it. But after three failed attempts to secure a loan, it was ultimately made possible thanks to a carefully controlled ground transportation plan that was designed to eliminate almost all vibrations, aided by the political will of French President Emmanuel Macron. The latter was intent on making a strong diplomatic statement of friendship with the UK. In exchange, France will receive the Sutton Hoo archaeological ship burial and the Lewis Chessmen set from the British Museum. However, as Le Monde’s Roxana Azimi pointed out, “the Sutton Hoo treasure does not resonate at all with the French public,” and the French people “are getting objects that are certainly valuable, but not very impressive.”

As for the Bayeux Tapestry, it is believed to have been made in Canterbury following the coronation of William the Conqueror as king of England in 1066. It tells his side of the Norman Conquest, which was one of the most pivotal moments in English history. Meanwhile, British Museum director Nicolas Cullinan responded frankly to Azimi’s point in Le Monde. “Yes,” he said. “It’s very hard to beat the Bayeux Tapestry.”

There's plenty going on in the audio Black Friday deal world today, so I thought I'd cut through the noise and bring you a short curated list of three IEMs (in-ear monitors – that is, earphones) that I personally own, and would have loved to have bought at these prices.

And the kicker? Although the sit in three different price categories, I believe that price in this case does not correlate to 'better' sound. They offer different sound profiles that will suit different listeners. In my view, each IEM is excellent in their sound profiles are excellent at nailing their respective sound goals.

Want more budget IEM ideas? I've got a buying guide for that. Or, if you're feeling fancy, I've also got a list of the best IEMs up to $500.

Note: All three of these IEMs are sold through HiFiGo, but that is a pure coincidence. I'm not getting any kickback from them for this, and this article is not a promotion of any sort... I just genuinely love these IEMs, as you can see from my in-depth reviews on each of them.

I've put this one up top, because it's the cheapest, and also because it offers the best value of the three IEM deals on the page.

The Defiant is an engaging, exciting IEM that I think most people will have a blast listening to. It doesn't do anything fancy with its midrange; it's not interested in conjuring soundstage with tuning tricks. What it gives you is a crisp, bassy V-shape tuning done really well.

As I explain in my glowing Juzear Defiant review.

This was a surprise to me when I got hands on it in September. I called it one of the most compelling IEMs of 2026, and I stand by that. I say surprising, because I'm not a fan of its looks. But the sound is anything but jarring. It offers excellent midrange detail, smooth treble and a whopping bass boost. One of the better 'neutral with bass boost' IEMs out there.

As far as a 'audiophile' tuning, this is one of the best I've ever heard. That high definition, elevated treble, micro-detail, clearly positioned instruments – all of that – the EP321 nails.

It is possible that it's too bright for some listeners. But for me it's an exceptionally well-balanced IEM that brings a crystal clear take on my favourite music.

The Juzear Defiant is a loud, proud, V-shaped crowd-pleaser. It chooses pure fun over nuance, delivering a contrasty slam with boosted bass, slightly lean lower mids, and an airy, fatigue-free treble. When I’m grabbing something for a noisy morning commute or long gaming sessions, this is what I reach for, especially with its really useful modular USB-C and 3.5mm switchable cable.

Stepping up to the Juzear Light Shuttle and things get more sophisticated. Even though JM-1 "neutral with bass boost" isn't my favourite tuning, I love how well this nails the brief. It’s a warm, sub-bass-focused all-rounder with natural mids and crisp/smooth treble that dodges every sibilant hot spot. It’s the easy choice if you want an engaging, balanced daily driver, and you're serious about your music listening.

Finally, there's the Binary EP321 MEMS which is all about analytical, treble-forward snap. I’ve been treble-shy in the past, yet I love how this fast silicon driver reveals micro-detail without feeling glaring. Backed by a dependable wad of bass, it’s built for detail-hunters who want pocket-sized audiophile precision on the train, even if it sacrifices a touch of pure midrange warmth.

Picture this: you're settled into your seat on a United flight out of LAX, the Pacific stretching endlessly outside your window, and you know — you genuinely know — that the person next to you paid $400 for this exact seat while you paid **7,500 miles**. That's the Hawaiian sweet spot, and it's one of the most quietly powerful redemptions available to anyone building a travel rewards strategy. Hawaii has always been the aspirational American vacation. It's the honeymoon destination, the bucket-list family trip, the anniversary getaway. And because of that demand, flights from the mainland — especially during spring break, summer, and the holidays — rarely go on sale. A round-trip economy ticket from Los Angeles to Honolulu will routinely run **$400–$700**, and during peak travel windows, prices can push past $1,000 for a family of four. That's real money. FI-community money. Now consider what Turkish Airlines Miles & Smiles charges for that same seat: **7,500 miles one-way**. At the low end of cash pricing ($200 for a one-way), you're extracting **2.7 cents per point**. At the high end ($500 during peak season), that same 7,500 miles is worth **6.7 cents per point** — a figure that makes even seasoned travel rewards enthusiasts do a double-take. For context, most people in the points world consider 1.5–2 cents per point a solid redemption. **Getting 6.7 cents per point is extraordinary.** It's not a fluke or a loophole — it's a structural pricing inefficiency baked into the Turkish award chart, which treats all short-haul domestic U.S. flights (including Hawaii, which is technically a domestic route) at the same rock-bottom rate. This is the fundamental insight behind every great travel rewards redemption: **loyalty programs price awards based on their own logic, not cash fares.** Turkish Miles & Smiles sees LAX→HNL as a short Star Alliance partner flight. The fact that cash fares on that route are elevated because of destination demand is irrelevant to their award chart. That gap — between what Turkish charges in miles and what the market charges in dollars — is exactly where you save. For a ChooseFI community member who already holds Citi ThankYou Points, this redemption is within reach right now. You don't need to fly Turkish. You don't need to connect through Istanbul. You just need availability on United, 7,500 miles, and about 20 minutes.

The magic here comes down to one core concept: Star Alliance partner pricing on a domestic U.S. route.

Turkish Airlines is a Star Alliance member, and like most alliance programs, they allow their members to book award flights on partner airlines — including United. Where Turkish gets interesting (and generous) is in how they price those partner awards. Their award chart uses a fixed, distance-based or zone-based structure, and for short-haul U.S. domestic flights, the price bottoms out at 7,500 miles one-way in economy.

Here's the pricing inefficiency in plain language: Turkish Miles & Smiles doesn't care that Hawaii is an aspirational, high-demand destination. To their award chart, LAX→HNL is just another short domestic United flight. Meanwhile, United's own MileagePlus program charges significantly more for the same route — often 13,000–22,500 miles one-way depending on the fare bucket. Turkish is pricing the same seat at less than half what United charges its own members. That's the gap you're exploiting.

No fuel surcharges — ever. This is a critical detail that makes Turkish a standout program. Many European programs (we're looking at you, Lufthansa Miles & More) pile on hundreds of dollars in fuel surcharges that nearly erase the value of the award. Turkish charges zero fuel surcharges on any award flight, including partner redemptions. Your out-of-pocket cost when booking this redemption is taxes and fees only — typically $5–$15 for a domestic U.S. itinerary.

The most accessible path to 7,500 Turkish miles runs through Citi ThankYou Points, which transfer to Turkish at a 1:1 ratio. The transfer is instant — meaning you can see award availability, confirm your plan, and have the miles in your Turkish account within minutes, not days. That speed matters because Hawaii saver availability can disappear quickly.

You can also transfer from Bilt Rewards at 1:1 (also instant), or Marriott Bonvoy® at a 3:1 ratio (takes 1–5 days and is far less efficient — avoid Marriott for this transfer unless you have no other option).

The best Citi cards for earning ThankYou Points include the Citi Strata Premier, which earns 3x on dining, groceries, hotels, and airfare — categories that make accumulating 7,500 points genuinely fast for most households.

Turkish's award chart is fixed, meaning the price doesn't fluctuate with demand, time of year, or how close you are to departure (beyond the booking window). A saver economy award on a short domestic U.S. United flight is always 7,500 miles. No dynamic pricing surprises. No "off-peak vs. peak" tiers to navigate. This predictability is itself a feature — you can plan around it.

The booking window opens 355 days in advance, giving you nearly a full year of search runway to find the availability you need.

Here's exactly how to execute this redemption from zero to booked.

Before you transfer a single point, confirm that saver economy availability exists on your target route and dates. Go to united.com, enter your origin and destination (for example, LAX to HNL), and select your travel dates. When the results appear, look specifically for fares labeled "Saver" — these are the award inventory buckets that partner programs like Turkish can access. Citi and Bilt transfers to Turkish are instant. Your miles will appear in your Turkish account within minutes. Do not transfer until you've confirmed availability in Step 2 — points transfers are one-way and non-refundable.

Return to the Turkish award booking tool with your miles now loaded. Complete the booking for your confirmed flight. You'll pay only taxes and fees at checkout — typically $5–$15 for a domestic U.S. itinerary. Enter your payment details for that small amount and complete the reservation.

Let's make this concrete. It's late February, and you're planning a spring getaway to Honolulu with your partner. You pull up United.com and search LAX→HNL for mid-April — not peak spring break week, but the week after, when families have gone home and the island is quieter. You find saver economy availability on a direct United flight departing at 8:45 AM and arriving in Honolulu before noon local time.

The cash price for that ticket: $389 per person one-way. For two travelers, that's $778 before you've booked the return.

The points price: 7,500 Turkish Miles & Smiles miles per person, plus roughly $11 in taxes and fees. For two people, you're spending 15,000 miles and about $22.

You already have 20,000 Citi ThankYou Points sitting in your account from everyday spending on your Citi Strata Premier — groceries, dining, a couple of utility bills. You transfer 15,000 points to Turkish Miles & Smiles (instant transfer), log into the Turkish booking portal, and complete both seats in a single transaction.

Your CPP on this redemption: $389 ÷ 7,500 = 5.2 cents per point. That's more than three times what most people consider a strong redemption.

Now for the experience itself: you're flying United Economy on a widebody aircraft — typically a Boeing 767 or 777 on the Honolulu route from LAX. The flight is approximately 5.5 hours. Economy isn't business class, but United's Pacific routes are comfortable — you'll find decent legroom in Economy Plus if you want to upgrade your seat selection for a modest fee, complimentary entertainment, and meal service on this longer domestic segment. The flight across the Pacific, even in economy, has a different feel than a 2-hour domestic hop. The water below you turns that impossible shade of blue. You land in Honolulu at mid-morning, cleared customs quickly (domestic flight — no customs required), and you're at your hotel before lunch.

Total cost for two one-way tickets: 15,000 miles + $22. Cash equivalent: $778. Money saved: $756. That's a car payment, a month of groceries, or a head start on your next investment contribution — redirected from airline revenue to your FI journey.

The 7,500-mile rate is available year-round — Turkish doesn't have a separate peak pricing tier for this redemption. Turkish's booking window opens 355 days in advance. United releases the bulk of its saver award inventory when the schedule first opens — roughly 11 months before departure. This is the single most common mistake. Points transfers to Turkish are irreversible. Turkish miles expire after 36 months of account inactivity. Even one small miles transaction — earning or redeeming — resets the clock. Transfer a small batch of points or book a cheap award every few years to keep your account alive.

The math behind one of travel rewards' best-kept secrets

Turkish Airlines Miles&Smiles uses a distance-based award chart that treats Hawaii as a domestic U.S. destination. Since flights from the West Coast to Hawaii are under 3,000 miles, they fall into the lowest pricing tier at just 7,500 miles each way. Compare this to United MileagePlus, which charges 22,500 miles each way for the same route through its own program. The Turkish chart effectively gives you a 67% discount for the identical seat on the identical United flight. This pricing anomaly is one of the most valuable in travel rewards and has persisted for years.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Before transferring miles, verify award space exists. Search on United.com for saver-level award space to Hawaii on your preferred dates. If United shows availability at the saver level, it should be bookable through Turkish.

After booking, you will receive a Turkish Airlines confirmation. Add your United MileagePlus number to the reservation for elite benefits. You can manage the booking through either Turkish or United once ticketed.

Availability depends on United releasing Star Alliance partner award space (sometimes called "saver" availability). Searching 2-4 months in advance, on weekdays, or during shoulder season (April-May, September-October) significantly improves your chances.

Yes, but the miles cost increases with distance. From the East Coast, flights to Hawaii price at 10,000-12,500 miles each way depending on routing distance. Still an excellent deal compared to United's own pricing, though the West Coast offers the absolute lowest redemption.

This redemption was built for the ChooseFI member who's just starting to take travel rewards seriously — someone who has a Citi credit card, has been accumulating ThankYou Points on everyday spending, and wants their first "I can't believe this worked" moment.

Families planning a Hawaii vacation. At 7,500 miles per person, a family of four needs just 30,000 miles one-way — an achievable balance for anyone who's been strategic with a single Citi card for 6–12 months. The savings versus paying cash for four tickets can easily hit $1,500–$2,000, which is serious FI-community money.

Couples looking for a meaningful but accessible trip. Hawaii is aspirational without requiring long-haul international travel. This is the redemption that converts skeptical partners into believers.

Minimum points balance needed: Just 7,500 Citi ThankYou or Bilt points per one-way flight. That's genuinely achievable — even a single welcome bonus on an entry-level Citi card exceeds this threshold.

This redemption is less ideal for travelers on the East Coast (positioning flights eat into the simplicity), anyone without access to Citi or Bilt points (other transfer paths are inefficient), and travelers who need guaranteed availability on specific peak dates — the saver inventory just isn't reliable enough for inflexible itineraries.

The **earning side is straightforward** — 7,500 Citi ThankYou Points is a modest target that most people hit within a few months of regular spending on a Citi Strata Premier. The program prices this incredibly cheaply *because* the airlines release limited seats at this level. The **booking interface** adds minor friction. The Turkish Miles & Smiles website works, but it's not as polished as booking directly on United.com. Expect a slightly clunky experience — search patiently, and don't be surprised if you need to refresh or try slightly different date combinations. **Three tips to overcome the main challenges:** 1. **Be flexible with dates.** Saver availability is the limiting factor. If you can move your trip by 2–3 days, your chances of finding a seat increase dramatically. 2. **Search early.** Start 10–11 months out. The availability you can't find at 3 months may have been wide open at 11 months. 3. **Confirm before you transfer.** Check the Turkish booking tool *first*, then move your points. This keeps the process clean and stress-free. If you're willing to be slightly flexible on dates, this redemption is genuinely beginner-accessible — and the payoff, especially for a family, makes the modest extra effort completely worthwhile.

#8996. German Museum Transforms Permanent Collection Galleries into Gym to Attract Youth

We’ve seen dance and musical performances in museums, as well as yoga classes, but a full array of gym equipment and gear? Beginning earlier this month and running through February 21, 2027, the Kunstpalast in Düsseldorf, Germany, has set up weight machines, mats, treadmills, ellipticals, and all manner of gym equipment in its permanent exhibition galleries, so that visitors can work out beside the historic and contemporary artworks, reported the Times of London. Whether or not participants are able to take in the art hanging in front of them while bench pressing, is anyone’s guess, but the idea has its fans, some of whom show up to the museum appropriately dressed in workout clothes. Related Articles Museum Wiesbaden Will Be Germany's First Institution to Return Colonial-Era Human Remains to Indonesia The Netherlands and Germany Agree to Return 2,000 Artifacts to Ghana

What artworks do these health-conscious visitors get to enjoy while sweating away? The program titled “Gym. Fit with Art” unfolds across 20 stations beside the museum’s collection of over 800 works, which span pieces by Peter Paul Rubens to Gerhard Richter. It was conceived as a tribute marking the centenary of the GeSoLei, which was the largest trade fair held during the Weimar Republic, which was also dedicated to health.

“We want to target people who might prefer going to the gym rather than a museum on weekends,” and this particularly includes younger audiences, said Alina Fuchte, who has led the project. To wit, “the museum is transforming its collection into an extraordinary fitness circuit,” states the museum website. “Instead of just strolling from painting to painting and admiring the art, visitors will soon be able to get active,” it adds. The endeavor is sponsored by TARGOBANK in cooperation with Technogym, which makes fitness equipment, according to the website.

“Anyone who would rather simply take in the art is equally welcome,” continues the website. This, however, begs the question of whether that simple act may be tough to do while standing beside someone jogging on a treadmill in front of large busts of Johann Wilhelm, Elector Palatine, and his wife, Anna Maria Luisa de’Medici, per just a few examples of the works on view.

One visitor, Kai Heimes, 25, tells the Times of London, “It’s cool to work out in the collection,” and if it feels “awkward” for some, “I don’t think it’s a big deal,” he added.

However, another, Moritz Rossmanith, 40, admitted to being “a bit confused by it all.” Rossmanith was visiting from Rome, and thought it was “very strange to see kids holding thick barbells while there’s old Italian art on the wall.” Children are reportedly the biggest fans of the gym gear.

As for bringing water bottles to the museum-gym, given that many other museums sternly scold visitors for taking covert sips of water inside art galleries, that rule doesn’t seem to apply here.

“Coming here and realizing this is also a space for me, I can feel comfortable here, I can be free here, I can try new things—that, for me, is the first step,” said Fuchte.

Did we mention there is also a range of scheduled fitness classes at the museum? You can sign up here.

#8995. Toot Toot! 6 Tips to Prevent Protein Farts

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Protein farts are a common, albeit smelly, side effect of high-protein diets. They happen because of how proteins are digested. But(t) don’t worry! We have some tips to help you say goodbye to those pungent protein toots without giving up your gains.

Protein farts are episodes of flatulence that don’t smell too pleasant! They’re generally due to upping your protein intake from supplements like protein shakes.

And while these butt whistles may be embarrassing, you’ll be glad to know they’re generally harmless.

Farts consist of different gases. The most stinky odors usually come from your gut bacteria, producing sulfur-containing compounds as they break down food. The main culprit is hydrogen sulfide, which gives off a characteristic rotten egg smell, yum!

But why do your protein choices lead to thunder from down under?

Well, there’s not much evidence that a high-protein diet causes protein farts. However, there’s some anecdotal evidence that supplementary protein — like protein bars, protein shakes, and powder powders — increases flatulence, but it’s likely due to non-protein ingredients like lactose.

Supplements containing whey protein or casein are derived from milk and are high in lactose, which can increase flatulence. If your body can’t properly digest lactose, it ends up in your colon, where bacteria feast on it, producing — you guessed it — more gas and cheek flapping.

So, whey protein can throw a curveball for those who are lactose intolerant or sensitive. Surprisingly, it might also stir up digestive drama even for folks who typically handle dairy like champs, potentially due to additives like fart-inducing sweeteners or thickeners.

Some people may also have more significant issues digesting protein. Proteins are big, complex molecules — breaking them down is no small task for your gut. Plant-based protein supplements, like those based on soya beans, may also worsen flatulence.

FYI: Another reason why flatulence is common with protein powders and supplements is due to the addition of artificial sweeteners in the powders and bars, like sugar alcohols, sucralose, sorbitol, xylitol, and stevia.

If you’re looking to continue your protein regimen without becoming a walking, talking whoopee cushion, here are some strategic adjustments you can make:

Don’t just dive into the deep end with your protein intake — wade in slowly. Gradually increasing the amount of protein you consume allows your digestive system to adjust without getting overwhelmed. This step-by-step approach can help minimize the likelihood of excessive gas.

Keep the water flowing. Drinking plenty of water is crucial as it helps your digestive system handle higher protein levels more efficiently. Proper hydration aids in the breakdown and absorption of nutrients, which can help prevent gas buildup.

Sometimes, your body needs a little extra help. Enzyme supplements like Beano or Lactaid can be game-changers, especially if you consume proteins that your body struggles with. These supplements help break down proteins and lactose, making digestion smoother and less gassy.

Variety isn’t just the spice of life — it can also be the solution to your protein fart problems. If whey protein tends to upset your stomach, explore other options like plant-based or animal-based proteins that might be easier to digest. Diversifying your protein sources can also ensure you get a broad range of nutrients.

What you blend your protein powder with can make a big difference. If you’re whipping up a protein shake, be mindful of adding high-fiber fruits and vegetables, as these can also increase gas production. Try to find a balance that allows you to enjoy the benefits of protein and fiber without the extra flatulence.

Introducing probiotics into your diet can improve your gut health, which can help manage and reduce gas production. Whether through supplements or probiotic-rich foods like yogurt, kefir, or sauerkraut, boosting your gut flora can aid in better overall digestion and less discomfort from gas.

Protein farts are a rather windy side effect of a high-protein diet, but they don’t have to knock you off course. Try easing into your protein consumption, staying hydrated, diversifying your protein sources, and integrating enzyme supplements or probiotics to max those gains, minus the stink bombs!

Big discounts and impressive specs can be tempting, but after years of testing drawing tablets, here's my advice on finding the creative tech that's actually worth buying.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Black Friday and Cyber Monday are a funny time for everyone, but artists can feel more tempted than most, because there are definite things, particularly drawing tablets, you’ve likely had your eye on. Everything you've vaguely thought about buying for six months suddenly has a big red discount sticker.The tablet you've been eyeing is £200 cheaper, a new stylus promises twice the pressure sensitivity, and maybe this time you need an Android drawing tablet. For some reason, you now really need an Android drawing tablet.

I've spent years testing the best drawing tablets, and even I get swept up in the Cyber Monday FOMO. My advice is simple: spend on things that will make you a better or happier artist, not on whatever has the biggest discount.

Cyber Monday is a time when headline discounts could be misleading. That 40% off looks impressive, but what did the product cost a month ago? Some retailers inflate discounts, so check the price history.Then ask whether you need it at all. Upgrading everything at once adds up fast, and the best upgrade is often duller: a comfortable chair, a decent desk lamp, fresh nibs or a bigger external drive.Do you really need an OLED tablet? Some specs target pros who work 10-hour days; if you’re a hobbyist like me, you don’t need a 27-inch drawing tablet. It’s great, but you don’t need one.

Manufacturers love big numbers. One tablet offers 8,192 pressure levels; another, 16,384, as if the second must be twice as good. It isn't, and 8,192 is plenty for most artists. Read my article on the 7 mistakes everyone makes when buying a new drawing tablet. I've added some advice below:

Screenless 'graphics' tablets like the Wacom Intuos Pro are cheaper and more portable, and once you're used to drawing by glancing up at a monitor, they're perfectly good. Some people even prefer them, since they force you to sit upright in a better posture. These are often a good alternative to using a mouse. If you do want a display, focus on size and resolution rather than buying the biggest one you can afford. Do you need 4K on a 27-inch screen? Will a huge screen work for travel?One of my favourites is the Huion Kamvas 22 (Gen 3); it's a good size, 2.5K and 90Hz. Standalone Android drawing tablets are also worth a look, as they free you from your computer. New ones like XPPen’s Magic Pro 13 can connect to a PC and work as a standard pen display. With Android tablets, check that your apps are supported, because the experience won't match an iPad or desktop.

It's easy to buy for the artist you imagine becoming, the one who sculpts in 3D or draws every day. An expensive drawing tablet, iPad Pro or new stylus won't make that happen. Beginners, an affordable tablet is fine. Professionals, a better stylus or screen may improve your workflow. Either way, pay only for features you'll use and the specs you need.

I know this is a creative tech newsletter, but traditional materials are also a good value in sales. Pencils, brushes, sketchbooks and paints may give you more enjoyment than more hardware. Consider some of these:

#8993. Russia Is Erasing Memories of the Gulag and Reframing Stalin’s History

All over Russia, memories of the Soviet Union and its former dictator Joseph Stalin are being manipulated to tell a new story by the government of President Vladimir V. Putin. An investigative report by The New York Times details how the horrors of Gulag camps are being reframed to depict the Soviets as the victors of World War II and the fight against Nazism. Russia is also using the memory of WWII to act as an extension of its fight against Ukraine.

Efforts to rewrite the story of Russia were already in play before the country’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine on February 24, 2022. Notably, Memorial, an organization dedicated to memorializing the camps, was dissolved and labelled an “extremist organization” by Russia’s Supreme Court, forcing the group to move its operations abroad. Memorial was also awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2022. Related Articles EU Countries Renew Call To Exclude Russia from Venice Ahead of 2027 Architecture Biennale Russian Teenager Detained After Posting Neo-Nazi Threats on TikTok, Targeting Moscow Museum

The Gulag was established by Vladimir Lenin in the late 1910s and early 1920s, but Stalin was the one who expanded the operation from the 1920s to the early 1950s. Nearly 1.5 million people were imprisoned in the Gulag and died from extreme cold, starvation, disease, and intense labor. Monuments that preserved its painful history are now being erased or censored. Examples include the shuttering of Moscow’s Gulag Museum earlier this year and the disappearance of at least 26 memorials dedicated to Gulag victims since 2022.

Additionally, in the summer, a Gulag memorial plaque was removed from the Arctic village Yur-Shor, and more symbols of the Gulag are starting to vanish. Under the power of the Kremlin, Russia is undergoing its own modern-day “digital gulag,” according to the Independent. To wit, a mandate now requires that all new digital devices be equipped with the messenger app Max, launched last year by the Russian tech company VK, which allows Russia’s Federal Security Service access to materials from the app.
