#8924. Rucking Benefits: Add Weight to Your Walk to Boost Fitness and Strength

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Weightlifting isn’t the only way to build muscle. Rucking, or walking with a weighted backpack, is also highly effective. It’s easy to start, can be done anywhere, and helps build muscle, burn fat, and boost endurance.

Curious? Keep reading to discover why rucking might become your new favorite workout!

Rucking is like taking your regular walk and cranking up the intensity with heavy cargo. It’s as simple as strapping on a weighted backpack (aka rucksack) and hitting the pavement, the trail, or wherever you like to roam. Originally dreamed up by the military to toughen up soldiers, rucking, or a rucksack march has, er, marched into civilian life as a killer workout.

What makes it awesome? The extra weight transforms a casual stroll into a workout that means business. Plus, it’s customizable — you can load up as much or as little weight as you want, making it perfect for any fitness level. And the best part is that you can ruck just about anywhere.

Rucking easily fits into a busy schedule. Ruck yes! Rucking is a low-impact, full-body workout that kicks butt.

#8923. Spring Allergies Can Cause Headaches. Here’s How to Deal

A stuffy nose and itchy, watery eyes are spring-allergy cornerstones—but they’re not the only symptoms that herald a pollen influx for some people. You might not immediately suspect a pulsing headache is due to allergies, but experts say it’s a common occurrence.

In fact, the same immune response that fills your nose with snot or leaves you sneezing up a storm can make your head throb. That’s especially true “if you have multiple seasonal allergies, for instance to grass and tree pollen; live near farms; or spend a lot of time outside during allergy season, being bombarded by pollen,” says Beth Oller, MD, a family medicine physician in Stockton, Kansas. Keep reading to learn why allergies can spark headaches, plus how to tell if your head pain is allergy-related and find relief.

If you have spring allergies and breathe in pollen, “your immune system perceives it as a foreign invader,” Dr. Oller says, and releases a bunch of inflammatory chemicals like histamine. The resulting inflammation triggers swelling in your nasal cavities, which are connected to your sinuses, says Rekha Raveendran, MD, allergist and immunologist at The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center. The sinuses extend behind the cheekbones, eyes, and bridge of the nose, and up into the forehead—so when they get puffy, you can wind up with a sensation of facial pressure and also headache, she explains.

At the same time, experiencing the effects of spring allergies may spark migraine attacks in those with migraine. The surge of inflammation and congestion can irritate a nearby nerve that plays a role in migraine, and allergy-driven fatigue and insomnia can be migraine triggers in and of themselves. Research suggests that among people with migraine, those who also have allergies tend to have worse, more frequent attacks than those who don’t.

An allergy headache typically feels like a dull throbbing in your temples, cheeks, or forehead, and makes your face feel heavy. It comes along with congestion, Dr. Oller says, and lying down or tilting your head can increase the pressure. (FYI: This is the same kind of pain as you’d get with a sinus headache, which is caused by a viral or bacterial infection in your sinuses—both lead to mucus buildup and swelling within the sinuses.)

By contrast, migraine attacks (whether or not they’re precipitated by allergies) trigger intense pain on one side of the head. They often come along with nausea, and sensitivity to light and sound, which you would not typically find with allergy headaches, Dr. Raveendran says. Meanwhile, tension headaches tend to feel more like a band squeezing around the head, and cluster headaches spark a surge of pain in or around one eye.

If you get walloped with allergy headaches each year, Dr. Oller suggests starting on an oral antihistamine medication before pollen counts rise. That's because antihistamines take a week or two of daily use to kick in, she explains. The non-drowsy options work best for daytime—think: cetirizine (Zyrtec), levocetirizine (Xyzal), loratadine (Claritin), or fexofenadine (Allegra). You can use the sleepiness-inducing diphenhydramine (Benadryl) at night, but just know that you shouldn’t make a habit of relying on it as a sleep aid.

Both doctors suggest pairing oral allergy meds with a nasal corticosteroid spray like fluticasone (Flonase) or triamcinolone (Nasocort). “They hit those mucus membranes and help decrease inflammation in that region,” Dr. Oller says. It’s best to take both drugs daily throughout allergy season, she adds, not just when you think you need them. (If your headaches are barely alleviated, or the pollen counts in your area are sky-high, you may also be able to safely increase your dose of these allergy meds to boost their efficacy.)

The less pollen that enters your airspace, the fewer symptoms you’ll experience. But you don’t have to stay cooped up to cut your exposure. Keeping your windows closed, using a high-efficiency particulate air (HEPA) filter in your HVAC system (or a portable air purifier that has one), and vacuuming often can make a difference, according to Dr. Oller.

Whenever you do spend ample time outside, Dr. Oller says to rinse off once you get home. This way, you’re not inhaling pollen any longer than you have to. While you’re at it, “shower your sinuses too,” Dr. Oller adds, with a nasal saline spray or Neti Pot. This helps clear some mucus to release pressure and offer temporary relief, Dr. Raveendran says.

If the congestion is making it feel like your face is chock-full of mucus, you might be tempted to reach for an OTC oral decongestant. But take note: While pseudoephedrine (Sudafed) can be helpful, it’s not recommended to use it more than a few days in a row, and isn’t a good choice if you have high blood pressure, Dr. Raveendran says. It’s a stimulant that can make some people feel jittery, or cause a fast heart rate or insomnia.

Nasal decongestants, which include phenylephrine- or oxymetazoline-based sprays (like Afrin and Vicks Sinex), can open up your nose fast but should only be used for three days at a time max, Dr. Raveendran adds. “There’s a risk of rebound congestion that leads to overall worsening of symptoms and addiction to the nasal decongestants,” she says.

Sometimes you just need in-the-moment relief for the head pain. In that case, you can pop an OTC pain reliever like ibuprofen (Advil), naproxen (Aleve), or acetaminophen (Tylenol), Dr. Oller says. The former two may be better at resolving allergy headaches because they combat inflammation. But it’s not advised to take these non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for more than 10 days straight (unless your doctor tells you otherwise) because of potential effects on your stomach and kidneys. Tylenol, by contrast, is generally safer to take long-term, though shouldn’t be combined with alcohol due to the risk for liver damage.

If you find that your allergy headaches have you reaching for pain relievers more than a few days in a row, check in with your primary care doctor or allergist. They may recommend a more intensive treatment, like prescription steroids, or suggest seeing an ear, nose, and throat doctor or neurologist, in case something else might be behind your head pain.

#8922. "How did young designers become so convinced of their own powerlessness?"

In the face of planetary collapse, design education and practice need to change to show young designers that it’s possible for them to make a difference, writes Céline Semaan.

The last time I taught a design class, at the School of Visual Arts (SVA) in New York, I remember sitting in my car after the two-hour workshop feeling quite honestly distraught. How had these young designers become so convinced of their own powerlessness?

During class, we discussed the political, ecological and economic infrastructures that make design possible: mineral extraction, exploited labour and the colonial systems sustaining much of what we produce and consume.

Having assumed these conversations had become an expected part of design education, I was taken aback by how little the students cared. Instead, they were far more concerned with securing and keeping jobs in an increasingly precarious industry.

Perhaps the profession needs to reconsider its relationship with obedience

“How do you expect us to make any difference if this is how the industry works?” one asked. Another just wanted to know how to earn a living, without upsetting their employers.

These were excellent questions, particularly as designers now compete with artificial intelligence capable of executing instructions at extraordinary speed. If design is reduced to following briefs and producing outputs, what space is there for a designer to effect any structural change?

Perhaps the profession needs to reconsider its relationship with obedience. Designers are trained to solve problems, yet rarely encouraged to question who defined them, whose interests they serve, or whether they should exist at all. They are commissioned to make products more sustainable without questioning production volumes, or improve services without examining the policies that make them inaccessible.

I often say design is a series of well-informed decisions. Every object, building and service emerges from decisions about resources, labor, budgets and the conditions of life.

Designers participate in these decisions, although they rarely control all of them. So where does their power begin and end?

Imagine a design studio commissioned by a city to address extreme heat in a low-income neighborhood. The brief requests solar-powered cooling shelters and shaded public spaces, with a fixed budget and deadline.

During research, the designers discover that the proposed shelters would be too far from elderly residents most vulnerable to heat, while existing community centers could accommodate cooling facilities at a lower cost. What should they do? Follow the brief, collect their fees and pretend their hands are tied? Refuse the commission, leaving another studio to complete the work, perhaps feeling rebellious for a moment?

There is a third possibility. They could show the city why its proposal would fail to reach its intended beneficiaries and present an alternative within the same budget. Working with residents and community organizations, they could identify accessible locations, compare costs and demonstrate how the alternative better meets the city’s objectives.

The difficult part is to make these commitments part of everyday practice, rather than optional gestures dependent on a sympathetic client

Here we see a tangible expansion of design as a civic responsibility. Designers can use their expertise to bring communities into decisions that affect their lives, improving outcomes while sharing decision-making power.

And if the city insists on its original proposal? The client controls the budget. A junior designer acting alone may have little negotiating power.

But a studio can incorporate community research into its contracts before work begins, negotiate a paid investigation phase and require the client to review evidence and alternatives before approving the design. Of course, this doesn’t guarantee agreement, but it makes critical inquiry a recognised part of the commission.

Design is a practice of applied imagination: understanding interconnected systems to intentionally shape the conditions of life. In this example, designers would examine the relationships between urban planning, public health, housing, energy and community governance. Their value lies partly in identifying what the original commission overlooked and developing viable possibilities with the people affected.

Thanks to the work of people like Victor Papanek, Tony Fry, Ezio Manzini and Arturo Escobar, by now it’s well understood that design has the capacity to shape the world but remains complicit in ecological and social destruction. The challenge today is to translate that knowledge into professional authority, economic leverage and meaningful participation in the decisions that will determine our collective futures.

Likewise, advocates of participatory design have long argued for involving people affected by design decisions. The difficult part is to make these commitments part of everyday practice, rather than optional gestures dependent on a sympathetic client.

Meeting these challenges requires rethinking design education. Designers need to learn to investigate the historical conditions behind a problem, understand ecological and economic relationships, and work alongside communities to develop alternatives.

Design can shape community-owned infrastructure, food systems and forms of local governance as well as products and buildings. These are tangible fields of work requiring collaboration and shared authority.

We should not ask young designers to compensate for structural failures through personal bravery alone

Of course, clients may refuse evidence, and insecure workers cannot always risk confrontation. Already there is too much pressure on Gen Z to save the world; we should not ask young designers to compensate for structural failures through personal bravery alone.

Studios, educators and commissioners must create paid roles and decision-making processes that give designers genuine influence. What if, for example, investigating the risks and assumptions behind a brief became an essential professional service, one that designers were commissioned and compensated to provide?

I keep thinking about those students at SVA, afraid of being considered difficult. We have taught them how to execute decisions without adequately preparing them to participate in making them. If designers are to take responsibility for their role in shaping the systems that govern our lives, they need a say in the decisions that produce those systems.

In the near future, success would mean residents gaining influence over where public money goes, with designers helping turn their priorities into lasting changes in public planning. This is design as a civic responsibility, and a meaningful distinction from machines optimized to execute instructions. To design possible futures, we must grow the agency designers hold, and the collective power they can help communities to build.

Céline Semaan is a Lebanese-Canadian designer, artist, writer, educator and speaker based in New York City, whose work focuses on climate issues and social justice. She is the founder of Slow Factory, a non-profit education and research platform that teaches about regenerative design. Her writing has appeared in The Cut, Vogue, Elle, Refinery29 and New York Magazine, among others. Her first book, A Woman Is a School, was published in 2024. Her upcoming book, Designing Possible Futures, explores the issues discussed in this article, and is due for publication in 2027.

#8921. Why Does My Side Hurt When I Run? Causes and Prevention Tips

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Side stitch, stomach cramp, side ache — whatever you wanna call it, that mid-run pain in your tum can seriously *cramp* your runner’s high.

This pesky prob that plagues runners and athletes all over has a scientific name: Exercise-related transient abdominal pain (ETAP). Though experts don’t know exactly what causes it, they have some ideas and tips about how to stop it.

Before you double-over during your next marathon, here’s what to know.

That fateful stab in your side is most likely to happen during exercise where your upper bod says tight and upright for an extended period, such as when you run, jog, bike, hike, play soccer, etc.

This common prob has been around for ages — the first historical mention is from ancient Roman philosopher Pliny the Elder. Yet, scientists still haven’t reached a consensus on its exact cause. We know that it affects up to 70% of runners each year.

It’s also more likely to occur on the right side.

A stiff spine or poor posture (according to older research from 2010) could contribute to side stitches – but TBH, the pros don’t know for sure.

According to a 2022 review, researchers also think a side stitch might be caused by your right foot hitting the ground while you breathe out, irritating a phrenic nerve. Researchers think this, in turn, may bother the lining of your abdomen (particularly on the lower right side). Since most people are right-foot dominant, this is one possible explanation.

Experts also theorize that it could be triggered by the boost of blood flow around the diaphragm when running.

Furthermore, fueling up before a big race is excellent — but eating or drinking large quantities right before running may boost your risk of getting a side stitch, anecdotal reports suggest.

When a side stitch strikes, don’t stress – there are steps you can take, including:

To stop a side stitch before it begins, here are some ideas FTW:

Side stitches are usually harmless. But it’s always a good idea to visit a pro if you experience any of the following probs:

Side stitches are a common issue and not typically the reason for concern. Though pros don’t know what causes them, they think issues with breathing, posture, or nerves may play a role.

Consider working on your running form or breathing to reduce the risk of experiencing a side stitch. Staying hydrated and avoiding huge meals pre-run may also help. Consider working with a physical therapist or personal trainer if your issues persist.

If you experience pain under your breastbone when running, visit a doctor asap.

#8920. Carlo Ratti and AI assistant to curate Seoul Biennale of Architecture and Urbanism 2027

Italian architect Carlo Ratti has been named the curator of next year’s Seoul Biennale of Architecture and Urbanism, for which he plans to take “an unconventional, AI-based” approach.

Taking place from 24 September 2027, the biennale will be used by Ratti as an opportunity to question the role of a curator today through the lens of architecture.

However, the event’s title, theme and full curatorial team will not be unveiled until 8 December.

What Ratti has revealed so far is that he plans to take “an unconventional, AI-based” approach to the event.

Specifically, he will use an AI assistant, aiming to challenge traditional approaches to developing exhibitions by highlighting emerging tools that can help curators.

“I am delighted to take on the direction of the Seoul Biennale and to explore the future of cities together with the Seoul Metropolitan Government,” says Carlo Ratti.

“Seoul is perhaps the best place in the world to ask how artificial intelligence and the collective wisdom of its citizens might shape the city together,” he continued.

“At the upcoming pre-biennale event, we will begin to introduce the people who will join us, and I think there will be a few surprises – one assistant curator isn’t even human!”

Ratti is an Italian architect and engineer, and director of his eponymous studio Carlo Ratti Associati. He is also a professor at Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT).

He was appointed by Seoul mayor Oh Se Hoon, succeeding British designer Thomas Heatherwick, who curated the 2025 event.

Heatherwick centred the event on a long, four-storey-high wall displaying images that reflected the ideals of his Humanise campaign.

The Seoul Biennale was established in 2017 by the Seoul Metropolitan Government as a festival of international architecture and urbanism.

“The Seoul Biennale is a place where architects and citizens from around the world think together about the future of cities and explore new possibilities,” said mayor Oh.

“Together with general director Carlo Ratti, who has connected architecture, cities, and technology, we will prepare so that the sixth Seoul Biennale offers a new perspective on cities and architecture and a meaningful experience for citizens.”

Ratti’s previous curatorial experience includes the Venice Architecture Biennale in 2025, for which the theme was Intelligens. Natural. Artificial. Collective. It explored how architecture can be adapted to increasingly unstable living environments through cross-disciplinary collaboration.

At the time, Ratti said, “Dezeen killed the traditional form of the biennale“.

The architect’s other recent projects include the French Pavilion at Expo 2025 Osaka and a proposal for a children’s hospital housed in a one-kilometre “green ring”.

Picture this: you've just landed in Honolulu after a long transcontinental flight. You've got four days on Maui planned, and then a few nights on Kauai before heading home. The problem? Those interisland flights add up fast — Hawaiian Airlines will gladly charge you $150–$250 *per person* for a 20-to-40-minute hop between islands. For a family of four, that's easily $600–$1,000 in airfare just to island-hop, on top of everything else you've already spent to get to Hawaii. Now imagine paying 7,500 HawaiianMiles per person instead — miles you transferred from your American Express Membership Rewards account at a 1:1 ratio just a day or two before booking. Suddenly, that $150–$250 ticket costs you points worth less than a nice dinner. At 3.3 cents per point on the high end, you're extracting extraordinary value from miles that most people leave sitting in an account doing nothing. This is what the ChooseFI community means when we talk about finding pricing inefficiencies in loyalty programs. Hawaiian Airlines prices these interisland segments on a dynamic award chart — but because these are short, regional hops operated almost entirely on 717s and A321s between islands most people aren't cross-shopping for redemptions, the program hasn't inflated the price the way major international carriers have. The sweet spot holds. The math is simple and satisfying: a cash ticket from Honolulu (HNL) to Kahului, Maui (OGG) or Lihue, Kauai (LIH) typically runs $100–$250. You're redeeming 7,500 miles to cover that cost, which means you're getting **1.3 to 3.3 cents per point** in value — above what most programs deliver on domestic redemptions. And because Hawaiian charges **zero fuel surcharges** on its own-operated flights, every mile goes toward the ticket price, not toward fees. For the FI-minded traveler who planned a multi-island Hawaii trip anyway, this redemption doesn't just save money — it reframes how you think about points. These aren't bonuses. They're a currency, and knowing where to spend them is the skill.

The core insight here is deceptively simple: HawaiianMiles prices interisland flights at a flat 7,500 miles in economy, and that price is shockingly stable relative to what these tickets actually cost in cash.

Here's why this works as a pricing inefficiency. Hawaiian Airlines operates a near-monopoly on interisland travel in Hawaii. There's limited true competition for these routes (go! Mokulele operates turboprops on some routes, but Hawaiian dominates the jet service). Because cash demand is inelastic — visitors need to get between islands — Hawaiian charges a premium in cash. But the HawaiianMiles award program hasn't kept pace with those cash price increases in the same aggressive way that programs like United MileagePlus or Delta SkyMiles have. The result: 7,500 miles per segment, consistently, while cash prices climb.

Now let's talk about how you actually get those miles into your account.

The primary transfer path the ChooseFI community uses is American Express Membership Rewards → HawaiianMiles at a 1:1 ratio. If you have the Amex Gold, Platinum, or a no-annual-fee Amex Everyday card earning MR points, you can transfer directly to Hawaiian. Transfer speed is 1–2 days — not instant, so plan accordingly and don't wait until the last minute.

Two other paths exist if you're working with different currencies:

One critical nuance: HawaiianMiles are earned primarily through flying, not credit card spend. Hawaiian does have a co-branded credit card, but it's not a top earner for most people's daily spend. This means your primary accumulation strategy is transfer partners — Amex MR and Bilt are your best levers.

Another key detail: Hawaiian miles never expire. This matters because you can slowly accumulate miles across multiple statement cycles, transfer when you're ready to book, and not feel rushed. There's no expiration clock running against you.

Finally, the no fuel surcharges policy is a genuine differentiator. Many programs — particularly those involving European carriers — tack on $300–$600 in surcharges that gut your redemption's net value. HawaiianMiles charges no fuel surcharges on Hawaiian-operated flights. Your 7,500 miles covers the flight. Taxes and fees on interisland tickets are minimal, often just a few dollars. What you see is what you get.

Go to hawaiianairlines.com and use the 'Book' tool, selecting 'Reward Travel' as your travel type. Enter your route — for example, HNL to OGG (Honolulu to Kahului, Maui) or HNL to LIH (Honolulu to Lihue, Kauai). Plug in your desired travel date and search. You're looking for economy award space priced at 7,500 miles. Availability on interisland routes is almost always wide open — this is one of the best availability scores (5/5) of any sweet spot in this guide series, but it costs nothing to confirm before you transfer.

If you don't have a HawaiianMiles account, create one at hawaiianairlines.com — it takes about two minutes and is free. Note your HawaiianMiles number. You'll need it for the transfer step.

From Amex Membership Rewards: Log into your Amex account, navigate to 'Membership Rewards,' select 'Transfer Points,' and choose Hawaiian Airlines HawaiianMiles as the destination. Enter your HawaiianMiles number and the number of miles you want to transfer (at minimum, 7,500 per person you're booking). Transfers process in 1–2 days.

From Bilt Rewards: Log into your Bilt app or biltrewards.com, navigate to 'Redeem,' select 'Transfer to Airline Partner,' and choose Hawaiian Airlines at 1:1. Same 1–2 day transfer window.

From Marriott Bonvoy®: Use this only as a last resort due to the 3:1 ratio. Navigate to Bonvoy's transfer portal and select HawaiianMiles. Allow up to 5 days.

Once your miles land (check your HawaiianMiles account balance), return to hawaiianairlines.com, log in, and re-run your award search. Select the flight you want, confirm the 7,500-mile price, and proceed through checkout. Taxes on interisland awards are typically just a few dollars — no fuel surcharges apply.

HawaiianMiles opens its booking window 330 days out. If you're planning a Hawaii trip far in advance and have specific flight times in mind, you can search and book early. That said, given the excellent availability on these routes, booking 2–4 weeks out is usually fine.

This is rare for interisland routes, but if it happens, try: searching adjacent dates, looking at different departure times on the same route, or checking alternate routing (e.g., OGG to LIH instead of HNL to LIH directly). Interisland availability doesn't fluctuate the way transatlantic business class does.

Let's make this concrete. You're planning a two-week Hawaii trip for two people. You've booked your Honolulu arrival flight separately, and now you need to connect the dots between islands: Honolulu (HNL) to Kahului, Maui (OGG) mid-trip, and then Maui (OGG) to Lihue, Kauai (LIH) before heading home.

The cash price check: Pull up hawaiianairlines.com and look at what these tickets retail for. On a typical mid-trip travel day, the HNL→OGG segment is priced at $189 per person. The OGG→LIH hop runs $149 per person. For two travelers, that's $676 in cash — before you've bought a single plate of shave ice.

The points price: Each segment costs 7,500 HawaiianMiles per person in economy. Two passengers, two flights: 30,000 HawaiianMiles total, plus roughly $10–$20 in taxes and fees across both bookings. No fuel surcharges.

The CPP calculation: You're replacing $676 in cash spending with 30,000 miles. That's 2.25 cents per point — well above the 0.8–1.2 cpp you'd expect on typical HawaiianMiles redemptions, and solidly within the 1.3–3.3 cpp sweet spot range for this redemption.

What the experience looks like: Hawaiian's interisland product is no-frills — these are 20-to-40-minute flights on Boeing 717s. You won't get a meal or premium service. But you will get a reliable, on-time carrier, clean aircraft, and the undeniable satisfaction of hopping between two of the most beautiful island destinations on Earth without opening your wallet at the gate.

For the ChooseFI traveler, the win isn't the in-flight experience — it's the mental accounting shift. You budgeted for interisland flights; now that budget goes to a sunset sailing charter or a snorkeling excursion instead. The points paid for the planes. The cash funds the memories.

Do: Transfer Points in the Right Batch Size HawaiianMiles doesn't allow you to transfer partial miles back out, so calculate exactly how many you need before initiating a transfer. For two passengers on two flights, that's 30,000 miles. Transfer exactly that amount — or a small buffer — rather than dumping your entire MR balance into a program you may not use frequently.

Do: Use Amex MR or Bilt as Your Primary Earning Strategy Since HawaiianMiles are earned primarily through flying, your accumulation plan should center on transferable currencies. The Amex Gold Card (4x on dining and groceries) and Amex Platinum (5x on flights) are elite MR earners. Bilt's no-annual-fee card earning on rent is underused by the ChooseFI community for exactly this kind of transfer.

Do: Search for Availability Before You Transfer This is worth repeating as a pro tip because new points travelers make this mistake constantly. Transfer speeds are 1–2 days for Amex MR and Bilt. Don't transfer points and then discover the flight you wanted is sold out. Always confirm availability first, then transfer, then book immediately once miles land.

Avoid: Using Marriott Bonvoy® for This Transfer At a 3:1 ratio, you'd spend 22,500 Bonvoy points for a 7,500-mile award. Bonvoy points are worth approximately 0.7–0.9 cpp on their own best redemptions. The math doesn't hold here — save your Bonvoy points for hotel redemptions.

Do: Consider the Merger Context Hawaiian Airlines is in the process of merging with Alaska Airlines, and HawaiianMiles may eventually transition into Alaska Mileage Plan. Pay attention to program announcements. This could change transfer partners, award pricing, or program structure. The current sweet spot exists now — book it while the program operates under its current rules.

Avoid: Waiting for a 'Better' Redemption on These Miles HawaiianMiles are a limited-use currency. They're excellent for interisland and mainland-to-Hawaii flights, but they don't transfer to other airlines and don't unlock international business class sweet spots. If you've got miles in this program, use them for exactly what they're designed for — Hawaiian flights — rather than letting them sit hoping for a better opportunity that may never come.

Do: Book Multiple Segments in a Single Trip If you're doing a true multi-island itinerary, every interisland hop is 7,500 miles. Three islands means two hops — 15,000 miles per person. Plan your island sequence to minimize backtracking, and book all segments at once once your miles transfer.

Make multi-island trips affordable with the right points strategy

Most visitors to Hawaii stick to one island because interisland flights add $100-$400+ per person to the trip cost. By using points for these short hops, you unlock a fundamentally different Hawaii experience — island-hopping from Oahu to Maui to the Big Island to Kauai without the airfare costs stacking up. This is a multiplier strategy: you are not just saving on one flight, you are enabling an entirely different type of trip. Combining a points-funded mainland-to-Hawaii flight with points-funded interisland hops creates a nearly free (in cash) multi-island Hawaiian vacation.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Decide which islands you want to visit and in what order. The most common combinations are Oahu + Maui, Oahu + Big Island, or a three-island itinerary. Map out how many interisland hops you need so you know the total points required.

Check Hawaiian Airlines (7,500 miles each way), Southwest (variable, typically 4,000-8,000 points), and United (5,000-7,500 miles) for each interisland segment. Southwest often offers the best flexibility with no change fees and no blackout dates.

For Hawaiian Airlines, transfer Amex Membership Rewards. For Southwest, earn Rapid Rewards directly or transfer from Chase (transfer to Southwest is currently limited). For United segments, transfer from Chase or use Turkish Miles&Smiles for even lower pricing.

Book each interisland hop as a separate one-way award. This gives you maximum flexibility to mix airlines and optimize pricing per segment. One-way awards have no penalty compared to round trips on these short routes.

Align your interisland hops with your arrival and departure flights. Arrive on one island and depart from a different one (open-jaw booking) to avoid backtracking. For example, arrive Honolulu, hop to Maui, depart Maui to the mainland.

Hawaiian Airlines has the most extensive interisland network and offers the most daily frequencies. Southwest Airlines also operates key interisland routes (Honolulu-Maui, Honolulu-Kona, Honolulu-Lihue). United flies select interisland segments as well. Each airline has different award pricing and transfer partner access.

Hawaiian Airlines interisland awards typically price at 7,500 HawaiianMiles each way. Southwest varies by cash fare but generally costs 4,000-8,000 Rapid Rewards points each way for interisland hops. United interisland segments can be booked for 5,000-7,500 miles using various Star Alliance partner programs.

Yes, especially when booking multiple hops. A family of four making two interisland hops at $150 each way would spend $1,200 in cash. Converting that to points frees up significant cash for accommodations, activities, and dining. The per-point value (1.5-2.5 cents) is reasonable, and the trip flexibility gained is substantial.

A popular strategy is to fly into Honolulu (Oahu), hop to Maui for beaches and Haleakala, then continue to the Big Island (Kona) for volcanoes and snorkeling, and optionally finish on Kauai for dramatic scenery. Each hop is 30-60 minutes. Allow 2-3 days minimum per island.

This redemption was built for families and couples planning a multi-island Hawaii vacation — full stop. If you're visiting multiple islands (which most Hawaii first-timers and repeat visitors do), you're already mentally budgeting for interisland flights. This sweet spot simply redirects that cash budget back into your pocket and replaces it with points.

Families get a 5/5 Family Friendly score here for good reason: availability is wide open, booking is simple, and the economics scale beautifully. Four people, two hops = 60,000 miles to cover potentially $1,200+ in interisland airfare. That's an extraordinary displacement of vacation cash.

Beginners are explicitly welcomed by this redemption's design. There's no partner airline complexity, no fuel surcharge math to calculate, no routing rules to decode. You search on Hawaiian's website, you transfer points, you book. The 5/5 Beginner Friendly and Easy to Book scores reflect that this is genuinely one of the simplest award redemptions you can execute.

Minimum points needed: 7,500 HawaiianMiles per person per segment. For a solo traveler doing two hops, that's 15,000 miles. For a family of four doing two hops, that's 60,000 miles.

This is NOT for: Travelers who don't have an Amex MR or Bilt account and no path to earning HawaiianMiles quickly. It's also not ideal for travelers who only need a single interisland flight — the opportunity cost of setting up the transfer relationship for 7,500 miles may not be worth it unless you're already accumulating MR points for other redemptions.

This redemption earns a **Beginner** rating — and it genuinely deserves it. In a world of waitlists, fuel surcharges, routing rules, and phone-only bookings, Hawaiian interisland awards are refreshingly clean. **What makes it easy:** Award availability is consistently excellent (5/5). The booking portal is functional and user-friendly. There are no fuel surcharges to calculate. Miles never expire, so there's no pressure. You can complete the entire redemption — from transfer initiation to confirmed booking — in about 48 hours. **The one genuine friction point:** Earning HawaiianMiles isn't as straightforward as earning Chase Ultimate Rewards or Amex MR. Hawaiian doesn't have a widely-used co-branded credit card for most people's everyday spend. This means you're dependent on transfer partners, and the Amex MR and Bilt paths are your primary options. If you don't have either, this redemption becomes harder to access. **Tip 1:** Start with an Amex card that earns Membership Rewards — the Amex Gold is the ChooseFI community favorite for everyday earning. Once you're accumulating MR points, you have a direct path to Hawaiian via a 1:1 transfer. **Tip 2:** Always search award availability before transferring. It takes 30 seconds and protects you from the one mistake that could derail an otherwise smooth booking. **Tip 3:** Don't overthink the merger situation. Hawaiian and Alaska remain separate programs today. Book what's in front of you. If you can earn Amex MR points, you can execute this redemption. It's the perfect first award booking for a ChooseFI member who wants to see how the system works without risking complexity.

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

Interisland awards are the key that unlocks multi-island Hawaii vacations without the stacking airfare costs that keep most travelers on a single island. At 7,500-10,000 miles per hop, the points cost is modest, and the trip transformation is significant. Whether you use Hawaiian Airlines miles, Southwest Rapid Rewards, or United partner programs, the strategy is the same: let points handle the short hops so your cash stays in your pocket for experiences. Combined with a points-funded mainland-to-Hawaii flight, interisland awards make a multi-island Hawaiian vacation one of the most achievable aspirational trips in travel rewards.

#8917. Does Magnesium Help You Lose Belly Fat?

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

We include products we think are useful for our readers. If you buy through links on this page, we may earn a small commission. Here’s our process

Magnesium is found in fatty fish, leafy greens, whole grains — and the supplement aisle.

The mighty mineral plays many essential roles in our bodies, but can it help tighten the belt buckle?

While magnesium can sneakily support weight loss in a few ways, that’s not its main gig.

“Magnesium alone is not a magic bullet for weight loss,” says Paunel Vukasinov, MD, a dual board-certified internist and obesity medicine specialist with Medical Offices of Manhattan.

“A comprehensive approach including diet, exercise, and other lifestyle changes are essential,” Vukasinov adds.

Here are a few ways magnesium may support weight loss, as explained by Vukasinov.

“Magnesium is not classified as an appetite suppressant,” Vukasinov says.

“However, by potentially stabilizing blood sugar and insulin levels, magnesium may reduce cravings and help prevent overeating. This effect can indirectly support weight loss.”

Vukasinov reminds us that no specific magnesium dosage is prescribed solely for fat loss.

With that in mind, the Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA) for magnesium is:

Vukasinov says that sticking to the RDA ensures you meet your body’s needs without over-supplementing.

“Excessive intake does not enhance weight loss and may lead to adverse effects,” he adds.

According to Vukasinov, it’s best to get magnesium from food since a nutrient-dense diet, including whole foods, boosts your intake of other extra essentials like fiber, which improves overall health.

Here are some foods you can gobble up for the most magnesium:

If you know your diet isn’t cutting it, you can find magnesium supplements at major retailers, like Wal-Mart and Target, drug stores, or Amazon.

PSA: The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) does not check the safety or effectiveness of dietary supplements, so it’s important to choose a reputable brand that undertakes third-party testing to prove the purity and quality of their products.

For some, magnesium supplements may cause a few unsavory side effects, including diarrhea, stomach upset, or cramping.

Remember that there are many forms of magnesium. Vukasinov points out that magnesium citrate or magnesium oxide can have a laxative effect (yikes).

Be sure you’re taking the best dose based on your RDA, and consider taking it with a meal to better avoid side effects.

Magnesium is not a miracle solution for weight loss, but getting enough of it can ensure that your body produces enough energy and gets enough sleep — both play a big hand in weight management.

Taking too much will have you gripping your belly with stomach pain or diarrhea, so stick to the daily recommended amounts.

Last medically reviewed on August 31, 2024

#8916. RSHP centres cantilevered office building Sąvaržėlė around glass atrium

UK studio RSHP has revealed its first project in the Baltic region, a mixed-use office building in Lithuania designed as “a landmark that is unmistakably forward-looking”.

Named after the Lithuanian word for paperclip, the seven-storey Sąvaržėlė is located in central Vilnius, between the UNESCO-listed Old Town and the city’s commercial district.

The stacked building has a cantilevered design and houses office space, a conference hall, a restaurant and a cafe across its 19,000-square-metre space.

“At Sąvaržėlė, we wanted to create a workplace that extends into the city – one that welcomes people, encourages collaboration and contributes new public spaces to Vilnius,” RSHP associate director Jack Evans-Newton said.

“Occupying a unique position between the historic centre and the city’s emerging business district, the building brings these two identities together through a calm and contemporary architectural expression,” he continued.

“Clarity of form, generous public spaces and carefully crafted detailing create a landmark that is unmistakably forward-looking, reflecting the ambition of a growing business district while respecting the scale and character of its historic setting.”

Sąvaržėlė has large, adaptable floorplates, designed to create a flexible interior.

The building has a stacked, rectangular shape and was made from prefabricated steel components that were bolted together on site. On the east and west facades, RSHP placed external ribs that the studio said “echo the tones” of Vilnius’ historic architecture.

Sąvaržėlė is arranged around a central glass atrium with a striking yellow-lined elevator. It can be accessed via a number of different entrances that connect to the surrounding streets.

To enhance the building’s environmental performance, RSHP added a double-skin facade. This uses energy-efficient chilled beam cooling and automated natural ventilation to help reduce energy demand.

In addition, Sąvaržėlė has a 2,897-square-metre fully landscaped green roof.

RSHP has also recently designed a 45-storey skyscraper in Shenzhen and a curved-roof railway hub.

#8915. Can You Actually ‘Boost’ Your Metabolism?

Few bodily processes are as focused on and as misunderstood as metabolism. It seems like just about everyone wants to “boost” or “speed up” their metabolism in the hopes of burning more calories and, as a result, losing body fat. In reality, this is not an easy task, but you wouldn’t know that from the countless TikToks claiming it’s as simple as taking a shot of apple cider vinegar, hopping into an infrared sauna, or braving a cold plunge.

The truth? Many of these supposed hacks don’t have much research backing them up, and the ones that do won’t meaningfully move the needle when it comes to your weight. Improving your metabolism actually boils down to a few basic tenets that aren’t flashy or sexy but can have long-term benefits for your overall health and well-being. We’ll get into all that, but first, a little background on what your metabolism even is.

Metabolism is commonly thought of as the mechanism that controls your weight. Having a “fast” metabolism means your body burns calories rapidly, making it easier to maintain or lose weight, while having a “slow” metabolism means you gain pounds more easily and have a harder time taking them off. This isn’t wrong, per se, but it doesn’t tell the whole story. Your metabolism is the way your body turns food into energy. This energy is then used to power your heart and lungs, build and repair tissue, regulate hormones, and perform other critical functions.

Put more succinctly, “metabolism is all the chemical processes that keep our body alive and functioning,” explains Jonathan Gabison, MD, an assistant professor of family medicine at the University of Michigan who is board-certified in obesity medicine.

For example, about 20% of the energy your metabolism provides goes to your brain, building neurotransmitters and keeping signals going, so having an efficient metabolism is critical for cognitive health.

In short, yes. Your metabolism is influenced by loads of factors, from genetics and age to weight. But that doesn’t mean your metabolism is fixed. It’s actually highly modifiable, says Shebani Sethi, MD, a clinical associate professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Stanford University and the founding director of the world’s first academic metabolic psychiatry clinical program.

That said, taking shots of apple cider vinegar in the morning or picking up “metabolism-boosting” supplements won’t do the trick. Research shows that improving your metabolism requires consistent long-term habits. Here are five that can make an impact.

Every time you move your body, it burns calories and raises your metabolism—both during the moment and for a period afterward. Think of your metabolism like a pie: Two thirds of the energy you use every day is devoted to keeping you alive (that’s your basal metabolic rate), and the rest goes toward digesting food and moving your body. Being more active is the most straightforward way to up your metabolism. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends that adults get at least 150 minutes of moderate intensity physical activity a week.

This can include dedicated exercise, like a jog, hike, or workout class. (The CDC recommends that adults get at least 150 minutes of moderate intensity physical activity a week.) But it also extends to all the movement you do outside of formal exercise, known as NEAT (non-exercise activity thermogenesis). Increasing your daily step count, prioritizing physical hobbies like gardening and walking your dog, or even taking on more household chores and grocery runs all count toward upping your overall movement.

Strength training helps build and maintain muscle mass. Muscle tissue is metabolically active, which means sustaining it burns more calories than maintaining fat tissue. Therefore, having more muscle mass will give your metabolism a slight boost.

By strength training you’re also improving your overall health. For instance, since muscle tissue uses the majority of the glucose in your bloodstream, more muscle mass can increase your body’s capacity to use glucose and help prevent blood sugar spikes. Plus, research has shown that having more muscle helps improve insulin sensitivity, including in individuals without diabetes.

Those same CDC exercise guidelines suggest including at least two days of strength training every week. That can include body-weight moves like push-ups and lunges; lifting weights with dumbbells, kettlebells, barbells, or cable machines; or utilizing resistance bands. Dr. Gabison says what’s most important is being consistent with your exercise routine, so it’s best to choose workouts you’re likely to stick with. And remember, if you’re just starting out, it’s important not to push yourself too hard early on and risk injury.

Protein is having a major moment right now. While things may be getting a little out of hand (hello, protein popcorn), consuming sufficient amounts of high-quality protein has well-established benefits for your metabolism. That’s because the nutrient is the building block of muscle, so eating enough of it helps support muscle growth and maintenance, especially if you’re resistance training.

Protein also has the highest thermic effect of all three macronutrients, meaning digesting it burns more calories than carbohydrates or fats. Plus, it’s the most satiating macro, so increasing your protein intake can help you feel fuller and fend off cravings, which may help with weight management.

However, balance is key. Sun Kim, MD, MS, a board-certified endocrinologist and associate professor of medicine at Stanford, says doctors and health care providers have different viewpoints on how much protein is enough for optimal health. In her opinion, “most Americans eat plenty of protein without trying,” she says, cautioning that consuming excessive amounts won’t magically speed up your metabolism and could even worsen insulin sensitivity in some cases. So unless you’re extremely active, there’s no need to get hundreds of grams a day.

For most healthy adults, the recommended dietary allowance for protein is 0.8 grams per kilogram of body weight per day. That means a 120-pound person needs roughly 43 grams of protein a day, which is about what you’d find in two four-ounce hamburger patties. If you incorporate some protein into every snack and meal throughout the day, you should easily hit the mark. That said, some groups need more. People who are pregnant, breastfeeding, or highly active may need up to 2 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight per day. Older adults and those taking GLP-1s should also be mindful of their intake, as reduced appetite can lead to inadequate protein intake and muscle loss, particularly when coupled with reduced physical activity.

An often-overlooked habit for better metabolism is getting quality sleep. A lack of sleep dysregulates your metabolism, causing a cascade of issues, including worsened glucose management, more intense hunger the next day, and reduced energy expenditure. (Sleepy people are less likely to move their bodies.) When this happens consistently, it can lead to an increased risk of obesity, type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, and heart disease. Sleep also has an impact on hormones that can slow down the metabolism.

There isn’t a specific number of hours you should sleep each night, but research shows that most adults do best with seven to nine hours of quality rest most evenings.

Prolonged stress keeps your cortisol (stress hormone) levels chronically elevated, which can break down muscle tissue and slow your metabolism. Constantly pulling out your hair can also disrupt your appetite-regulating hormones, triggering cravings that may prompt you to eat more. All of these things can affect your weight. Research shows chronic stress can increase your risk of obesity, type 2 diabetes, and related cardiometabolic complications too.

There is, sadly, no quick fix for reducing stress, so some trial and error might be required to figure out what works best for you. Some places to start are doing yoga, meditating, practicing breathing exercises, going for walks outside, journaling, spending time with loved ones, engaging in relaxing hobbies, or starting therapy to talk through whatever is weighing on you.

Sure, supporting a healthy metabolism can increase the number of calories you burn and help with weight management. But it can also improve what’s known as your metabolic health, which encompasses measures such as blood pressure, cholesterol, insulin sensitivity, and total body fat. Having good metabolic health is essential for preventing chronic diseases such as type 2 diabetes and heart disease. The healthier your metabolism, the more calories you burn and the better your metabolic health.

#8913. Meet BC Architects & Studies & Materials, Marina Tabassum's pick for the most influential architect of the next 20 years

In this interview for Dezeen’s 20×20 project in partnership with Kohler, two of BC Architects & Studies & Materials’ founders discuss how their ideas have gone from being perceived as the product of “young idealism” to being taken seriously by the construction sector.

The Brussels-based studio is at the forefront of bio-regional and circular design, with a whole arm of its practice dedicated to the development of new materials, often making use of construction waste.

Recently, the studio worked with UK studio Assemble and circular design lab Atelier Luma to create Le Magasin Électrique at Luma Arles in France, with a palette that included everything from rammed earth and construction waste to salt and algae.

Alongside these likeminded practitioners, BC Architects & Studies & Materials is at the forefront of a recent wave of interest in bio-based materials and vernacular methods – ideas that the studio has been championing for some 15 years, pushing for systemic change in the industry.

Founded between 2009 and 2012 by Ken De Cooman, Wes Degreef, Nicolas Coeckelberghs and Laurens Bekemans, the origins of BC Architects & Studies & Materials were – as its tripartite name suggests – not particularly conventional.

The studio is comprised of three different legal entities: BC Architects, an architecture cooperative; BC Studies, a non-profit “education laboratory”; and BC Materials, a material production co-operative.

BC Architects & Studies & Materials’s approach and outlook was borne out of a series of early projects in Burundi, Morocco and Ethiopia – where the studio briefly had a satellite office – which were grounded in working with local communities and materials.

“A lot of our first experiences in architecture were linked to different construction cultures,” said De Cooman. “I lived in Ethiopia for five years, others were in Morocco for a long time, and at the same time, we were finding our way in Belgium.”

“It was a different path to learning architecture as a practitioner,” he continued. We learnt to work with local materials and short supply chains, to make do with what you find around.”

The studio’s first built project was the Library of Muyinga in Burundi, developed using an open-source template from the OpenStructures network and constructed from compressed earth bricks alongside members of the local community.

It feels much more valid to be doing this in our own construction culture

BC Architects & Studies & Materials also designed several school buildings and a women’s shelter in Morocco, often using the construction process itself as an opportunity for the sharing of knowledge around vernacular construction techniques and materials.

According to De Cooman, however, this strand of the studio’s work was never intended to be long-term.

Challenging a tendency in the industry to view these methods and techniques as solely belonging to the realm of “humanitarian” architecture, BC Architects & Studies & Materials’s aim was to apply them to the business-as-usual processes of architecture and construction back home in Belgium.

“It feels much more valid to be doing this in our own construction culture,” said De Cooman.

“It was a huge learning process, and now we’re really focussing on the here and now because it’s here that we need to actually change the most.”

While a big part of this change is the studio’s use of alternative materials, it was also based on the idea of building being an opportunity for shared learning, driven by BC’s belief in the the need for architects to be more engaged with the construction process.

We’re still trying to emulate what our first experiences were: creating shared learning environments with people that can bring together different skills and learn from each other by really engaging with other field

Several of the studio’s early projects in Belgium the result of these learning workshops. Maison de Chasse, a rammed-earth hunting house, was constructed over the course of the first rammed earth workshop in Belgium, based on the techniques of Martin Rauch and Anna Heringer.

In 2017, the renovation of a series of warehouses in Ghent into an artist’s studio for Pascale Marthine Tayou was achieved via a five-week “Urban Construction Camp”, in which volunteers created a new hempcrete structure inside an existing metal shell.

“We’re still trying to emulate what our first experiences were: creating shared learning environments with people that can bring together different skills and learn from each other by really engaging with other fields, not on paper, but with the heart and the hands included,” explained De Cooman.

“It is crazy that we now have a system where, as an architect, you draw all the execution files and send them to a contractor to execute it exactly how you drew it.”

“The magic happens when everyone can get together – you can draw it together, find a passionate contractor to make it with.”

BC Architects & Studies & Materials was keen, however, to not be defined by this smaller-scale work, with the whole point being to demonstrate how these techniques and materials could be scaled up into larger contexts.

The idea of BC is to not only do small projects but also to change the building culture by making these materials available to big contractors and buildings

A key means to achieving this was the formal establishing of BC Materials in 2018, enabled by the interest generated by their earlier projects. Alongside consultancy, workshops and training, the BC Materials arm also offers its own range of earth and clay products, Léém.

“The idea of BC is to not only do small projects but also to change the building culture by making these materials available to big contractors and buildings,” says Wes Degreef.

“I think we were very surprised that the idea of working with a certain bioregion and its materials is something that we forgot in Europe.”

“Some of it still exists, but you really have to search for it. And with earth materials, for example, those crafts don’t exist anymore in Belgium. So we had to do it; we became the craftsmen.”

Sure enough, the scale of the projects involving BC Architects & Studies & Materials – whether they are engaged as architects or as craftspeople – is growing.

“In the beginning, we were just like young, crazy people who are doing these weird things on Belgium,” said De Cooman.

“There was a bit of interest in it, but it was also seen as, young, idealist energy. Now, we’re operating at a scale where we are actually seen as serious partners in the construction sector here in Belgium.”

There was a bit of interest in it, but it was also seen as, young, idealist energy. Now, we’re operating at a scale where we are actually seen as serious partners in the construction sector here in Belgium

In Brussels, BC Architects & Studies & Materials worked alongside EVR-architecten to convert a former barracks into the Usquare Feder university district, the materials for which were sourced in part by the dismantling of several neighbouring buildings.

With numerous other residential and office projects in the works – including a new bioregional materials hub and workspace in the centre of Brussels, Stadsatelierdeville, that will be its future office.

If it at times felt like BC Architects & Studies & Materials were up against the world, it is projects like La Magasin Électrique, which was a finalist for the 2026 Mies van Der Rohe Award, that reveal a growing international network who share their outlook, one that De Cooman is quick to credit with a lot of their own success.

“I think the dial is shifting, but I don’t think it is us who did it,” said De Cooman.

“There are all kinds of practises, organisations, material developers, and so on, who see a different construction sector – it’s a wave, a societal shift.”

“We’re very happy about it, but it’s broader than our practice. The construction sector is very conservative and we’re not there yet at all.”

Degreef adds that external social and economic pressures have also had a hand in forcing change to some degree.

“After Covid and the impacts on material prices, the gap between contemporary materials and the materials we want to promote is not so big anymore.”

Asked if there is a particular type of building that represents a dream project, however, they remain resolutely focused on processes and systems.

“I think, for us, it’s not in the buildings itself. It’s not what we build, but how we build and how everybody needs to build.”

To celebrate Dezeen’s 20th birthday, we asked 20 of the most influential architects and designers of the last 20 years to identify someone they think will have a major impact in the next 20 years. Over the next four weeks, we’ll reveal their picks in a series of profile interviews. The series is presented in partnership with Kohler.

#8910. "Europe's largest museum development" opens in 1930s Citroën garage in Brussels

Photography by Koen Van Damme unless otherwise stated. Video by Eyes–Screen.

Brussels‘ former Citroën Garage has been transformed into Kanal, a 40,000-square-metre museum for modern art and architecture with an exhibition programme developed with the Parisian art institution Centre Pompidou.

The transformation was designed by Atelier Kanal, a consortium made up of architecture studio EM2N, NoAarchitecten and Sergison Bates Architects, with a team of construction workers, who restored the 1930s industrial building and added three new volumes within its structure.

Claiming to be “Europe’s largest museum development”, Kanal – sometimes referred to as Kanal-Centre Pompidou – hopes to provide space for people to gather to enjoy visual art, performance, dance, music, film and architecture.

Opening to the public on 28 November, the canal-side building was originally built in 1934 as a garage and showroom for the car company Citroën.

Atelier Kanal aimed to keep the industrial character of the building by implementing a “light touch” approach, restoring most of the building fabric, repairing and upgrading parts where needed, and replacing other parts to improve climatic and acoustic conditions.

The garage’s former showroom, a modernist curved glass building with 20-metre-tall interiors, was converted into a gallery space topped with a publicly accessible rooftop.

“Rather than a spectacular gesture, our proposal offers an attitude of ‘radical optimism’ – open and non-prescriptive, spontaneous and instinctive – much like the spirit of modern progress in which it was created,” said Atelier Kanal.

“The interior is a fine example of elegant industrial engineering, while the glass facades clearly express early modernism,” it continued.

“Our ambition has been to trust the building as we found it, embracing its industrial character and many layers of use.”

Three new buildings were added inside the existing structure, including a four-storey volume with a basement level that contains art galleries, and another volume housing a 378-seat auditorium and the Kanal offices.

The third volume is the new home for Brussels’ museum and archive of architecture, Kanal Architecture, which was formerly known as CIVA.

Rising nine stories on the north-east side of the campus, across from the art galleries, the structure includes exhibition spaces, a library, archives, research centre, bookshop and workshop spaces.

Architecture collective Assemble designed an indoor playground on the first floor of the museum, which features playscapes informed by volcanoes, planets, and piles of coal that were once transported on the canal.

Elsewhere in the building are a library, bookshop, rooftop bar, restaurants and an in-house bakery.

Kanal’s year-round programme of exhibitions was developed in collaboration with the Centre Pompidou art museum in Paris.

“Kanal invites citizens, organisations, collectives and communities to appropriate and inhabit large parts of the building, for production, performances, events, informal gatherings or simply to spend time,” said Atelier Kanal.

“The museum extends beyond curated art, becoming part of the city and its fabric,” it continued. “In this sense, Kanal departs from the traditional museum and instead offers a place for civic gathering, responding to the growing absence of shared public spaces in our cities today.”

Other museums that have recently opened in historic buildings include the London Museum, located in a transformed Victorian market building, and a bank in Santander that was transformed into the Faro Santander museum.

Photography by Koen Van Damme unless otherwise stated. Video by Eyes–Screen.

#8908. How to Use Jojoba Oil for Hair: Expert Tips for Stunning Results

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Jojoba oil is a must-have for moisturizing shampoos and skincare products.

The slippery oil is squeezed out of jojoba plant seeds. These plants are shrubs that pop up around the desert-y spots ofArizona, southern California, and Mexico.

Though it’s been used as a natural remedy for centuries, jojoba oil is having a major hair moment right now.

Keep reading to learn how to use it for strong, shiny hair and a healthy scalp.

“Jojoba oil is incredibly nourishing,” says Mayara Macedo, a hairstylist and scalp specialist in NYC. “It’s a natural oil that closely resembles the sebum our skin and scalp produce,” Macedo explains.

Because of this, Macedo says it’s super compatible with our bodies and works great as a balancing treatment — whether you have an oily or dry scalp.

While its proven benefits mainly revolve around its help with scalp health, jojoba oil can also strengthen and moisturize hair. However, it’s not the go-to pick for improving hair loss (that’s usually minoxidil).

If you’re dealing with dryness, jojoba oil is fantastic for adding moisture to your scalp,” Macedo says.

“Its natural hydrating properties help restore balance, leaving everything healthier and more manageable.”

“Jojoba oil has been known for its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties in addition to its conditioning and emollient properties,” says Kseniya Kobets, MD, board-certified dermatologist and Director of Cosmetics Dermatology at Montefiore Einstein Advanced Care.

These properties help out with dry, irritating dandruff.

This also explains jojoba oil‘s Mexican Indian history as a treatment for sores, which eventually caused researchers to flag its potential for improving skin conditions like acne and psoriasis (but please see a dermatologist for proven treatment options).

Though many say that jojoba oil grows hair, this claim is probably tossed around because it helps moisturize hair follicles — which can keep dryness at bay.

A dry environment can be a breeding ground for breakage, hair loss, and dandruff.

Also, your split ends say hello — jojoba oil can help by restoring hair health overall.

“If your scalp gets oily quickly after washing,” Macedo says, “It could be because your scalp is overcompensating, thinking it doesn’t have enough moisture and needs to produce more oil.”

She says adding jojoba oil helps signal to your scalp that it has enough, which can slow down excess oil production.

Although you can apply jojoba oil to the length and tips of your hair, Macedo says she prefers to use it only for the scalp, saying that other oils, like argan oil, will work better for the length.

Here;s how Macedo recommends using jojoba oil:

You can also buy shampoos or conditions that already have it!

Macedo says you can apply jojoba oil to wet or dry hair, depending on your goal.

“If you want to lock in moisture and add shine, you can try applying it to damp hair.” However, she doesn’t recommend this because it’s easy to accidentally apply too much or distribute it unevenly on wet hair, which she says can leave your hair feeling heavy and greasy.

“Applying it to dry hair reduces frizz and adds a light shine to styled hair,” she suggests.

Kobets recommends using oils overnight for extended exposure. However, she points out this can get messy (RIP pillowcases), so you can always apply them for a few hours and wash them off before bed.

Macedo also suggests being mindful of the amount you use — too much can make your hair look greasy, especially true for fine hair. “For a lightweight finish, start with a small amount and focus on the ends of your hair. But again, I’d recommend jojoba oil for the scalp and argan oil for the hair,” Macedo adds.

“If you’re using jojoba oil as a pre-wash treatment to balance scalp oil or as a deep conditioner, apply it before washing,” Macedo explains. “If you’re using it as a leave-in conditioner or frizz-tamer, you can apply it to freshly washed hair — careful not to apply too much.”

Kobets suggests washing the scalp after using oils, noting that her patients don’t always prefer to use them because they can reduce hair volume for some.

Kobets says that someone with a dehydrated scalp and coarse hair may want to leave the oil in to hydrate the scalp better. “People with fine or oily scalps usually want to wash the oils out,” she adds.

Jojoba oil is a natural moisturizing ingredient known for improving scalp health. It can also add shine and help strengthen your locks.

It’s not the move for improving hair loss, however.

Do a patch test to make sure you aren’t allergic first! Then you’re good to glow.

Last medically reviewed on August 31, 2024

#8907. Base Design gives Visa a brand refresh "for the next generation"

Design agency Base Design has created a more compact version of credit card company Visa’s logo and worked with Displaay Type Foundry on a new typeface, as part of a refresh of the brand’s visual identity.

While the 2021 Visa wordmark remains unchanged, the refresh included creating a shortened symbol for the brand, rolling out the new Visa Sans typeface, and creating a blocky hero graphic to market towards a younger generation.

“When you’re working with a brand as iconic as Visa, the challenge isn’t recognition – it’s relevance,” said Base Design executive creative director Min Lew.

“Our ambition was to build on Visa’s extraordinary equity while giving it a renewed sense of energy and expression, one that feels as relevant to the next generation as it does to the generations who have grown up with it.”

As part of this strategy, the studio cut the V out of the existing wordmark to function as its own symbol. It will be used on credit cards and appear across digital platforms.

The studio also wrapped it in colourful bar, which will also be used on graphic elements such as posters, and to frame text.

“More than a framing device, the hero graphic device brings movement, direction, and possibility to the identity,” said Lew.

“This simple gesture becomes the foundation for a visual language that can be energetic at a global sporting event, confident and bold in a B2B environment, or vibrant and elevated for affluent audiences.”

For Visa Sans, Base Design and Displaay Type Foundry also based the design on the existing logo.

The typeface features rounded edges akin to the rounded corner of the Visa V, and overall, extends “the logo’s character across the wider identity”.

Ultimately, the new identity was created to be used across different smaller, touchpoints according to the team, such as at tap-to-pay stations, at checkout, or online, as the brand appears “for only a moment” in day to day life.

“We have deep trust and recognition as a brand,” said Visa chief marketing officer Frank Cooper III. “This refresh gives us an opportunity to build on that.”

A more subtle approach to logo and branding updates has been popular in recent years, such as at Walmart and Google.

In contrast, the US restaurant chain Cracker Barrel recently took a hard swing at a logo update, which was immediately met with online backlash and promptly scrapped in favour of the original design.

#8904. 6 Signs Your Skin Needs Medical Attention, Stat

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Your skin is your most visible organ, so it’s easy to notice when something seems off. It’s normal to experience some skin issues from time to time, like itchiness, breakouts, or ingrown hairs. But when these skin symptoms stick around, it could be a sign that something more serious is going on.

Many of these skin issues get better with the right at-home remedies or changes in your skin care routine. For example, if dryness pops up when Old Man Winter comes along, slathering on a more intense moisturizer may help.

But if skin symptoms don’t go away with a little self-care — or they return frequently — a chronic skin condition might be the culprit. However, just because you have a lasting symptom or two doesn’t necessarily mean you have a chronic health issue.

Here are the symptoms you should watch for and what they might mean. And if they don’t improve, consider checking in with a dermatologist for a proper diagnosis and a plan of action.

If you wish you had cat claws to satisfy your skin itch, you could be dealing with eczema. Eczema is an umbrella term for several conditions that impact the skin, with atopic dermatitis being the most common.

With most forms of eczema, your skin may show signs of inflammation, such as:

These symptoms may flare up occasionally and then go into periods of remission, where your skin isn’t as irritated.

Allergies can also lead to itchiness. For example, if you’re allergic to a skin care ingredient, a fabric type, a pet, or another allergen, your skin might react as a way to tell you to avoid this trigger.

Ongoing or regular periods of itchiness are a reason to see a dermatologist.

A rash can affect the skin in various ways, including:

A one-off or temporary rash might result from friction or chafing from a new outfit item. It could also be a heat rash when sweat gets trapped in skinfolds or bodily creases.

A persistent rash could be a sign of eczema or allergies. However, different types of rashes can be a sign of other things. For example, a butterfly-shaped (malar) rash across the face is a common sign of an autoimmune disease known as lupus.

If you frequently experience skin rashes, talk with a dermatologist to help you get to the bottom of the issue.

Dry skin can be just that — dry skin. Common causes include:

But if your skin is so dry it makes you want to bathe in a vat of thick moisturizer, it could be a sign of psoriasis.

Psoriasis is an inflammatory skin condition potentially caused by an overactive immune system. It can lead to dry, cracked, or scaling skin. In fact, psoriasis often involves a buildup of scales or plaques on areas like the elbows or knees — though they can occur anywhere.

Psoriasis and eczema are different conditions, but they have overlapping symptoms that mimic each other. So if you experience these symptoms, it’s important to see a dermatologist to identify and treat the underlying cause.

Changes in skin color — including red, brown, gray, or purple patches of skin — can be a sign of various skin issues, including eczema, psoriasis, or allergies. But it can also be a sign of rosacea.

Rosacea typically involves persistent redness that looks like a sunburn or blushing. It may also lead to skin thickening.

The good news? Rosacea is highly treatable. So working with a dermatologist can help you address it.

No one is immune from developing the occasional pimple or ingrown hair. But sometimes, skin bumps can be a sign that something else is going on.

Acne is one of the most common skin conditions that could bring skin bumps like pimples.

Hidradenitis suppurativa (HS) is another condition that causes painful, boil-like lumps to form underneath the skin. These bumps can turn into pus-filled pockets that may connect via tunnels. HS typically shows up in areas of high friction or where skin meets skin, such as the armpits or groin.

Other types of skin bumps may include ingrown hairs, which can get infected and turn into folliculitis.

Talk with a dermatologist to help you address any bothersome skin bumps you may experience.

Common moles are growths that develop when pigment cells (melanocytes) grow in clusters. The average adult has between 10 to 40 common moles.

An irregular mole, also known as a dysplastic nevus, is a type of mole that looks different from your common moles. If you have a dysplastic nevus (or several), schedule regular skin checks with a dermatologist to look for anything suspicious. Be sure to mention any changes in:

These types of changes could be a sign of a form of skin cancer such as melanoma, which occurs in melanocytes. Melanoma can develop anywhere, including on normal-looking skin, a common mole, or a dysplastic nevus.

Skin symptoms — like rashes, bumps, discoloration, dryness, or itchiness — may come and go. But if symptoms stick around or return frequently, consider seeing a dermatologist for an evaluation. Your skin may be telling you that there’s an underlying issue that needs to be addressed.

A dermatologist can provide a proper diagnosis and treatment plan to help reduce, or, in some cases, resolve your skin symptoms. If you don’t currently have a dermatologist, your primary care physician or nurse practitioner can refer you to one.

Last medically reviewed on February 12, 2025

#8903. Caring for Life Across Scales: The XIV Ibero-American Biennial in Brasília

Read the original version in Portuguese here.

Caring for life: this was the motto of the XIV edition of the Ibero-American Architecture Biennial (BIAU) held in Brasília from November 3 to 6, 2026. The choice of care as a theme is significant, as is its presentation as an infinitive verb—lacking tense or mood—serving as an urgent call to action. Structured around the thematic axes of water, vegetation, housing, communities, and new territories, the discussions made it clear that these elements are not mere resources or means for caring for life. Rather, they must be understood as subjects of care, demanding an attentive and respectful consideration of their natural and social cycles within architectural practice.

The event addressed shared urgencies on both sides of the Atlantic: the crisis of housing access compounded by the climate emergency. In this context, the ultimate goal of the Biennial was to build a lasting collaborative network extending far beyond the four-day event, combating urban exclusion and demonstrating that architectural practice cannot be decoupled from politics.
